item.title: [商汤 日日新] SenseNova-Loop-9B
item.content:encoded:
You need to agree to share your Hugging Face information to access this model

This repository is publicly accessible, but you have to accept the conditions to access its files and content.

Log in or Sign Up to review the conditions and access this model content.

SenseNova-Loop-9B

English | 简体中文

🌐 Architecture

📣 News

🔥 2026-11-18: Added download links for the AWQ and GGUF weights.

🔥 2026-11-17: We release SenseNova-Loop-9B, with model weights and code available to the community.

🔥 2026-10-31: We release SenseNova-Loop-9B-Preview, with model weights and code available to the community.

🚀 SenseNova-Loop-9B: Deeper Computation with Fewer Parameters

We officially release SenseNova-Loop-9B. Building on the Preview's exploration of parameter efficiency, the model reuses layer weights through a looped architecture and combines them with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC) to expand computational depth within a compact parameter budget. It is designed for complex reasoning, coding, tool use, and multimodal tasks.

Since the Preview release, we have received community interest and feedback on model use, inference deployment, and ecosystem integration. The official release retains the looped architecture and two-stream mHC, further improving performance on agentic, coding, and data analysis tasks while continuing to explore the capabilities of looped computation.

SenseNova-Loop-9B has approximately 9B parameters. By repeatedly executing shared middle layers, it extends 32 physical decoder layers into 56 layer executions. The model accepts text and images and generates text, supporting long-context understanding and multi-step tasks. In agentic and data analysis evaluations, the model is competitive with Qwen3.8-27B: it scores 41.36 versus 44.60 on NL2Repo and 65.31 versus 65.01 on AIDABench.

Model Highlights

  • Shared looped block: 24 decoder layers are executed twice in sequence, producing 56 layer computations from 32 distinct layers per forward pass.
  • Two-stream mHC: learned mappings route and combine information between two residual streams within the looped block.
  • Hybrid attention: the decoder interleaves linear and full attention in a repeating four-layer pattern.
  • Long-context multimodal training: the training recipe includes text, images, code, and tool-use trajectories, with the context length extended to 512K tokens.
  • Low-memory deployment: With 4-bit weights and an 8-bit KV cache, multimodal inference at a 256K context length requires approximately 15 GiB of GPU memory.
  • Official quantized release: An official AWQ 4-bit version is available on launch day for easier deployment.

🎬 Showcase

3D

SVG + Web

Poster

Web

Design

📊 Model Performance: From Preview to Release

We evaluate SenseNova-Loop-9B on agentic, coding, and data analysis tasks, comparing the release with the Preview and other models.

The release outperforms the Preview on all seven benchmarks shown. AutomationBench rises from 14.33 to 36.67, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 40.45 to 59.55, and GAIA from 37.86 to 69.90.

Compared with Qwen3.8-27B, the release matches its 36.67 on AutomationBench and scores 65.31 versus 65.01 on AIDABench. On NL2Repo, it scores 41.36 versus 44.60. Its BIRD score of 72.34 is 0.96 percentage points above the Preview's 71.38.

🧠 Model Architecture

SenseNova-Loop-9B is built on a 32-layer multimodal decoder combining shared-weight looped computation, hybrid attention, and two-stream manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC). It extends computation depth by reusing middle-layer parameters, accepts text and images, generates text, and supports a context length of up to 512K tokens.

Model Specifications

PropertySenseNova-Loop-9B
ArchitectureAutoregressive multimodal decoder; looped block with two-stream mHC
Parameter scaleApproximately 9B total parameters; approximately 14.6B inference-equivalent parameters
Input / outputText and images / text
Distinct decoder layers32
Looped layer range / passes[4, 28) / 2, with shared weights
Decoder layer executions56 per forward pass
mHC residual streams2
Context length512K tokens
Weight precisionBF16 backbone; FP32 mHC routing parameters

Looped Decoder

Inputs first pass through layers 0–3, then through the same block of layers 4–27 twice, and finally through layers 28–31 and the output head. If B denotes the looped block and h its input, the looped computation can be written as B(B(h)).

During inference, each forward pass performs 56 decoder-layer computations while storing only 32 sets of decoder-layer weights. The looped block shares the same weights across both passes, with the output of the first pass serving as input to the second.

Hybrid Attention

The decoder interleaves linear attention and full attention. Each group of four layers contains three linear-attention layers followed by one full-attention layer. The loop boundaries align with complete four-layer groups, so both passes preserve the same attention pattern.

Two-Stream mHC

Within the looped block, mHC uses two residual streams to carry information around decoder-layer computations. Learned mappings determine how each layer reads from the streams, mixes information between them, and writes its output back to the residual state. The stream-mixing map is constrained with Sinkhorn normalization, using 20 iterations in the model configuration.

The two streams can be viewed as two sets of hidden states carried in parallel. A looped layer reads from the streams, applies attention or feed-forward computation, and writes its output back. Repeated row and column normalization constrains how information is mixed between the streams. These 20 normalization iterations are internal to mHC and are separate from the two passes through the looped block.

The loop range, number of passes, and mHC routing parameters together define the checkpoint's execution configuration. A compatible inference implementation must load these parameters and preserve the same computation order.

ConfigurationValue
Distinct decoder layers / executions32 / 56
Looped layer range / passes[4, 28) / 2
Hidden dimension4,096
Feed-forward dimension12,288
Vocabulary size248,320
Full-attention heads / KV heads16 / 4
mHC residual streams / Sinkhorn iterations2 / 20

🔬 Loop Scaling: Exploring the Benefits of Looped Computation

Looped Transformers show promising performance scaling, offering another way to expand model capability through repeated computation. Using the original 9B model with a standard single forward pass (Loop 1) as the baseline, we vary the number of loops while holding the training data and other settings constant. Overall performance improves across the four tasks, with the best results at three or four loops. AIDABench-QA and Workbuddy-office peak at three loops, improving by 6.42% and 16.93% relative to the baseline; LiveCodeBench V6 and AIDABench data visualization peak at four loops, improving by 8.10% and 8.55%.

To balance inference efficiency, both the Preview and the release use two loops by default. Deeper loops nevertheless provide further gains: moving from two to four loops improves LiveCodeBench V6 by 1.04 percentage points and AIDABench data visualization by 1.35 percentage points. These experiments cover one to four loops, leaving the potential of deeper looping open for further study.

Different tasks respond differently to loop depth. We will continue exploring deeper computation and Dynamic Loop architectures that adapt the number of loops to each input, allocating computation according to task complexity.

💾 Low-Memory Deployment

The shared looped architecture uses approximately 9B distinct parameters. With 4-bit weight quantization, the model weights occupy approximately 4.9 GB. Using an 8-bit or 4-bit KV cache can further reduce memory requirements for long-context inference. The estimated minimum GPU memory requirements for deployment are:

Context length8-bit KV cache4-bit KV cache
64K~10 GiB~9 GiB
128K~12 GiB~10 GiB
256K~15 GiB~12 GiB

Get Started

Model Weights

WeightsDownloadFiles
BF16Hugging Face · ModelScopeRelease weights in Safetensors format
AWQHugging Face4-bit AWQ weights and matching MTP draft
GGUFHugging FaceBF16, Q8_0, Q5_K_M, and Q4_K_M

Text Generation with Transformers

Use Transformers to load the model from a Hugging Face repository or a local model directory. The examples below cover single-GPU text generation and serving with inference engines.

Requirements

The checked Preview environment uses Transformers 5.18.0, PyTorch 2.11.0, and CUDA 13.0. The model directory must include the configuration, tokenizer, chat template, custom model code, and all weight shards.

First install a CUDA-compatible build of PyTorch, then install the remaining dependencies:

python -m pip install "transformers==5.18.0" accelerate safetensors

Set model_id to the release model directory or repository ID, then run:

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "/path/to/SenseNova-Loop-9B"
device = "cuda:0"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map={"": device},
).eval()

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 13 times 7?"}]
prompt = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tokenize=False,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    enable_thinking=True,
)
inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
with torch.inference_mode():
    outputs = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=512,
        do_sample=False,
        use_cache=True,
    )
response = tokenizer.decode(
    outputs[0, inputs.input_ids.shape[1]:],
    skip_special_tokens=True,
)
print(response)

The example enables thinking mode, uses greedy decoding, and generates up to 512 new tokens. Set enable_thinking to False to disable thinking, or change device to select a GPU. trust_remote_code=True loads the custom SenseNova Loop model implementation.

Deployment

The following commands are adapted from the Preview deployment examples. Replace the model path with the release checkpoint directory; the release engine versions and configurations will be updated with the model.

LightLLM

Four-GPU deployment example:

docker pull ghcr.io/modeltc/lightllm:main

docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host -p 8000:8000 \
  -v /path/to/SenseNova-Loop-9B:/model \
  -e LOADWORKER=4 -e LIGHTLLM_TRITON_AUTOTUNE_LEVEL=1 \
  ghcr.io/modeltc/lightllm:main \
  python -m lightllm.server.api_server \
    --model_dir /model --model_name SenseNova-Loop-9B \
    --tp 4 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

Once the service is running, send an OpenAI-compatible request:

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model": "SenseNova-Loop-9B", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 128}'

SGLang

Use the version from SGLang PR #47281, which includes the SenseNova Loop implementation, and replace the model path:

git clone https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang.git
cd sglang
git fetch origin pull/47281/head
git checkout -b sensenova-loop FETCH_HEAD
python -m pip install -e ./python

sglang serve --model-path /path/to/SenseNova-Loop-9B

vLLM

For text generation, build vLLM from the SenseNova Loop branch in vLLM PR #64832, which supports the published AWQ checkpoint.

git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git
cd vllm
git fetch origin pull/64832/head
git checkout -b sensenova-loop FETCH_HEAD
python -m pip install -e .

To serve the BF16 checkpoint:

vllm serve sensenova/SenseNova-Loop-9B \
  --served-model-name sensenova_loop \
  --tensor-parallel-size 4 \
  --dtype bfloat16

To serve the 4-bit AWQ checkpoint on a single GPU:

vllm serve sensenova/SenseNova-Loop-9B-AWQ \
  --served-model-name sensenova_loop \
  --dtype bfloat16

vLLM detects AWQ from the checkpoint configuration.

Inference Acceleration

SenseNova-Loop supports MTP speculative decoding. DSpark and DFlash2 draft model training instructions are available in SenseSpec; available release draft weights and launch settings will be updated with the model.

🏋️ Training

For model fine-tuning, refer to the SenseNova-Loop examples in OpenSenseNova/torchtitan.

Training scripts for DSpark and DFlash2 speculative decoding draft models are available in OpenSenseNova/SenseSpec.

⚠️ Known Limitations

Given its size and development time, SenseNova-Loop-9B has room for improvement in the following areas:

  • Complex instruction following: The model may misunderstand or miss requirements when given many complex tool definitions or multiple constraints.
  • Coding and general agent tasks: Performance can be inconsistent on coding and general agent tasks. The model can correct some errors through additional steps, but its ability to handle complex, long-horizon tasks still needs improvement.
  • Complex web generation: Websites with complex 3D scenes and rich animations may not be completed in a single turn. Some examples require user feedback and two to three rounds of refinement.

We will continue to improve the model and plan to apply the Loop architecture to larger models in the future. We welcome community feedback and reports of issues.

📄 License and Citation

The model project is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Gemini 3.7 Flash: What's New, Benchmarks & API Guide
item.content:encoded:
Gemini 3.7 Flash: What's New, Benchmarks & API Guide

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Gemini 3.7 Flash is Google’s Flash-tier reasoning model. It takes text, images, video, audio and PDF files as input, returns text, and has a 1,000,000-token context window on DeepInfra. Google DeepMind released it on August 13, 2026, about three weeks after Gemini 3.6 Flash, and positioned it as its workhorse model for coding and agents.

It is a closed model. DeepInfra serves it as a partner model through Google’s API, so you call it with the same OpenAI-compatible endpoint, API key and bill you already use for open models such as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3 and MiMo-V2.6-Flash. DeepInfra charges $0.75 per 1M input tokens and $3.75 per 1M output tokens, the same as Google’s current discounted standard price.

Google has since shipped newer Flash releases. Artificial Analysis now marks Gemini 3.7 Flash as deprecated and suggests Gemini 3.8 Flash instead. If you already run 3.7 Flash, or want it next to open models under one API, this guide covers what changed, how it benchmarks, what it costs and how to call it.

Model string: google/gemini-3.7-flash

What changed from Gemini 3.6 Flash

Gemini 3.7 Flash keeps 3.6 Flash’s 1M-token context and input types. The changes are in agentic work, speed per task and price.

Agentic coding (Google-reported). Google’s launch figures, as summarised by MindStudio, show the largest gains on long-horizon software engineering: DeepSWE rises from 49% to 65.3%, and FrontierCode from 34.4% to 43.6%. Web Dev Arena moves from about 1538 to about 1588 Elo.

Agents and knowledge work (independent). Artificial Analysis attributes most of the improvement to agentic evaluations: Terminal-Bench v2.1 up 8 points, Tau3 Banking up 3 points, GDPval-AA v2 up 103 Elo to 1525, and its AA-Briefcase knowledge-work evaluation up 169 Elo to 1132.

Speed per task. Artificial Analysis measured about 340 output tokens per second at launch and an average of 1.7 minutes per Intelligence Index task at high reasoning. That put 3.7 Flash on its Intelligence vs. Time per Task Pareto frontier.

Cost per task. At Google’s discounted price, Artificial Analysis put Gemini 3.7 Flash (high) at $0.40 per Intelligence Index task, 30% less than Gemini 3.6 Flash. At medium reasoning, the figure fell to $0.26.

Reasoning levels. Google exposes three reasoning levels (high, medium, low), and Artificial Analysis benchmarked all three. The DeepInfra parameter for this is covered under Parameters.

Benchmarks

Google-reported: Gemini 3.7 Flash vs 3.6 Flash

These are vendor-reported figures from Google’s launch, via MindStudio’s write-up.

BenchmarkGemini 3.6 FlashGemini 3.7 Flash
DeepSWE (long-horizon software engineering)49%65.3%
FrontierCode34.4%43.6%
Web Dev Arena (Elo)~1538~1588
AutomationBench~17%~30%

AutomationBench shows the biggest relative jump, though the model still fails most tasks on Google’s version of the test. DeepSWE is the strongest absolute result.

Artificial Analysis at launch (August 13, 2026)

Artificial Analysis benchmarked the model ahead of release. These scores come from the version of the Intelligence Index in use in August 2026. They aren’t comparable with scores on the current index (v5.0.1), where Artificial Analysis no longer reports a score for this model.

Metric (AA, August 2026)Gemini 3.7 Flash
Intelligence Index, high reasoning56 (+4 vs 3.6 Flash)
Intelligence Index, medium / low reasoning53 / 51
Output speed~340 tokens/s
Average time per Index task (high)1.7 min
Cost per Index task (high / medium, discounted price)$0.40 / $0.26
AutomationBench-AA62.7% (highest at launch)
AA-AnalystAgent, pass^560% (highest at launch)
AA-Briefcase1132 Elo
GDPval-AA v21525 Elo

Where it led and where it didn’t. At launch, Gemini 3.7 Flash led AA’s AutomationBench-AA, ahead of Kimi K3 (53%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (51.2%), and AA-AnalystAgent, ahead of Claude Opus 5 (54%) and Fable 5 (49%). On the overall Index it sat just behind GPT-5.6 Terra and Muse Spark 1.2 (both 57). On GDPval-AA v2 its 1525 was level with GLM-5.2 (1506) and below DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (1558).

AutomationBench-AA (62.7%) is Artificial Analysis’s own version of the benchmark, so it doesn’t line up with Google’s AutomationBench figure above.

Where it stands now

Artificial Analysis now lists Gemini 3.7 Flash as deprecated: it still benchmarks the model, but every 18 hours instead of every 6, and points to Gemini 3.8 Flash. Its current leaderboard is led by closed frontier models such as Claude Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5. Gemini 3.7 Flash’s strengths are throughput and price per task on agentic and document work, not the top of that table.

Modalities and context

SpecGemini 3.7 Flash on DeepInfra
InputText, images, video, audio, PDF
OutputText
Context window1,000,000 tokens
ReasoningYes (reasoning model)
FeaturesOpenAI-compatible API, JSON mode, structured output, function calling, OCR
WeightsProprietary (no open weights)

PDF and OCR support make it a practical pick for document-heavy agent steps: reading contracts, invoices or slide decks and returning structured JSON. That matches its lead on AA-AnalystAgent, which tests questions about spreadsheets and documents.

Pricing

Pricing as of 2026-11-17. The model page always shows current rates.

TierInput / 1MOutput / 1MCached input / 1M
Standard$0.75$3.75Not listed
  • Same price as Google’s discounted rate. DeepInfra’s $0.75 / $3.75 matches the discounted standard price Google offers on its own API. Google’s undiscounted standard price is $1.50 / $7.50 (Artificial Analysis).
  • Fewer tiers than Google’s API. Google also offers a 90% discount on cached input, plus Flex and Batch tiers at half the standard price, and DeepInfra lists none of these for this model. For high-volume batch work with heavily repeated prompts, Google’s own API is cheaper.
  • No Flex or Priority on DeepInfra. DeepInfra’s Flex (0.8×) and Priority (1.5×) tiers apply only to models that carry those tags, and this one doesn’t.

What DeepInfra offers for this model is consolidation, not a lower price. One API key, one invoice and one OpenAI-compatible client for Gemini and for open models. You don’t need a Google Cloud project, a second SDK or a second billing relationship.

Costing an agent step

A document-extraction step that sends 20,000 input tokens and returns 2,000 output tokens costs:

  • Input: 20,000 × $0.75 / 1M = $0.015
  • Output: 2,000 × $3.75 / 1M = $0.0075
  • Total: $0.0225 per call, or $22.50 per 1,000 calls

Reasoning tokens are billed as output, so higher reasoning effort raises the output side of that sum.

Getting started

Gemini 3.7 Flash uses DeepInfra’s OpenAI-compatible API:

  • Base URL: https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai
  • Endpoint: POST /chat/completions
  • Auth header: Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY (create a key in the dashboard)

The model requires a signed-in account with an API key; anonymous free calls aren’t available.

Parameters

The full schema is on the model’s API page.

ParameterTypeDefaultNotes
modelstring—google/gemini-3.7-flash
messagesarray—Chat history; supports multimodal content
reasoning_effortstring—DeepInfra accepts none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Lower values cut reasoning tokens and latency
max_tokensinteger—DeepInfra doesn’t publish a maximum output for this model, so set this explicitly for long outputs
temperaturefloat0.7Sampling temperature
top_pfloat0.9Nucleus sampling
streambooleanfalseServer-sent events
stoparray—Up to 16 stop strings
ninteger1Up to 4 completions
presence_penalty / frequency_penaltyfloat0−2 to 2
response_formatobject{"type": "text"}json_object or json_schema for structured output
tools / tool_choicearray / string—Function calling: none, auto or required
seedintegerrandomDeterminism not guaranteed

reasoning_effort is part of the OpenAI SDK’s standard arguments, so you can pass it directly. Test the levels on your own prompts and compare quality, latency and output-token counts before choosing one for production.

Python

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="google/gemini-3.7-flash",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Extract fields as JSON."},
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Invoice 4417 from Acme GmbH, dated 2026-10-02, total EUR 1,240.00. "
                       "Return invoice_number, vendor, date and total.",
        },
    ],
    reasoning_effort="low",
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    max_tokens=2048,
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(response.usage)copy

Switching between Gemini 3.7 Flash and an open model is a one-line change to model. This is useful for A/B tests on cost and quality, and for two-tier agents that send mechanical steps to a cheaper model and keep a stronger one for the hard steps.

Output limits

The model page sets 1,000,000 tokens as the maximum context, counting input and output together. DeepInfra doesn’t state a separate maximum output for this model, so pass max_tokens whenever you expect long answers, and check finish_reason for "length" to catch truncated responses.

Conclusion

Gemini 3.7 Flash brought real gains over 3.6 Flash on agentic coding and document work, and was fast per task at launch. Artificial Analysis now points users to newer Gemini releases, so it’s the right choice mainly when you’ve already validated it, or need its PDF, audio and video input next to open models under one API.

On DeepInfra it costs the same per token as Google’s discounted rate, and it shares a key, an invoice and a client with the rest of your stack. If cached-input discounts or batch pricing drive your bill, compare Google’s own API before committing.

Next steps

  • Plan for model retirement. Keep the model ID in config and set up an eval to compare a replacement; see how to build an LLM app that survives model retirement.
  • Pair it with an open model. Route bulk agent steps to an open model and keep Gemini for multimodal or document steps. Our guide to the best open-source models for coding compares the candidates.
  • Try it. Open the Gemini 3.7 Flash model page, create an API key, and run the example above.

Related articles

Best API Providers for GLM-5.1 in 2026<p>Updated November 2026. GLM-5.1 has been retired on DeepInfra. Its successor, GLM-5.3, is available now; see the best GLM-5.3 API providers for current options. The comparison below is kept for reference. GLM-5.1 is available across a growing number of API providers, and the choice between them materially affects cost, latency, and what features you can […]</p>

Best Open Source LLM API Providers in 2026<p>Updated November 2026. Picking an inference vendor used to be a short conversation. You wanted Llama behind an HTTP endpoint, three companies served it, and their prices sat close enough that the decision came down to whoever had capacity. The market has since split into a dozen serious operators running truly different businesses. The best […]</p>

Best Jev Alternatives: Hosted APIs and Open Models (2026)<p>Jev had competitors before it was even a month old. TypeSafe launched it on September 15, and by the first week of October OpenAI had announced a Decisions API, Cloudflare and AWS had shipped open-weight decision models, and GitHub had a shelf of open-source Jev alternatives: Laya, OpenJev, Kev, AnyJev. We ran Jev and the […]</p>

item.description: Full title: DeepInfra Partners with Opper AI: 100+ Models on the Opper Gateway
item.content:encoded:
DeepInfra Partners with Opper AI: 100+ Models on the Opper Gateway

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Palo Alto, California, November 2026. DeepInfra and Opper AI are partnering to make DeepInfra’s open-model inference available through Opper’s EU-hosted AI gateway. Developers can now call more than 100 DeepInfra-hosted models through the Opper API, from Kimi K3, GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash to MiniMax M3, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and FLUX.2 Pro, and apply Opper’s spend, retention and routing Rules to every call.

What this means for developers

If you already run on DeepInfra, nothing changes on your existing integration. The partnership adds a second route to the same models: through Opper, alongside the other providers you may already use there.

One model string per tier. Every DeepInfra chat model on Opper has a standard tier, and many also come as flex and priority:

Opper model stringWhat it’s for
deepinfra/…Standard tier, for everyday calls
deepinfra:flex/…About a fifth cheaper, for evaluations and background work
deepinfra:priority/…Interactive traffic that must answer first

Large jobs can go through Opper’s Batch API at the flex price. Per-tier prices for each model, plus DeepInfra’s image, speech, video and embedding models, are listed on Opper’s DeepInfra provider page.

The catalog. Through Opper you can reach the open models agents run today: DeepSeek V4 and V4.1, Moonshot’s Kimi K3, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, the Qwen3.5 to Qwen3.8 lineup, Google’s Gemma 4, Meta’s Llama and Thinking Machines’ Inkling. The same route covers image models from Black Forest Labs, ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 for video, Qwen3 TTS for speech and embeddings for search, as well as NVIDIA’s Nemotron family, from Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to Nemotron 3 Ultra.

Price. According to Opper, DeepInfra is currently the cheapest route on the Opper gateway, in any region, for MiniMax M3, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, DeepSeek V3.2 and Qwen3 235B Instruct 2507.

Data handling. Every DeepInfra route on Opper runs in the United States. On standard, flex and priority calls, prompts and completions are not logged or used for training, and a DPA is available. Batch jobs hold requests until they run, as any batch API must. DeepInfra owns and operates its GPU infrastructure and is SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certified. Opper’s provider page lists residency and retention for each route.

A first call

Opper is OpenAI-compatible, so switching to a DeepInfra model is a change of base URL and model string:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["OPPER_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.opper.ai/v3/compat",
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepinfra/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3",  # or "deepinfra:flex/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3" for background work
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)copy

Why Opper: Rules for every call

Opper describes itself as the European AI gateway for agents. Based in Stockholm, it gives developers more than 700 models through one EU-hosted, GDPR-compliant API. Routing is only part of what it does. Every call through Opper can run under your Rules: spend limits, data retention, model access, content checks and routing order, set once for the organization or per project.

For DeepInfra users, that means you can:

  • pin DeepInfra’s flex tier for evaluation runs,
  • set DeepInfra as a fallback behind another provider, or the other way round,
  • cap spend and limit which models a project can call, without changing application code.

Opper or DeepInfra’s API directly?

Both routes reach the same DeepInfra models. The choice depends on what sits around the call.

Use Opper when you use models from several providers through one key, want spend caps, model allowlists and retention rules managed centrally, or want routing and fallback between DeepInfra and other providers handled by the gateway.

Use DeepInfra’s API directly when your workload runs only on DeepInfra models and you don’t need a gateway in the request path. You get the full DeepInfra model catalog, the pricing listed on each model page, and the Flex service tier for work that can wait.

Quotes

“DeepInfra runs one of the deepest open-model catalogues anywhere, at prices that make it a natural home for high-volume work. With standard, flex, priority and batch on the same models, builders on Opper can match every call to the speed and price it needs.” — Göran Sandahl, Co-founder and CEO, Opper AI

“We built DeepInfra to run open models at production scale on our own GPUs, at a price that works for every token. Opper puts that catalogue in front of a wide community of builders through one API, next to every other model they already use.” — Nikola Borisov, Co-founder and CEO, DeepInfra

Availability

DeepInfra models are live on Opper today. To get started:

  • Read Opper’s announcement: Opper AI partners with DeepInfra to bring 100+ AI models to the gateway
  • See models, tiers and per-route prices on Opper’s DeepInfra provider page
  • Browse the DeepInfra model catalog and pricing

About DeepInfra

DeepInfra is an inference cloud founded in 2022 and based in Palo Alto, California. It owns and operates its GPU infrastructure and serves open models for text, speech, image, video and embeddings through OpenAI-compatible APIs, with zero data retention and SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification. item.title: [DeepInfra] Kimi K3.1 Pro: Model Overview, Benchmarks & API Guide
item.content:encoded:
Kimi K3.1 Pro: Model Overview, Benchmarks & API Guide

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI’s flagship open-weight model, released on October 23, 2026 and built for long-horizon agent work: coding, 3D creation, financial research and document-heavy tasks. It is a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104B parameters active per token, takes text and images as input, returns text, and has a 1,048,576-token context window.

K3.1 Pro is not a new pre-training run. Moonshot post-trained it from Kimi K3 “with substantially larger post-training compute” and large-scale reinforcement learning across hundreds of domains, and swapped K3’s full-attention layers for sparse attention to make long contexts cheaper to serve. It is the first model in the K3.1 series.

On DeepInfra the model runs behind an OpenAI-compatible API with zero data retention, JSON and structured output, function calling and image input. If you need a cheaper model for simpler agent steps, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 is on the same API. The model string is:

moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro

What changed from Kimi K3

Moonshot’s claims below are vendor-reported unless marked otherwise.

Post-training and coding

  • Long-horizon coding: on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, an internal Moonshot benchmark, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2 against K3’s 55.95 (release post).
  • Independent check: on LiveBench 2.0 (November 6, 2026 table), coding rises from 53.1 for Kimi K3 to 67.8, and long-horizon agentic work from 36.0 to 38.7. That is a real coding gain, though K3.1 Pro still sits mid-pack among open-weight models on LiveBench coding.

Factual accuracy

  • On Moonshot’s internal Kimi Hallu Bench Hard, the claim-level hallucination rate falls from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%. Moonshot calls the benchmark a deliberate stress test, so the rate does not describe everyday error rates.

Finance and business work

  • Moonshot’s internal finance benchmarks improve by 7.2 points (financial modeling) and 11.6 points (financial research), and its Business Operation simulation scores about 4.2 times K3’s result. On the public OfficeQA Pro v2, K3.1 Pro scores 64.4, the top score in Moonshot’s table.

Attention and long context

  • K3.1 Pro replaces K3’s full-attention Gated MLA layers with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention (Gated DSA): 24 of its 93 layers now use sparse attention with a top-k of 2,048 indexed tokens, and the other 69 use KDA linear attention. The point is cheaper long-context modeling at the full 1M window.

Cyber capability, deliberately capped

  • For the open-weight release, Moonshot removed cyber-related data from mid-training and RL. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, the unfiltered checkpoint solves 90.5% of tasks at pass@3; the released model solves 81.0%. Moonshot says K3.1 Pro’s offensive cyber capability remains behind frontier proprietary models.

Price on DeepInfra

  • Kimi K3 is still listed at $2.85 input and $14.25 output per 1M tokens. K3.1 Pro’s promotional rate of $1.90 / $9.50 is a third lower on both, and K3.1 Pro adds a Flex tier.

Technical architecture

ComponentKimi K3.1 Pro
ArchitectureMixture-of-Experts
Total / active parameters2.8T / 104B
Layers93 (1 dense)
Attention69 KDA + 24 Gated DSA layers
Experts896 routed, 16 selected per token, 2 shared
Hidden dimension / attention heads7,168 / 96
Vocabulary160K
ActivationSiTU-GLU
Vision encoderMoonViT-V2 (401M parameters)
Released weightsMXFP4 weights / MXFP8 activations (quantization-aware training)
Context window1,048,576 tokens
LicenseKimi K3.1-Pro License (modified MIT)

Source: Hugging Face model card.

The license is MIT-style with two conditions. Companies running a model-as-a-service business with more than $20 million in group revenue over any 12 months need a separate agreement with Moonshot before commercial use. Products with more than 100 million monthly active users or $20 million in monthly revenue must display “Kimi K3.1-Pro” in their interface. Internal use is exempt from both. If your product could cross either threshold, read the license text before you ship.

Benchmarks

Moonshot ran K3.1 Pro at reasoning effort max, temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95, mostly inside the Claude Code or Kimi Code harnesses. Several comparison scores are cited from leaderboards or other labs’ reports, closed models ran with fallback, and rows marked “internal” use Moonshot’s own benchmarks. Treat everything in this table as vendor-reported. The rows below are a selection; the model card has all 47.

BenchmarkKimi K3.1 ProClaude Opus 5.5GPT-6 AstraClaude Fable 5.1DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017GLM-5.3
Terminal-Bench 4.065.766.458.257.942.341.8
SWE Marathon v1.151.746.342.545.640.042.5
DeepSWE v1.175.574.274.167.477.066.9
ProgramBench31.565.050.053.529.119.0
HLE-Full (no tools)51.159.853.657.642.643.0*
HLE-Full w/ tools70.067.757.265.658.862.5
GPQA-Diamond94.293.996.193.792.291.7
BrowseComp92.190.891.5———
Agents’ Last Exam (all)43.242.641.8—37.726.2
AutomationBench-AA73.369.568.559.466.662.2
GDPval-AA v2.1 (Elo)184618661573175417461650
APEX-Agents69.473.564.768.669.856.6
OfficeQA Pro v264.462.254.454.540.431.1
OSWorld V2.179.681.875.880.769.3—
MMMU-Pro w/ python90.089.887.888.482.5—
ExploitGym20.734.542.430.4—15.0
Kimi Hallu Bench Hard w/ tools (internal, lower is better)8.315.05.523.323.322.6

Source: Kimi K3.1 Pro model card. Bold marks the best score in each row. GLM-5.3’s HLE score is on the text-only subset.*

Who leads which row. K3.1 Pro has the top score on agentic and tool-using work: SWE Marathon, HLE with tools, BrowseComp, Agents’ Last Exam, AutomationBench, OfficeQA Pro v2 and MMMU-Pro with Python. Claude Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-Bench 4.0 by 0.7 points, plus ProgramBench, HLE without tools, GDPval-AA, APEX-Agents and OSWorld.

Where it loses. The widest gaps are on ProgramBench (31.5 against Opus 5.5’s 65.0), HLE-Diamond without tools (39.4 against GPT-6 Astra’s 65.8) and the cyber rows, where Moonshot capped capability on purpose (ExploitGym 20.7 against 42.4). Among open-weight models in the table, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 beats it on DeepSWE (77.0 against 75.5) and APEX-Agents (69.8 against 69.4) at a small fraction of the price.

Independent view. Artificial Analysis scores K3.1 Pro at 46 on its Intelligence Index v5.0.1, first of 29 open-weight models of similar size (class median 23). The same page calls it “particularly expensive when comparing to other open weight models of similar size” and “somewhat verbose”: 113M output tokens to run the index against a 104M median. You can compare it against other models on DeepInfra on the model comparison page.

Pricing

Pricing as of 2026-11-17, per 1M tokens (model page, pricing page):

TierInputOutputCached input
Standard, promotional (5% off)$1.90$9.50$0.19
Standard, list$2.00$10.00$0.20
Flex (0.8×)$1.52$7.60$0.152
Priority (1.5×)$2.85$14.25$0.285

How the discounts stack. The 5% promotion comes off list, and Flex takes a further 20% off the promotional rate: $1.90 × 0.8 = $1.52 input, $9.50 × 0.8 = $7.60 output. Priority applies 1.5× to the promotional rate. Cached input is 10% of the input rate in every tier. No end date has been published for the promotion.

Against other providers. On Artificial Analysis’s provider benchmarks, DeepInfra’s $1.90 / $9.50 is the second-lowest input, output and blended price of the providers it measures, and the lowest of those that returned no errors: DeepInfra’s measured error rate is 0.0%, while the one cheaper endpoint (PrimaLabs, $1.80 / $9.00) failed 15.4% of requests. Most providers charge Moonshot’s own $2.00 / $10.00, and high-speed tiers run $4.00–$6.00 input and $20–$30 output. If response speed is your product, test DigitalOcean or Baseten, which measure around 200 and 183 tokens per second at the standard $2.00 / $10.00 rate against DeepInfra’s 47; for batch, agents and cost-sensitive work, the per-token gap compounds over long outputs.

Flex is the cheapest way to run the model if your work can wait. Send "service_tier": "flex": when capacity is short, the request waits up to 10 minutes and then returns HTTP 429, and a rejected Flex request is not charged. Overnight evaluations, batch extraction and background agents are a good fit. The Flex service tier announcement covers the details.

Priority ("service_tier": "priority") is for traffic that should not queue. At $2.85 / $14.25 it costs more than Moonshot’s list price, so use it only where queueing costs you more than the premium.

Caching matters with a verbose model and long agent sessions: cached input costs $0.19 against $1.90 for fresh input. Use prompt_cache_key to route repeated prefixes to the same cache, and prompt_cache_options to keep it warm for longer (see prompt cache retention).

For worked monthly cost scenarios, see the Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing guide. Startups can apply for free credits through DeepStart.

Getting started

The API is OpenAI-compatible:

  • Base URL: https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai
  • Endpoint: POST /chat/completions
  • Auth header: Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY

The full request schema is on the model’s API page.

Parameters

Model-specific parameters first. Send non-standard fields through extra_body in the OpenAI Python SDK.

ParameterDefaultNotes
reasoning_effortmodel defaultnone, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max. "none" turns thinking off. Moonshot’s benchmarks use max. Reasoning tokens bill as output
reasoning—Object form: {"effort": "...", "enabled": true/false}
temperature1Moonshot’s evaluations use 1.0
top_p1Moonshot’s evaluations use 0.95
service_tierstandardflex (0.8×, may queue up to 10 min, then 429) or priority (1.5×)
fail_fastfalseReturn 429 immediately instead of queueing
models—Up to 4 fallback models, tried in order if this one has no capacity
prompt_cache_key, prompt_cache_options—Share a prompt cache across requests; e.g. {"ttl": "1h"}
model(required)moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro
messages(required)Chat messages; user content can include images
max_tokensmin(context − input, 65,536)Up to 943,718
streamfalseServer-sent events
stop—Up to 16 sequences
n1Up to 4
top_k, min_p0Optional sampling controls
presence_penalty, frequency_penalty0−2 to 2
response_formattextjson_object, json_schema or regex
tools, tool_choice—OpenAI-style function calling

Python

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior equity research analyst."},
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize the revenue trend in this chart and list three risks."},
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/revenue-chart.png"}},
            ],
        },
    ],
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
    max_tokens=32768,
    extra_body={
        "reasoning_effort": "high",  # none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh | max
        "service_tier": "flex",      # remove this line for the standard tier
    },
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(response.usage)copy

For short, well-defined steps such as classification, extraction or routing, start with "reasoning_effort": "low" or "none". K3.1 Pro is verbose at high effort, and reasoning tokens are billed as output at $9.50 per 1M on the standard tier.

Output limits

There is no 16,384-token output cap on this model. You can request up to 943,718 output tokens. If you leave max_tokens unset, DeepInfra uses the smaller of 65,536 tokens and whatever remains of the 1,048,576-token window after your input. Input and output together must fit in that window.

Moonshot’s published results use max effort, and long agent runs at that setting can spend tens of thousands of tokens reasoning before the final answer starts. To get closer to Moonshot’s setup, set max_tokens explicitly above the 65,536 default, use max effort, and stream the response so long generations don’t hit client timeouts. Exact reproduction isn’t guaranteed, because Moonshot ran most benchmarks inside its own harnesses.

Conclusion

Kimi K3.1 Pro has the highest Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score among the 29 open-weight models of its size, and Moonshot’s own table puts it at or near the top on agentic, tool-using and document work. Its weak spots are clear too: closed models still lead on knowledge without tools, ProgramBench and cyber tasks, and it is verbose, so output tokens drive most of the bill.

That makes price per output token the number to watch. On DeepInfra, K3.1 Pro costs $9.50 per 1M output tokens at the current promotion, or $7.60 on Flex. That is below Moonshot’s list price and below the model it replaces, with a measured 0% error rate.

Next steps

  • Cut the bill for batch and evaluation traffic with Flex and longer-lived prompt caching.
  • Build agents with function calling, structured output and reasoning_effort set per step.
  • Compare providers in the Kimi K3.1 Pro API benchmarks and the best Kimi K3.1 Pro API providers, or start from the Kimi K3.1 Pro launch post.
  • Coming from Kimi K3? The Kimi K3 overview covers the base model.
  • Need dedicated capacity? Deploy the model privately, or talk to sales.

Related articles

GLM-5.3-Flash API Is Now on DeepInfra<p>Z.ai’s GLM-5.3-Flash activates just 18 billion of its 320 billion parameters at inference time, and on Z.ai’s reported results it outscores Claude Opus 4.8 on DeepSWE v1.1 (63.4 vs. 58.0), a demanding software engineering benchmark. It’s the first natively multimodal model in the GLM-5 series, combining text, image, and video input with a one-million-token context […]</p>

Best OpenClaw Alternatives: Hermes Agent, ZeroClaw & NemoClaw<p>OpenClaw has 362,000 GitHub stars and a skill marketplace with over 44,000 community contributions. That kind of adoption doesn’t happen by accident. Still, the same teams running it in production keep running into the same complaint: the model list is fixed. OpenClaw’s guided setup wizard covers OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, and local Ollama. You can […]</p>

GLM-5.1 Pricing Guide: API Cost Comparison & Analysis<p>Updated November 2026. Provider choice for GLM-5.1 is a real economic decision. Across 10 benchmarked API providers, blended pricing runs from $0.74 to $1.70 per 1M tokens, output speed from 33.8 to 175.2 t/s, and the fastest provider is 5.2x quicker than the slowest. For teams deploying at scale, that spread determines whether this model […]</p>

item.title: [DeepInfra] Best Kimi K3.1 Pro API Providers (2026): Price, Tiers, Speed
item.content:encoded:
Best Kimi K3.1 Pro API Providers (2026): Price, Tiers, Speed

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Summary of the Best Kimi K3.1 Pro Providers

ProviderBest For
DeepInfraLowest price of the providers in this guide ($1.90 / $9.50), Flex and Priority tiers, 0% measured error rate, private endpoints
Moonshot AI (Kimi API)First-party access, plus the Highspeed variant and Moonshot’s own coding and work apps
DigitalOceanFast responses at Moonshot’s list price, with dedicated GPUs available
BasetenFast per-token Model API, with dedicated deployments for scale
ModalPer-token API wired into coding agents, with a low cost per agentic task
Amazon BedrockThe Highspeed variant inside an AWS account, with Flex and Priority tiers
OpenRouterOne API key across many hosts, with automatic failover
Featherless AIOne OpenAI-compatible key for K3.1 Pro and a large open-model catalog

Quick reference by priority

  • Lowest price per token among the providers in this guide: DeepInfra ($1.90 input / $9.50 output / $0.19 cached per 1M tokens; Flex $1.52 / $7.60)
  • Fastest answers at list price: DigitalOcean or Baseten
  • Fastest in this guide: Amazon Bedrock’s Highspeed variant, at twice the list price
  • First-party features and apps: Moonshot AI
  • One key with failover: OpenRouter

Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI’s open-weight agentic model, released October 23, 2026, with weights published on Hugging Face in early November. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 2.8T total and 104B active parameters, natively multimodal (text and image in, text out) and a 1M-token context window. It was post-trained from Kimi K3 with much larger reinforcement-learning compute, and it replaces K3’s full-attention layers with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention for cheaper long-context serving. On Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index it scores 46, the highest of the 29 open-weight models of its size. It is also verbose and reasons for a long time before answering, so where you run it shapes both the bill and the wait.

This guide compares the ways to run Kimi K3.1 Pro on what decides the choice: price and pricing tiers, features, deployment model, and who each option suits. Each entry gets one line on measured speed. The full speed and latency comparison is in the Kimi K3.1 Pro API benchmarks, including time to first token versus time to first answer token, which for this reasoning model ranges from about 25 seconds to over two minutes. Speed, blended price and error rates come from Artificial Analysis (reasoning effort max, pulled 2026-11-17), which benchmarks 16 endpoints from 14 providers for this model. Rates and features come from each provider’s own pages. Pricing as of 2026-11-17.

Hosted API Providers

1. DeepInfra

DeepInfra is the best pick when cost per token decides the choice and you want production reliability, service tiers and a path to dedicated capacity.

  • Current rates: $1.90 input / $9.50 output / $0.19 cached input per 1M tokens, a 5% promotional discount on the $2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20 list price
  • Flex tier: $1.52 / $7.60 / $0.152. Opt in with "service_tier": "flex". A request waits up to 10 minutes for capacity, then returns HTTP 429, and a rejected Flex request is not charged (how Flex works)
  • Priority tier: $2.85 / $14.25 / $0.285 with "service_tier": "priority", for requests that can’t queue
  • Blended price (Artificial Analysis, 7:2:1): $1.46, below every standard-price endpoint at $1.54 and every fast tier ($2.31 to $4.62). With the same weighting, Flex works out to about $1.17
  • Reliability: 0.0% error rate in Artificial Analysis’s runs. DeepInfra is the cheapest endpoint Artificial Analysis measures with a 0% error rate
  • Context and output: 1,048,576-token context; up to 943,718 output tokens per request. If max_tokens is unset, the default is the lesser of the remaining context and 65,536
  • Features: OpenAI-compatible API, image input, tool calling, JSON mode and structured outputs (JSON schema and regex), reasoning_effort from none (thinking off) to max, prompt caching with prompt_cache_key and a configurable TTL, up to 4 fallback models per request
  • Deployment: serverless per-token API, or a private endpoint on dedicated GPUs; zero data retention
  • Speed: 46.9 tokens/s output on Artificial Analysis. If response speed is your product, test DigitalOcean or Baseten; for batch, agents and cost-sensitive work, the per-token gap compounds.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is verbose: Artificial Analysis counted 113M output tokens to run its Intelligence Index, against a class median of 104M. Output tokens, including reasoning tokens, therefore drive most of the bill, and DeepInfra’s $9.50 output rate ($7.60 on Flex) is where the saving shows. It suits background agents, document and finance pipelines, evaluation runs and any workload that can absorb a longer wait for a lower price. One thing to measure on your own traffic: DeepInfra’s cache hit rate on Artificial Analysis’s agentic workload was 92.6%, below the 98–100% several hosts reached. Cache-heavy agent loops should set prompt_cache_key and check the hit rate before projecting costs.

A first call with the OpenAI SDK:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Reconcile these two revenue tables and explain each difference."}],
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
    extra_body={"reasoning_effort": "high", "service_tier": "flex"},
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)copy

The endpoint is /chat/completions and the auth header is Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY. Full parameters are on the Kimi K3.1 Pro API page.

2. Moonshot AI (Kimi API)

Moonshot’s own Kimi API is the best pick when you want first-party access, the Highspeed variant, or the model inside Moonshot’s products.

  • Model names: kimi-k3.1-pro and kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed (Moonshot release post)
  • Rates (Artificial Analysis): $2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20 cached; Highspeed $4.00 / $20.00 / $0.20
  • Highspeed: Moonshot says it delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro
  • Products: also available in Kimi.ai, Kimi Work and Kimi Code; zero data retention is available for API customers
  • Speed: 31.0 tokens/s on Artificial Analysis for the standard endpoint (Highspeed: 69.4 tokens/s)

The first-party API gets new Moonshot features first, and the Highspeed variant is the simplest way to cut response time without leaving Moonshot. It costs more than DeepInfra on every token category, and Artificial Analysis measured an 8.0% error rate on the standard endpoint in its runs, so build in retries.

3. DigitalOcean

DigitalOcean Serverless Inference is the best pick when users wait on every answer and you want to stay at Moonshot’s list price.

  • Rates: $2.00 input / $10.00 output / $0.20 cache read per 1M tokens
  • Billing: prepaid serverless credits; dedicated GPU inference billed per GPU-hour
  • Platform: model catalog, Inference Router and agent tooling in one console
  • Speed: 200.8 tokens/s and the lowest time to first answer token among standard-price endpoints on Artificial Analysis

DigitalOcean is the provider to test for chat UIs and interactive coding agents. It costs about 5% more per token than DeepInfra’s standard rate, and its pricing page lists only a Standard tier for this model.

4. Baseten

Baseten’s Model API is the best pick when you want a fast per-token API now and dedicated deployments when volume grows.

  • Model: Kimi K3.1 Pro, 1M context, text and image input
  • Rates (Artificial Analysis): $2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20 cached
  • Deployment: per-token Model API, plus dedicated deployments and engineering support for custom setups
  • Speed: 183.0 tokens/s on Artificial Analysis, among the fastest at list price

Baseten suits product teams that expect to move from shared to dedicated capacity. Its per-token rates match Moonshot’s list price, so it costs more than DeepInfra per token.

5. Modal

Modal’s Model APIs are the best pick when you run K3.1 Pro inside coding agents and want low cost per finished task.

  • Rates: $2.00 input / $0.20 cached input / $10.00 output per 1M tokens
  • API: OpenAI-compatible, with native integrations for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Hermes Agent
  • Inputs: text and images, 1,048,576-token context
  • Cost per task: $3.19 per Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index task, among the lowest measured, helped by a 100% cache hit rate
  • Speed: 118.0 tokens/s on Artificial Analysis

Modal’s high cache hit rate means agent loops that resend long prefixes pay less per task than the list price suggests. Per token it charges Moonshot’s list rate, about 5% above DeepInfra’s.

6. Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock is the best pick when your workloads already run in AWS and you want the Highspeed variant under AWS governance.

  • Model: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed (global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1), 1M context
  • Rates (Standard tier): $4.00 input / $20.00 output / $0.20 cache read on the global profile; $4.40 / $22.00 / $0.22 on the US and India profiles; cache writes $5.00 per 1M tokens
  • Service tiers: Flex at 0.5× and Priority at 1.75× the Standard rate
  • APIs: OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses, plus Converse and Invoke; reasoning effort none to max (default max)
  • Speed: 218.2 tokens/s on Artificial Analysis, among the fastest measured

Bedrock keeps data inside the AWS boundary, with regional profiles for US and India data residency. The standard rate is twice Moonshot’s list price for the Highspeed variant. Bedrock’s Flex tier brings it back to $2.00 / $10.00 for workloads that can wait, which is still above DeepInfra’s standard rate.

7. OpenRouter

OpenRouter is the best pick when you want one API key and automatic failover across the hosts that serve K3.1 Pro.

  • Model slug: moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
  • Hosts routed: over 20 endpoints, DeepInfra among them, each at the host’s own price
  • Routing: balanced, fastest or cheapest modes; you can pin a single host
  • Speed: whatever the selected host delivers; OpenRouter adds a network hop but no compute of its own

OpenRouter lists some smaller hosts with lower prices than DeepInfra, served at a range of precisions. Pin a host if output consistency matters. Teams that settle on one host usually go direct for its full feature set, service tiers and support.

8. Featherless AI

Featherless AI is the best pick when you already use its OpenAI-compatible API for many open models and want K3.1 Pro on the same key.

  • Rates (Developer plan): $2.00 input / $0.20 cached / $10.00 output per 1M tokens
  • Context: 256K on the Developer plan; the full 1M window on a dedicated instance
  • Data: no logging of prompts or completions
  • Deployment: serverless API, or dedicated GPU clusters
  • Speed: not tracked by Artificial Analysis for this model

The 256K window is a quarter of the model’s native context, which matters for whole-repository and long-document work. It fits teams consolidating many open models under one provider.

About the License

Kimi K3.1 Pro ships under the Kimi K3.1-Pro License, a custom license that allows commercial use with conditions. Model-as-a-service operators with group revenue above $20 million over any 12 months need a separate agreement with Moonshot, and products with over 100 million monthly active users or over $20 million monthly revenue must display “Kimi K3.1-Pro” in their interface. The license names exemptions for internal use and for some access routes. Read the full text, or ask your provider, if either threshold could apply to you.

Final Thoughts

  • Lowest price per token in this guide: DeepInfra, at $1.90 / $9.50 / $0.19, $1.46 blended on Artificial Analysis, and Flex at $1.52 / $7.60 for async work
  • Lowest price with a 0% measured error rate: DeepInfra
  • Fastest answers at list price: DigitalOcean or Baseten
  • Fastest in this guide: Amazon Bedrock’s Highspeed variant, at $4.00 / $20.00
  • Low cost per agentic task: Modal, helped by a 100% cache hit rate
  • First-party features and apps: Moonshot AI
  • One key, automatic failover: OpenRouter
  • One key across a large open-model catalog: Featherless AI

Speed and latency for this model shift week to week as hosts tune their serving stacks, as covered in why open models get faster after launch. Check the benchmarks guide for current numbers before committing.

The Best Overall Solution

For most teams running Kimi K3.1 Pro as an API, DeepInfra is the default choice. It has the lowest price of the providers in this guide at $1.90 input and $9.50 output, and a Flex tier at $7.60 output for anything that can wait. It is the cheapest endpoint Artificial Analysis measures with a 0% error rate, it serves the full 1M context with up to 943K output tokens, and it offers zero data retention and private endpoints, all on an OpenAI-compatible API you can switch to by changing a base URL. For lighter steps in an agent pipeline, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash runs on the same API for a fraction of the price.

For more detail, see the Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing guide for cost scenarios, the API benchmarks for speed and latency, and the model overview for architecture and parameters. If you are moving from Kimi K3, the Kimi K3 pricing and providers guide covers the previous generation. Startups can apply for free credits through DeepStart.

Kimi K3.1 Pro API Benchmarks: Providers, Speed & Cost

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI’s new open-weights flagship, and it tops the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index among open-weights models of its size. It is also a large, talkative reasoning model, so where you run it changes both the bill and the wait. This guide compares the Artificial Analysis data for the 16 endpoints from 14 providers covered here, price first.

Kimi K3.1 Pro Provider Comparison Data

Prices are per 1M tokens. Blended price uses Artificial Analysis’s 7:2:1 weighting of cache-hit, input and output tokens.

Provider (endpoint)InputOutputBlended (7:2:1)Error rateOutput speed (t/s)Time to first answer token (s)Cost per Index taskBest for
DeepInfra$1.90$9.50$1.460.0%46.9109.82$4.39Cost with reliability: lowest price of any endpoint with a 0% error rate; Flex tier
PrimaLabs$1.80$9.00$1.3915.4%109.821.16$2.94Lowest list price
Modal$2.00$10.00$1.540.0%118.044.64$3.19Cache-heavy agent runs
Baseten$2.00$10.00$1.540.0%183.025.53$3.26Throughput at list price
Databricks$2.00$10.00$1.541.9%111.769.25$3.29Databricks-native stacks
DigitalOcean$2.00$10.00$1.540.0%200.825.35$3.42Speed and latency at list price
Wafer$2.00$10.00$1.540.0%112.381.11$3.50Low time to first token (1.41 s)
Kimi (first-party)$2.00$10.00$1.548.0%31.0152.69$3.68Baseline; Moonshot’s own API
Parasail$2.00$10.00$1.540.0%112.154.07$4.22Mid-pack all-rounder
Nebius$2.00$10.00$1.542.0%94.661.52$4.38Mid-pack all-rounder
SiliconFlow$2.00$10.00$1.540.0%45.5105.62$4.68List-price fallback
Inco$3.00$15.00$2.315.8%134.238.91$4.79Faster than list price, below fast tiers
Amazon Bedrock (High Speed)$4.00$20.00$2.940.0%218.224.93$4.37AWS-native fast tier
Kimi High Speed$4.00$20.00$2.944.9%69.474.05$4.42Moonshot’s own fast tier
LithosAI (ULTRA)$6.00$30.00$4.410.0%258.517.87$6.32Fastest output and first answer
Inco (FAST)$6.00$30.00$4.620.0%187.027.22$9.55Premium speed tier

Methodology. Data from the Artificial Analysis providers page for Kimi K3.1 Pro at max reasoning effort, pulled November 17, 2026. Artificial Analysis uses its “Performance v3” method: headline speed and latency average single-request and multi-turn agentic workloads, and error rate pools those runs. Blended price weights cache-hit, input and output tokens 7:2:1. Cost and time per task come from Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index workload and depend on each endpoint’s measured cache hit rate as well as its prices. DeepInfra’s figures are its current promotional price (5% off its $2.00 / $10.00 list price). Figures change over time. Pricing as of 2026-11-17.

Kimi K3.1 Pro API Review Summary

  • Lab and release: Moonshot AI, released October 23, 2026; open weights followed in early November.
  • Intelligence: 46 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1, #1 of 29 open-weights models of similar size (class median 23).
  • Price on DeepInfra: $1.90 input / $9.50 output / $0.19 cached per 1M tokens (5% off list); Flex $1.52 / $7.60 / $0.152.
  • Blended price: $1.46 per 1M on DeepInfra, the lowest of any benchmarked endpoint with a 0% error rate.
  • Reliability: DeepInfra recorded a 0.0% error rate over Artificial Analysis’s measurement window.
  • Speed leaders at list price: DigitalOcean (200.8 t/s, 25.35 s to first answer token) and Baseten (183.0 t/s, 25.53 s).
  • Verbosity: 113M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, against a class median of 104M.
  • Context and output: 1,048,576-token context; up to 943,718 output tokens on DeepInfra (65,536 by default if max_tokens is unset).
  • Modality: text and image in, text out.
  • Size: Mixture-of-Experts, 2.8T total and 104B active parameters (Hugging Face).
  • License: custom Kimi K3.1-Pro License; commercial use allowed, with extra terms for very large model-as-a-service operators and very large consumer products.
  • Providers covered: 16 endpoints from 14 providers.

About Kimi K3.1 Pro

Kimi K3.1 Pro is post-trained from Kimi K3 with much larger reinforcement-learning compute. The main architecture change is in attention: K3’s full-attention Gated MLA layers are replaced with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention for cheaper long-context work, alongside its KDA layers. It keeps the 1M-token context and reads images through a 401M-parameter vision encoder.

Moonshot’s own results (vendor-reported, run at max reasoning effort) put it at the top of its comparison table on agentic tasks such as HLE-Full with tools (70.0), BrowseComp (92.1) and AutomationBench-AA (73.3). Closed models still lead on reasoning without tools (HLE-Full 51.1 vs Claude Opus 5.5’s 59.8), on Terminal-Bench 4.0 by a hair (65.7 vs 66.4) and on the cyber-security rows. Against its predecessor, Moonshot reports Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon at 61.2 vs Kimi K3’s 55.95. Our Kimi K3 API provider analysis covers the previous model.

Two serving details shape provider choice. First, the model reasons at length: Artificial Analysis counts 113M output tokens to complete its index, and reasoning tokens bill as output, so the output price dominates cost. Second, latency to the first answer is long on every endpoint (17.87 s to 152.69 s), so time to first answer token matters far more than time to first token.

DeepInfra: The Overall Recommended Provider

DeepInfra is the recommended Kimi K3.1 Pro API on price and reliability. At $1.90 input and $9.50 output per 1M tokens it is 5% below the $2.00 / $10.00 list price that 9 of the 16 benchmarked endpoints charge, and its $1.46 blended price is the lowest of any endpoint that recorded a 0% error rate. Among the providers Artificial Analysis benchmarks, only PrimaLabs lists a lower price.

The Flex service tier takes the price lower: $1.52 input, $7.60 output and $0.152 cached. That output rate is 24% below list. At the same 7:2:1 weighting Artificial Analysis uses, Flex works out to about $1.17 blended (our calculation). Send "service_tier": "flex"; a Flex request waits up to 10 minutes for capacity, then returns HTTP 429, and a rejected request isn’t charged. A Priority tier is also available at 1.5× the promotional rate.

Because output dominates this model’s bill, the per-token gap adds up. A batch job that generates 100M output tokens costs $950 on DeepInfra Standard, $760 on Flex, and $1,000 at list price.

If response speed is your product, test DigitalOcean or Baseten at the standard list price; for batch, agents and cost-sensitive work, DeepInfra’s per-token gap compounds.

  • Blended Price: $1.46 per 1M ($1.90 input, $9.50 output, $0.19 cached); Flex about $1.17
  • Output Speed: 46.9 t/s
  • Latency (TTFT): 2.09 s; 109.82 s to first answer token
  • Optimal Workload: batch reasoning, background agents and evaluation runs where price and a clean error rate matter more than seconds to first answer

The Kimi K3.1 Pro model page lists JSON mode, structured output, tool calling, image input, zero data retention and private endpoints. The API is OpenAI-compatible at https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions with Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY; parameters are on the API page.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Plan the migration steps for this schema change."}],
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,
    max_tokens=32768,
    extra_body={
        "reasoning_effort": "high",
        "service_tier": "flex",  # remove for standard tier
    },
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)copy

DigitalOcean: Speed and Latency Leader at List Price

DigitalOcean is the fastest endpoint at the standard $2.00 / $10.00 price: 200.8 t/s output and 25.35 seconds to the first answer token, with a 0% error rate. It finishes an Intelligence Index task in 6.0 minutes and costs $3.42 per task.

  • Blended Price: $1.54 per 1M
  • Output Speed: 200.8 t/s
  • Latency (TTFT): 1.71 s; 25.35 s to first answer token
  • Optimal Workload: interactive coding assistants and chat where users wait for the answer

Baseten: High-Throughput Alternative

Baseten is close behind at 183.0 t/s and 25.53 seconds to first answer, also at list price with a 0% error rate. A 99.6% cache hit rate on Artificial Analysis’s agentic workload brings its cost per task to $3.26, the third-lowest in the set.

  • Blended Price: $1.54 per 1M
  • Output Speed: 183.0 t/s
  • Latency (TTFT): 1.44 s; 25.53 s to first answer token
  • Optimal Workload: throughput-heavy agent pipelines that also need low latency

LithosAI ULTRA and Amazon Bedrock High Speed: Premium Speed Tiers

If speed matters more than price, two fast tiers lead the table. LithosAI ULTRA has the highest output speed (258.5 t/s) and the shortest time to first answer (17.87 s) at $6.00 / $30.00, three times list price. Amazon Bedrock High Speed reaches 218.2 t/s and 24.93 s at $4.00 / $20.00. Both recorded 0% error rates.

  • Blended Price: $4.41 (LithosAI ULTRA); $2.94 (Bedrock High Speed)
  • Output Speed: 258.5 / 218.2 t/s
  • Latency (TTFT): 1.75 / 4.00 s; 17.87 / 24.93 s to first answer token
  • Optimal Workload: latency-critical products with budget for a speed premium

PrimaLabs: Lowest Listed Price

PrimaLabs lists the lowest price on Artificial Analysis ($1.80 / $9.00, $1.39 blended) and the lowest cost per Index task ($2.94), with 109.8 t/s and 21.16 seconds to first answer. Its 15.4% error rate over the measurement window is the highest in the set, so plan retries or a fallback if you route to it.

  • Blended Price: $1.39 per 1M
  • Output Speed: 109.8 t/s
  • Latency (TTFT): 0.95 s; 21.16 s to first answer token
  • Optimal Workload: cost-first workloads with retry logic in place

Kimi (Moonshot First-Party API): The Baseline

Moonshot’s own API charges the $2.00 / $10.00 list price and measured 31.0 t/s with 152.69 seconds to first answer token and an 8.0% error rate. Moonshot also sells Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed at $4.00 / $20.00 (69.4 t/s on Artificial Analysis). The first-party API is the reference for pricing and for Moonshot-specific features.

  • Blended Price: $1.54 per 1M (Highspeed $2.94)
  • Output Speed: 31.0 t/s (Highspeed 69.4)
  • Latency (TTFT): 4.03 s; 152.69 s to first answer token
  • Optimal Workload: teams that want Moonshot’s own API and products

Technical Deep-Dive: What Developers Need to Know

1. Time to First Answer Token Is the Latency Number That Matters

Time to first token runs from 0.95 to 6.54 seconds across the 16 endpoints, but time to first answer token runs from 17.87 to 152.69 seconds, because the model reasons before answering. For anything user-facing, compare providers on time to first answer, and consider a lower reasoning_effort for interactive calls: DeepInfra’s API accepts none through max, and Artificial Analysis’s figures are all measured at max.

2. Output Price Drives the Bill

At 113M output tokens to run Artificial Analysis’s index (class median 104M), Kimi K3.1 Pro is somewhat verbose, and its output price is five times its input price. On output-heavy work, the output rate is the number to compare: $9.50 on DeepInfra, $7.60 on Flex, $10.00 at list price and $20.00–$30.00 on fast tiers.

3. Cost per Task Depends on Your Cache Hit Rate

Artificial Analysis’s blended price assumes 70% of tokens are cache hits, and its cost per task reflects each endpoint’s measured cache hit rate on a long agentic workload. If your traffic is mostly fresh prompts or output-heavy reasoning, per-token prices predict your bill better than the per-task figure. Use prompt_cache_key on DeepInfra to keep repeated context cached across agent turns.

4. Output Limits and Long Context

DeepInfra serves the full 1,048,576-token context and allows up to 943,718 output tokens. If you don’t set max_tokens, it defaults to the smaller of the remaining context and 65,536.

5. API Feature Parity

All the providers above serve the same open weights through OpenAI-compatible APIs, so you can route cost-sensitive traffic to one endpoint and latency-sensitive traffic to another by changing only the base URL and model name.

Conclusion

  • Lowest price with a 0% error rate: DeepInfra ($1.90 / $9.50, $1.46 blended; Flex $7.60 output)
  • Speed and latency at list price: DigitalOcean (200.8 t/s, 25.35 s to first answer); Baseten close behind
  • Fastest regardless of price: LithosAI ULTRA (258.5 t/s, 17.87 s) and Amazon Bedrock High Speed
  • Lowest listed price: PrimaLabs, with a 15.4% error rate to plan around
  • Baseline: Moonshot’s first-party Kimi API at $2.00 / $10.00

For full pricing scenarios, see the Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing guide; for the model itself, the Kimi K3.1 Pro model overview. Our roundup of the best open-source models for coding puts K3.1 Pro next to its open-weights peers. To start, call Kimi K3.1 Pro on DeepInfra, or deploy it on a private endpoint for dedicated GPU capacity.

Related articles

That kind of adoption doesn’t happen by accident. Still, the same teams running it in production keep running into the same complaint: the model list is fixed. Best MiMo-V2.5 API Providers Ranked<p>Executive Summary: Selecting the right API provider for Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 is critical for optimizing production workflows. Based on the benchmark research, DeepInfra is the best provider for raw speed and low latency (130+ tokens/second), while Xiaomi’s first-party API is the most cost-effective, offering unmatched prompt caching discounts.
