item.content:encoded:
Kimi K3.1 Pro Pricing: API Costs, Providers & Flex (2026)

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Kimi K3.1 Pro Executive Summary

Pricing as of 2026-11-17. DeepInfra’s Standard rate is promotional (5% off a $2.00 / $10.00 list price, no published end date). Budget against list if you’re planning past this quarter.

Best ForProvider RecommendationWhy
Lowest price with a 0% error rateDeepInfra Standard$1.90 input / $9.50 output / $0.19 cached per 1M tokens: the lowest price among the endpoints Artificial Analysis measured with a 0% error rate. One endpoint is cheaper (PrimaLabs, $1.80 / $9.00), with a 15.4% error rate.
Batch jobs, evals and backfillsDeepInfra Flex$1.52 / $7.60 / $0.152, 20% below Standard, for requests that can wait up to 10 minutes for capacity.
Agents and RAG with large repeated promptsDeepInfra StandardCached input bills at 10% of the input rate ($0.19), and agent traffic is mostly cached prefix.
First-party access and HighspeedMoonshot (Kimi API)$2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20 at list, plus a Highspeed variant at $4.00 / $20.00 that only Moonshot serves.
Fastest responses at list priceDigitalOcean or Baseten200.8 and 183.0 output tokens per second, about 25 seconds to the first answer token, at $2.00 / $10.00.
One API across many hostsOpenRouterRoutes Kimi K3.1 Pro across more than 15 providers at each provider’s own price, with failover.

Verdict: for most production traffic, DeepInfra Standard is the lowest-cost endpoint that didn’t fail requests in Artificial Analysis’s tests, and Flex takes another 20% off anything that can wait. Pay list price elsewhere only when response speed is the product.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI’s open-weight flagship, released on October 23, 2026 and on DeepInfra since November 2026. It is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 2.8T total and 104B active parameters, a 1,048,576-token context window, and text and image input. Moonshot post-trained it from Kimi K3 with much more compute and swapped K3’s full-attention layers for sparse attention to make long context cheaper to run. The weights ship under the Kimi K3.1-Pro License, an MIT-style license with two extra conditions for very large commercial operators (details below).

On Artificial Analysis, Kimi K3.1 Pro scores 46 on Intelligence Index v5.0.1, first of 29 open-weight models of its size (class median: 23). It is also a long-thinking model: it wrote 113M output tokens to run the index, against a 104M class median. That’s the pricing story in one line. The rate card is high for an open model, output is the expensive side of it, and this model writes a lot. The useful question is not whether it’s cheap, but which endpoint and which token mix keep your bill reasonable.

Understanding Tokens and How You’re Charged

You pay for what you send, what the model writes, and, at a 90% discount, what you send again.

Token typeWhat it isWhy it matters for Kimi K3.1 Pro
Input (uncached)New prompt tokens: user text, retrieved documents, tool results, images$1.90 per 1M on DeepInfra. A full 1M-token prompt costs about $1.99 uncached.
Cached inputPrompt prefix the provider has seen recently: system prompt, tool schemas, conversation history$0.19 per 1M, 10% of the input rate. Agent loops resend history every turn, so this line carries most of the volume.
OutputGenerated tokens, including reasoning$9.50 per 1M, 5× the input rate. Reasoning tokens bill here too.
Max outputThe cap on one responseUp to 943,718 tokens on DeepInfra. If you don’t set max_tokens, the default is 65,536, about $0.62 of output at most.
Context windowPrompt plus output, per request1,048,576 tokens. Long-context RAG fits without aggressive chunking, which is a capability, not a budget.

What this means in practice:

  • Output is where the money goes. At 5× the input rate, and with a model Artificial Analysis rates “somewhat verbose”, output usually decides the bill even when it’s a small share of tokens.
  • Reasoning effort is a cost dial. DeepInfra accepts reasoning_effort from none (thinking off) to max. Moonshot’s benchmark numbers use max. For extraction, classification and routing, a lower setting saves output tokens the task doesn’t need.
  • Cache hit rate matters as much as the cache price. On Artificial Analysis’s agentic Index workload, DeepInfra’s endpoint hit the cache 92.6% of the time, against 98–100% on several other endpoints. Even with lower token prices, that made DeepInfra’s cost per Index task $4.39, more than several $2.00 / $10.00 endpoints. Keep the stable parts of your prompt at the front and set prompt_cache_key so repeated prefixes stay cached.
  • Images bill as input. Kimi K3.1 Pro accepts images, which are tokenized and charged at the input rate.

Provider Token Cost Tradeoffs

Artificial Analysis benchmarks Kimi K3.1 Pro on 16 endpoints from 14 providers. Most standard endpoints charge Moonshot’s list price, $2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20. DeepInfra is $0.10 below that on input and $0.50 below on output. Prices are per 1M tokens.

Provider / routeInputOutputCachedAdvantageDisadvantageBest fit
DeepInfra Standard (promo)$1.90$9.50$0.19Lowest price among Artificial Analysis endpoints with a 0% error rate; zero data retention; JSON, structured output and tool callingPromotional rate (list $2.00 / $10.00); lower measured cache hit rate on Artificial Analysis’s agent workloadProduction apps, agents, RAG
DeepInfra Flex$1.52$7.60$0.15220% below Standard; a request Flex can’t place is rejected and not chargedWaits up to 10 minutes for capacity, then returns HTTP 429Batch jobs, evals, backfills
DeepInfra Priority$2.85$14.25$0.285Priority capacity when demand peaks1.5× Standard, above Moonshot’s list priceLatency-sensitive paths where queueing costs more than tokens
PrimaLabs$1.80$9.00$0.18Lowest price Artificial Analysis measured15.4% error rate on Artificial Analysis; OpenRouter lists its endpoint at $2.70 / $13.50Price-only workloads that can absorb failed requests
Moonshot (Kimi API)$2.00$10.00$0.20First-party; Highspeed variant at $4.00 / $20.0031.0 t/s and an 8.0% error rate on Artificial AnalysisTeams already on Moonshot’s platform
DigitalOcean, Baseten$2.00$10.00$0.20Fastest standard-price endpoints: 200.8 and 183.0 t/sList price on every tokenInteractive products where speed is the requirement
Fast tiers (Amazon Bedrock High Speed, LithosAI ULTRA, Inco FAST)$4.00–$6.00$20.00–$30.00$0.20–$0.60Up to 258.5 t/s2–3× the standard priceLatency at any cost
OpenRouterVaries by providerVariesVariesOne key, failover; some hosts Artificial Analysis doesn’t benchmark list lower pricesThe routed provider sets price, speed and cache behaviorMulti-provider fallback
Self-hostingGPU costGPU costn/aFull control over a 2.8T-parameter modelA multi-GPU cluster and an inference team; MaaS operators above $20M revenue need a separate agreement with MoonshotVery large, steady volume

Source: Artificial Analysis providers page, OpenRouter and the DeepInfra model page, accessed 2026-11-17.

Takeaways by workload:

  • Output-heavy work: DeepInfra’s $9.50 output rate is the lowest of the zero-error endpoints Artificial Analysis measures. Every 100M output tokens costs $50 less than at list.
  • Batch and async work: Flex at $7.60 output is 24% below list and needs one request field.
  • Agent loops: the $0.19 cache rate helps only if requests actually hit the cache. Structure prompts for it, then check your cached-token share in usage before you trust a forecast.
  • Off-benchmark routes: OpenRouter lists a few hosts that Artificial Analysis doesn’t benchmark at lower token prices. That’s why every price claim in this guide is scoped to the endpoints Artificial Analysis measures.

Cost trap to avoid: a broken cache. In Scenario 1 below, a cache hit rate of 80% instead of 90% raises the monthly bill from $1,653.00 to $2,166.00, with no change in traffic. Timestamps or request IDs at the top of a system prompt, or reshuffled tool definitions, are the usual culprits.

On speed: DeepInfra’s endpoint measured 46.9 tokens per second and 109.82 seconds to the first answer token at max reasoning. If response speed is your product, test DigitalOcean or Baseten at list price; for batch, agents and cost-sensitive work, the per-token gap compounds.

DeepInfra: The Lowest-Cost Zero-Error Route for Kimi K3.1 Pro

Model / listingBest use caseContextInput (per 1M)Output (per 1M)
Kimi K3.1 Pro, StandardAgents, coding, long-context RAG, document and image understanding1,048,576$1.90 ($0.19 cached)$9.50
Kimi K3.1 Pro, FlexBatch jobs, evals, backfills1,048,576$1.52 ($0.152 cached)$7.60
Kimi K3.1 Pro, PriorityLatency-sensitive production paths1,048,576$2.85 ($0.285 cached)$14.25

Kimi K3.1 Pro on DeepInfra runs behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions, model ID moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro, Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY). It supports JSON mode, structured output, tool calling, image input and reasoning control, with zero data retention and no minimums. DeepInfra owns its GPU infrastructure, and the same account can deploy the model on a private endpoint when shared capacity stops being enough. The /api page lists every parameter. This request uses Flex and a lower reasoning effort:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Extract the parties and dates from this contract as JSON: ..."}],
    max_tokens=2048,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    extra_body={
        "service_tier": "flex",
        "reasoning_effort": "low",
    },
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)copy

Why this matters: most endpoints charge Moonshot’s $2.00 / $10.00 list price for this model. DeepInfra’s promotional rate is 5% below that on every token type. Among the endpoints Artificial Analysis benchmarks, only one is cheaper, and it failed 15.4% of requests. For a reasoning model where a failed request can waste thousands of tokens of work, a 0.0% error rate is part of the price.

Real-World Cost Scenarios for Developers

All five scenarios use DeepInfra’s promotional Standard rate ($1.90 / $9.50 / $0.19) unless they say otherwise. Each compares the same workload at Moonshot’s list price ($2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20), which is also what most endpoints on Artificial Analysis charge and what DeepInfra charges if the promo ends. Token volumes are monthly. “M” means million.

Scenario 1: Repo-scale coding agent for a 25-person team

VolumeModelProviderInput tokensOutput tokensMonthly cost
25 developers, daily agent sessionsKimi K3.1 ProDeepInfra Standard3,000M (2,700M cached, 300M uncached)60M$1,653.00

Coding agents resend the repo map, tool schemas and conversation history on every turn, so input dwarfs output and most of it should hit the cache. This assumes a 90% cache hit rate and output at 2% of input. Moonshot reports 51.7 on SWE Marathon and 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for this model (vendor-reported), which is the kind of long-horizon coding this loop needs.

Why DeepInfra fits: the cached prefix bills at $0.19, and the uncached input and output are at the lowest zero-error rate Artificial Analysis measured.

Cost breakdown – Uncached input: 300M × $1.90/M = $570.00 – Cached input: 2,700M × $0.19/M = $513.00 – Output: 60M × $9.50/M = $570.00 – Total: $1,653.00/month

Same workload at list price ($2.00 / $10.00 / $0.20): $600.00 + $540.00 + $600.00 = $1,740.00, or $87.00 more. At an 80% cache hit rate, the DeepInfra bill rises to $2,166.00.

Scenario 2: Long-context RAG over a document library

VolumeModelProviderInput tokensOutput tokensMonthly cost
100,000 queriesKimi K3.1 ProDeepInfra Standard6,000M (5,000M cached, 1,000M uncached)80M$3,610.00

Each query sends a 60,000-token prompt: a 50,000-token cached prefix of instructions and core documents, plus 10,000 tokens of freshly retrieved passages. It returns an 800-token answer. The 1M-token window leaves room to grow the prefix before you need to chunk harder.

Why DeepInfra fits: the cached prefix is 83% of input but only $950 of the bill. The uncached retrieval tokens are where the 5% rate gap shows up.

Cost breakdown – Uncached input: 1,000M × $1.90/M = $1,900.00 – Cached input: 5,000M × $0.19/M = $950.00 – Output: 80M × $9.50/M = $760.00 – Total: $3,610.00/month (about $0.036 per query)

Same workload at list price: $2,000.00 + $1,000.00 + $800.00 = $3,800.00, or $190.00 more.

Scenario 3: Nightly agent evals and backfills on Flex

VolumeModelProviderInput tokensOutput tokensMonthly cost
Nightly eval sweeps and data backfillsKimi K3.1 ProDeepInfra Flex2,000M (1,600M cached, 400M uncached)100M$1,611.20

Regression suites for an agent product, synthetic-data generation and re-processing old tickets can all wait a few minutes for capacity. That’s exactly what Flex is for: the same model at 0.8× the price, in exchange for a queue of up to 10 minutes.

Why DeepInfra fits: Flex is one request field ("service_tier": "flex"), and a request it can’t place within 10 minutes returns a 429 without a charge.

Cost breakdown (Flex) – Uncached input: 400M × $1.52/M = $608.00 – Cached input: 1,600M × $0.152/M = $243.20 – Output: 100M × $7.60/M = $760.00 – Total: $1,611.20/month

On DeepInfra Standard, the same jobs cost $760.00 + $304.00 + $950.00 = $2,014.00, so Flex saves $402.80. At list price: $800.00 + $320.00 + $1,000.00 = $2,120.00, or $508.80 more than Flex.

Scenario 4: JSON and tool-calling backend

VolumeModelProviderInput tokensOutput tokensMonthly cost
500,000 requestsKimi K3.1 Pro (reasoning_effort low)DeepInfra Standard1,500M (1,000M cached, 500M uncached)200M$3,040.00

A backend turns tickets, invoices and form submissions into validated JSON and tool calls. Each request carries a 2,000-token cached prefix (instructions and JSON schema) and 1,000 new tokens, and returns 400 tokens. Reasoning effort is set low because extraction gains little from long thinking.

Why DeepInfra fits: structured output and tool calling are supported, and output, two-thirds of this bill, is at the lowest zero-error rate measured.

Cost breakdown – Uncached input: 500M × $1.90/M = $950.00 – Cached input: 1,000M × $0.19/M = $190.00 – Output: 200M × $9.50/M = $1,900.00 – Total: $3,040.00/month

Same workload at list price: $1,000.00 + $200.00 + $2,000.00 = $3,200.00, or $160.00 more. The bigger lever is the reasoning setting: every extra 1,000 reasoning tokens per request adds 500M output tokens, or $4,750.00 a month.

Scenario 5: Production agent platform with a Priority slice

VolumeModelProviderInput tokensOutput tokensMonthly cost
80% of trafficKimi K3.1 ProDeepInfra Standard6,400M (5,600M cached, 800M uncached)240M$4,864.00
20% of traffic (interactive)Kimi K3.1 ProDeepInfra Priority1,600M (1,400M cached, 200M uncached)60M$1,824.00
Total8,000M300M$6,688.00

A customer-facing agent platform runs most work on Standard and routes the interactive slice, where users are watching a spinner, to Priority.

Why DeepInfra fits: both tiers use the same model ID, endpoint and integration, so moving traffic between them is a request field, not a migration. A private endpoint is available on the same account if you later need dedicated capacity.

Cost breakdown – Standard: 800M × $1.90 + 5,600M × $0.19 + 240M × $9.50 = $1,520.00 + $1,064.00 + $2,280.00 = $4,864.00 – Priority: 200M × $2.85 + 1,400M × $0.285 + 60M × $14.25 = $570.00 + $399.00 + $855.00 = $1,824.00 – Total: $6,688.00/month

Everything on Standard would cost $1,900.00 + $1,330.00 + $2,850.00 = $6,080.00, so the Priority slice adds $608.00. At list price everywhere: $6,400.00. Priority sits above list, so use it where queueing costs you more than tokens do.

What these scenarios say about DeepInfra

  • The rate gap is small per token and steady in total. At 5% below list on every token type, DeepInfra saves $87 to $190 a month on the Standard scenarios here.
  • Flex is the larger saving. Moving schedulable work to Flex cut Scenario 3 by $402.80 against Standard, 24% below list.
  • Cache discipline beats provider choice. Scenario 1’s drop from a 90% to an 80% cache hit rate costs $513 a month, nearly six times what the rate gap saves.
  • Reasoning settings beat both. In Scenario 4, 1,000 extra reasoning tokens per request would cost more than the whole bill.
  • A 0% error rate is the condition on every “lowest price” claim. The one cheaper endpoint Artificial Analysis measures failed 15.4% of requests.

Conclusion

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the top-scoring open-weight model in its size class on Artificial Analysis, and one of the more expensive to run. Three decisions control the bill: where you run it, how much of each prompt hits the cache, and how much reasoning you let it do.

For where: DeepInfra’s $1.90 / $9.50 is the lowest price among the endpoints Artificial Analysis measured with a 0% error rate, and Flex ($1.52 / $7.60) is the cheapest way to run anything that can wait. Pay the $2.00 / $10.00 list price at a faster endpoint only when response speed is what you’re selling. For cache and reasoning: put stable content first, watch your cached-token share, and set reasoning_effort per task instead of leaving it at the maximum.

Moonshot’s license is MIT-style. Two conditions apply only to Model-as-a-Service operators with more than $20M in revenue and to products past 100M monthly users or $20M in monthly revenue, so read it before you build a hosted product on the weights.

If a step doesn’t need K3.1 Pro, a lighter model on the same API costs a fraction of the price. The best open-source models for coding roundup compares the options. For the previous generation’s numbers, see the Kimi K3 pricing guide, and for how Flex works, the Flex tier announcement. For speed and latency by provider, see the Kimi K3.1 Pro API benchmarks; for specs and parameters, the Kimi K3.1 Pro model overview.

Start with Kimi K3.1 Pro on DeepInfra, run your real prompt mix for a week, and read your cached-token share and output volume off the usage page before you commit to a forecast. Startups can apply for free credits through DeepStart.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Kimi K3.1 Pro on DeepInfra: Pricing, Benchmarks & API
item.content:encoded:
Kimi K3.1 Pro on DeepInfra: Pricing, Benchmarks & API

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro posts the top scores in its own comparison table on BrowseComp (92.1) and Humanity’s Last Exam with tools (70.0), ahead of the closed frontier models Moonshot tested against, according to the Kimi K3.1 Pro model card (vendor-reported). Independent testing backs up the headline: Artificial Analysis gives it 46 on its Intelligence Index v5.0.1, the highest of 29 open-weights models of its size, against a class median of 23.

Moonshot released K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026 and published the weights in early November. It’s a 2.8-trillion-parameter Mixture of Experts model with 104B active parameters, a 1M-token context window and native image input. It’s built for long-horizon agentic work: coding agents, browsing and research, and document-heavy office tasks such as finance, legal and spreadsheet work.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is now available on DeepInfra at $1.90 per 1M input tokens and $9.50 per 1M output tokens with the current 5% promotion. That’s below Moonshot’s own API list price of $2.00 / $10.00, and the Flex tier takes output down to $7.60. Artificial Analysis also recorded a 0% error rate on DeepInfra’s endpoint.

BenchmarkKimi K3.1 ProClaude Opus 5.5GPT-6 AstraDeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017GLM-5.3
BrowseComp92.190.891.5––
HLE-Full (with tools)70.067.757.258.862.5
AutomationBench-AA73.369.568.566.662.2
SWE Marathon v1.151.746.342.540.042.5
OfficeQA Pro v264.462.254.440.431.1
Terminal-Bench 4.065.766.458.242.341.8
DeepSWE v1.175.574.274.177.066.9
OSWorld V2.179.681.875.869.3–
HLE-Full (no tools)51.159.853.642.643.0*
GPQA-Diamond94.293.996.192.291.7
ExploitBench74.791.0100–54.4

All scores are vendor-reported from the Kimi K3.1 Pro model card. Moonshot ran K3.1 Pro at max reasoning effort and ran the proprietary models “with fallback”; some comparison scores are cited from leaderboards or other labs’ reports. Text-only subset.*

K3.1 Pro is strongest on agentic tasks that use tools. It leads the table on BrowseComp, HLE with tools, AutomationBench, long-running software work (SWE Marathon) and office document QA. In Moonshot’s own internal hallucination test with tools, its error rate fell to 8.3% from Kimi K3’s 23.4%.

It doesn’t win everywhere. Claude Opus 5.5 edges it on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (66.4 vs 65.7) and computer use (OSWorld V2.1), and the closed models are well ahead on reasoning without tools (HLE-Full and HLE-Diamond) and on cybersecurity, where Moonshot says it removed cyber training data from the open-weight release. Among open-weights models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 beats it on DeepSWE v1.1 (77.0 vs 75.5). Moonshot ran every number above, and the model card also includes internal benchmarks that nobody else can reproduce; those are left out of the table here.

What Makes This Model Different

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the first model in the K3.1 series. Moonshot post-trained it from Kimi K3 with “substantially larger post-training compute”, using large-scale joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of domains. That’s where most of the gains over K3 come from.

The architecture is a sparse Mixture of Experts: 2.8T total parameters, 104B active, 896 experts with 16 selected per token plus 2 shared experts, across 93 layers. Each token touches under 4% of the weights, so you get the capacity of a very large model at the per-token compute of a much smaller one.

Sparse attention for long context

The one architectural change from K3 is attention. K3.1 Pro replaces K3’s full-attention Gated MLA layers with Gated DeepSeek Sparse Attention (Gated DSA). The model now mixes 69 KDA layers with 24 Gated DSA layers, which makes long-context modeling cheaper. That matters at a 1M-token context, where long agent traces and large document sets add up fast.

Native vision

K3.1 Pro takes images as well as text. A 401M-parameter MoonViT-V2 vision encoder feeds the language model directly. Moonshot’s chart, document and multimodal results (CharXiv, MMMU-Pro, GDP.pdf) are strongest when the model can also run Python, which fits agent pipelines that read a chart, compute on it and write up the result.

Reasoning control and output length

It’s a reasoning model, and Moonshot ran its evaluations at max effort with temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95. On DeepInfra you control depth with reasoning_effort (from none, which turns thinking off, up to max). Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so set the effort per task: low for simple steps, max for hard agentic work.

If you leave max_tokens unset, DeepInfra uses the smaller of the remaining context and 65,536 tokens. For long reasoning runs, set it explicitly. The ceiling on DeepInfra is 943,718 output tokens.

License

K3.1 Pro ships under the Kimi K3.1-Pro License, a permissive MIT-style license with two conditions. Companies that offer the model as a service with more than $20M in group revenue over 12 months need a separate agreement with Moonshot first. Products with more than 100M monthly active users or more than $20M in monthly revenue must show “Kimi K3.1-Pro” in their interface. Internal use isn’t affected. Read the license if you’re building a large consumer product on it.

Where it’s not the right fit

Artificial Analysis calls K3.1 Pro “somewhat verbose”: it used 113M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, against a class median of 104M. Deep reasoning at max also takes time on every provider. Faster endpoints exist (DigitalOcean and Baseten lead output speed at the standard price on Artificial Analysis); if response speed is your product, test them. For batch jobs, agents and cost-sensitive work, the lower per-token rate and Flex add up. For simple, high-volume steps, a smaller model is the better tool (see the conclusion).

Getting Started on DeepInfra

Kimi K3.1 Pro is available now in DeepInfra’s text generation catalog. Pricing is per token with no minimums.

TierInputOutputCached input
Standard, promotional (5% off)$1.90$9.50$0.19
Standard, list$2.00$10.00$0.20
Flex (0.8×)$1.52$7.60$0.152
Priority (1.5×)$2.85$14.25$0.285

Per 1M tokens. Pricing as of 2026-11-17. Flex and Priority apply to the promotional rate. Source: model page and pricing page.

The promotion has no published end date, so budget against the $2.00 / $10.00 list price and treat the 5% as upside. Cached input costs 10% of the input rate, which helps agents that resend the same system prompt and tool definitions on every turn.

As an example, an agent workload of 10M input tokens and 2M output tokens costs $19.00 + $19.00 = $38.00 at the promotional rate. On Flex the same job costs $15.20 + $15.20 = $30.40.

Choosing a tier:

  • Flex costs 0.8× standard. Opt in with "service_tier": "flex". A Flex request waits up to 10 minutes for capacity and then returns HTTP 429, and rejected Flex requests aren’t charged. It suits batch jobs, evals and background agents. See how the Flex tier works.
  • Priority costs 1.5× standard. Opt in with "service_tier": "priority" for traffic that shouldn’t queue.

Model specs on DeepInfra:

  • Model ID: moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro
  • Context window: 1M tokens (1,048,576)
  • Max output: 943,718 tokens; default max_tokens is 65,536 if unset
  • Input: text and images. Output: text
  • reasoning_effort: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh or max
  • JSON mode, structured output and function calling are supported

The endpoint is OpenAI-compatible. Point your client at https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai, call /chat/completions and authenticate with Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY. DeepInfra runs a zero-retention data policy and is SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certified. If you need dedicated capacity, you can deploy a private endpoint from the model page.

Python

Get an API key from the DeepInfra dashboard and export it as DEEPINFRA_API_KEY. This example sends a chart image and asks for analysis:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Summarize the trend in this chart and flag any anomalies."},
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/revenue-chart.png"}},
            ],
        }
    ],
    max_tokens=131072,  # unset defaults to 65,536; the ceiling is 943,718
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=0.95,         # Moonshot's evaluation settings
    extra_body={
        "reasoning_effort": "high",  # none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh | max
        "service_tier": "flex",      # 0.8x price; drop this line for standard
    },
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)copy

To try prompts before writing code, open the interactive demo on the Kimi K3.1 Pro model page. The API reference lists every supported parameter, including reasoning_effort, service_tier, response_format and prompt-caching options.

Conclusion

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the strongest open-weights model on Artificial Analysis’s index for its size class, and its vendor results are best on agentic work with tools: browsing and research, long-running coding tasks, and office and document analysis. Teams building research agents, coding agents or document pipelines should evaluate it on their own tasks, since the benchmark table is Moonshot’s. If you’re running Kimi K3 today, K3.1 Pro is the natural next model to test.

Don’t route every step to it. For classification, extraction and other simple steps, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on DeepInfra costs a fraction of the price per token. Keep K3.1 Pro for the hard, multi-step work where its results are strongest.

For more context, see our Kimi K3 launch post and Kimi K3 overview, and how K3.1 Pro compares in our roundup of the best open-source models for coding. The rest of this package covers Kimi K3.1 Pro pricing, API benchmarks, the model overview and the best Kimi K3.1 Pro API providers.

Building a startup? DeepStart gives eligible startups about 50 billion free tokens (counted at DeepSeek V4 Flash prices) to spend on any model, including Kimi K3.1 Pro. Or head to the model page, grab an API key and make your first call.

With its native omnimodal architecture — supporting text, image, video, and audio — and a 1,048,576-token context window, it opens up new paradigms for agentic workflows, long-document analysis, and […]</p>

item.title: [DeepInfra] 9 Best Open-Source Models for Coding (November 2026)
item.content:encoded:
9 Best Open-Source Models for Coding (November 2026)

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) coding tools now analyze repositories, fix bugs, edit several files, run tests, and execute autonomous development loops. These agentic workflows generate millions of input and output tokens through continuous model calls, and that makes proprietary APIs costly at scale.

Open-source coding models offer a cost-effective alternative. You can run them on private infrastructure, choose your serving hardware, pin a specific model version, adjust inference settings, and reduce dependence on a single API provider. Hosted inference services like DeepInfra also let you use these models without managing GPUs yourself, at per-token prices that start under $0.10 per million input tokens for the top-scoring model in this guide.

In this guide, we compare the leading open-source models for coding as of November 2026. We evaluate them on coding benchmarks, context window size, license terms, and API cost, and we cover self-hosting options at the end. Scores and prices are as of November 17, 2026.

How to Evaluate Coding Models: Benchmarks That Matter

Watch the following benchmarks to judge how well a model will perform on the tasks you plan to automate.

  • HumanEval and MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems) measure function-level code generation. A model receives a short natural-language problem and must produce Python code that passes unit tests. They offer a quick measure of basic programming ability, but they do not test repository navigation, tool use, or multi-file changes, and current models have largely saturated them.
  • SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro assess how well a model resolves real GitHub issues within agentic coding workflows. The model has to work through an entire codebase, locate the source of a bug, write a patch across multiple files, and pass execution tests.
  • DeepSWE is the long-horizon software engineering benchmark that most of this year’s model cards report. Because DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi, Z.ai, and Qwen all publish a DeepSWE v1.1 score, it is the closest thing to a common yardstick across vendors, with the caveat that each vendor runs its own harness.
  • Terminal-Bench compares model performance on tasks related to shell commands, command-line interfaces (CLI), and DevOps. Vendors now report versions 2.1 and 4.0, and results change a lot with the agent harness used, so compare scores only within the same model card.
  • LiveBench is independent and regularly refreshed to limit training-data contamination. LiveBench moved to version 2.0 on November 6, 2026. The new version grades long-horizon work (bug fixes, apps that run for hours, research reports), and its scores are not comparable to the LiveBench figures published before that date.

Apart from the leaderboard, check the context window and license. A model that looks good on function-level completion can still be a poor choice for whole-repo refactors or private on-prem use.

  • Context window defines how much code, documentation, terminal output, and conversation history the model can process in a single request. A larger context window helps with repository analysis and long-running agent sessions.
  • License determines whether you can use the weights commercially, modify them, redistribute the model, or provide the model through a hosted service. “Open-source” is used loosely in this field. Several models below ship open weights under custom licenses with commercial conditions, and we note each one. Our guide to open-weight model licenses covers what to check.

Top 9 Open-Source Models for Coding: Comparison

Here is how the current top open-source models for coding compare on size, license, context window, and what they are best at:

ModelDeveloperParameters (total / active)LicenseContext windowBest for
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017)DeepSeek763B totalMIT1MBest coding score per dollar
Mistral Large 4Mistral AI1T / 49BMistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License1MEuropean-built generalist with near-top coding scores
GLM-5.3Z.ai753B totalGLM-5.3 License (custom)1MLong-horizon coding and security work
Qwen3.8-27BAlibaba Qwen27B denseApache 2.0262KSmall deployments and local use
MiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMax428B / 23BMiniMax Community License1MAgentic coding with image and video input
Kimi K3.1 ProMoonshot AI2.8T / 104BKimi K3.1-Pro License (custom)1MThe hardest long-horizon agent tasks
MiMo-V2.6-ProXiaomi1.02T / 42BMIT1MLong tool-use sessions on an MIT license
DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813)DeepSeek1.65T totalMIT1MDeep reasoning on large codebases
Muse Glimmer 30BMeta29.6B denseApache 2.0131KLocal coding agents on consumer hardware

1. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 is the October update to DeepSeek’s Flash line, and it is the strongest open-weight model on the current independent leaderboard. On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 80.4 in the coding category, the highest of any open-weight model and ahead of several proprietary ones.

DeepSeek’s own model card reports 77.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, both up from the original V4.1 Flash (74.2 and 31.2). The update also reduces task execution time and output length, which matters for agents that pay per output token. The model is MIT-licensed, multimodal, and supports a 1M-token context window.

It is also the cheapest serious coding model in this guide. On DeepInfra it is priced at $0.098 per million input tokens and $0.294 per million output tokens during a 51% launch promotion (list price $0.20 and $0.60), and it supports the Flex tier at 0.8× for work that can wait.

2. Mistral Large 4

Mistral Large 4 is Mistral AI’s largest model: about 1 trillion parameters with 49 billion active per token, natively multimodal, with a 1M-token context window. Mistral released the weights on October 29, 2026, and says the model was trained in its own data centers in Europe. It replaces Devstral as the Mistral model to consider for coding.

On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 79.4 in coding, one point behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 and well clear of the rest of the open-weight field. Its long-horizon agentic score is 24.7, which puts it mid-table on unattended work. (LiveBench lists two Mistral Large 4 entries; these figures are for the October 29 entry, which matches the open-weight release. The earlier entry scores 44.4 in coding.)

The Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License is a modified MIT license that allows commercial and internal use, with one condition: a company operating a model-as-a-service business needs a separate commercial license from Mistral. DeepInfra does not serve Mistral Large 4 at the time of writing, so the routes are Mistral’s own API or self-hosting, which at this size means a multi-GPU cluster.

3. GLM-5.3

GLM-5.3 uses the same base model as GLM-5.2, with all of the gains coming from post-training. Z.ai’s model card reports large jumps on long-horizon work: DeepSWE v1.1 rises from 46.2 to 66.9, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 81.0 to 88.2, and SWE-Marathon v1.1 from 19.4 to 42.5. It also reports the top CyberGym score in its comparison (84.5), which makes it a candidate for security-review agents.

The full GLM-5.3 is not yet listed on LiveBench 2.0. Its smaller sibling, GLM-5.3-Flash, is, and scores 70.9 in coding, third among open-weight models.

Check the license before you build a product on it. GLM-5.3 ships under a custom GLM-5.3 License that reads like MIT with one added condition: companies that run a model-as-a-service business with more than $10 billion in annual revenue must pass a Z.ai security review before commercial use. GLM-5.3-Flash is plain MIT. On DeepInfra, GLM-5.3 costs $0.563 input and $2.50 output per million tokens on a 38% promotion (list $0.90 and $4.00), with Flex available.

4. Qwen3.8-27B

Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27-billion-parameter model under Apache 2.0, and it is the small model to beat. Its hybrid architecture combines Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention layers, supports a 262K-token context natively, and includes a vision encoder.

On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 69.3 in coding, within two points of GLM-5.3-Flash despite being a fraction of the size. Qwen’s model card reports 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, 73.0 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and 90.3 on LiveCodeBench v6. Its DeepSWE v1.1 score is 42.2, well below the large models in this guide, which is the honest picture of a 27B model: strong on contained tasks, weaker on multi-hour ones. LiveBench shows the same thing, with a long-horizon agentic score of 15.9.

On DeepInfra it costs $0.15 input and $1.875 output per million tokens on a 25% promotion (list $0.20 and $2.50), with Flex and Priority tiers.

5. MiniMax M3.1 Flash

MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a native multimodal mixture-of-experts model for coding, agentic workflows, and computer use. It has about 428 billion total parameters with 23 billion active per token, accepts text, image, and video, and supports up to 1M tokens of context. It scores 68.8 in LiveBench 2.0 coding.

MiniMax reports 73.7 on DeepSWE v1.1, 38.1 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 61.2 on NL2Repo-Bench. Its card also publishes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017’s numbers alongside its own, and DeepSeek leads on all three.

Two things to know. First, the MiniMax Community License grants non-commercial use by default; commercial use requires displaying “Built with MiniMax M3.1-Flash”, notifying MiniMax, and getting written authorization once the product earns more than $20 million a year. Second, DeepInfra does not serve M3.1 Flash at the time of writing. It serves the earlier MiniMax-M3 at $0.28 input and $1.10 output per million tokens, with Flex.

6. Kimi K3.1 Pro

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the largest model here: 2.8 trillion total parameters with 104 billion active. It is post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale reinforcement learning, and it replaces K3’s full-attention layers with sparse attention for more efficient long-context work.

Its profile is the reverse of Qwen’s. On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 67.8 in coding, mid-pack, but 38.7 on the long-horizon agentic category, level with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 at the top of the open-weight field. Moonshot’s card reports 75.5 on DeepSWE v1.1, 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 51.7 on SWE Marathon v1.1. It improves on Kimi K3 in LiveBench coding by almost 15 points (67.8 against 53.1).

It is also the most expensive open-weight option: $1.90 input and $9.50 output per million tokens on DeepInfra (5% off a $2.00 and $10.00 list price), with Flex at 0.8×. The Kimi K3.1-Pro License is MIT-style with conditions: model-as-a-service operators above $20 million in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Moonshot, and very large consumer products must display the model name. Internal use, and use through Moonshot’s certified inference partners, is exempt.

7. MiMo-V2.6-Pro

MiMo-V2.6-Pro is Xiaomi’s trillion-parameter reasoning model: 1.02 trillion total parameters, 42 billion active, a 1M-token context window, and text, image, video, and audio input. It carries a plain MIT license, which makes it the simplest large model in this guide to adopt commercially.

The jump from the previous version is the largest in this guide. Xiaomi’s card reports DeepSWE v1.1 rising from 19.0 on MiMo-V2.5 Pro to 71.9, and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 65.2 to 89.9. On LiveBench 2.0 it scores 64.5 in coding and 36.4 on long-horizon agentic work, third among open-weight models on the latter.

On DeepInfra it costs $0.387 input and $0.783 output per million tokens (10% off a $0.43 and $0.87 list price). The low output price stands out: it is less than a tenth of Kimi K3.1 Pro’s for a model that sits close to it on agentic work.

8. DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813)

DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813 is the August production release of DeepSeek’s flagship, at 1.65 trillion parameters with a 1M-token context window and an MIT license. It is not yet listed on LiveBench 2.0, so the evidence here is vendor-reported.

DeepSeek’s card shows how far it moved from the preview: Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 72.1 to 87.9, DeepSWE from 12.8 to 62.7, and NL2Repo from 38.5 to 61.5. Note that the newer and much cheaper V4.1 Flash-1017 reports a higher DeepSWE v1.1 score (77.0). Choose V4 Pro when you want the larger model’s reasoning on hard, single-shot problems, and V4.1 Flash for agent loops.

On DeepInfra it costs $1.30 input, $0.10 cached input, and $2.60 output per million tokens, with Flex at $1.04 and $2.08. The cached-input rate is worth attention for coding agents, which resend the same repository context on every step.

9. Muse Glimmer 30B

Muse Glimmer 30B is Meta’s open model for agents that run on local or consumer hardware. It is a dense 29.6-billion-parameter model under Apache 2.0, released in August 2026, with image input and a 131K-token context window.

Meta reports 76.0 on SWE-bench Verified, 51.2 on SWE-bench Pro, and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. What sets it apart is the packaging. Meta ships two roughly 4-bit variants aimed at 32GB and 24GB of VRAM, reporting 0.2% and 1.0% average degradation, plus a speculative-decoding drafter that it says lifts generation on an RTX 5090 from 74.9 to 233.4 tokens per second. Qwen3.8-27B posts higher coding scores on Qwen’s own card (61.7 against 51.2 on SWE-bench Pro), so Glimmer is the pick when local speed and a ready-made quantized build matter more than the last few points.

If you would rather not run it yourself, DeepInfra serves it at $0.30 input and $1.20 output per million tokens.

Where the Open-Source Coding Models Stand Against Proprietary Models

To set the context, it’s worth understanding where open source stands relative to proprietary options.

Proprietary models provide reliable tool calling, polished IDE integrations, managed infrastructure, and consistent performance across coding tasks. The trade-off is control: usage-based pricing can be unpredictable, and closed APIs limit your choices on data handling and serving infrastructure.

Open-weight models give you more flexibility in deployment, fine-tuning, and provider choice. The trade-off is that self-hosting can require more infrastructure and engineering work to optimize, monitor, and maintain the model.

Here are the LiveBench 2.0 results for the open-weight models it lists, from the November 6, 2026 release. GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813, and Muse Glimmer 30B are not on the leaderboard yet, so they do not appear. The top proprietary score in each category is included as a reference line.

LiveBench 2.0 Coding

ModelOrganizationTypeCoding
Gemini 4 Carbon (reference)GoogleProprietary91.0
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017DeepSeekOpen weights80.4

GLM-5.3-FlashZ.aiOpen weights70.9

MiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMaxOpen weights68.8
Kimi K3.1 ProMoonshot AIOpen weights67.8
MiMo-V2.6-ProXiaomiOpen weights64.5

Kimi K3Moonshot AIOpen weights53.1

LiveBench 2.0 Long-Horizon Agentic

ModelOrganizationTypeLong-horizon agentic
Claude Fable 5.2 (reference)AnthropicProprietary82.9
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017DeepSeekOpen weights38.8
Kimi K3.1 ProMoonshot AIOpen weights38.7
MiMo-V2.6-ProXiaomiOpen weights36.4
Kimi K3Moonshot AIOpen weights36.0
MiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMaxOpen weights25.7
Mistral Large 4Mistral AIOpen weights24.7

The two tables tell different stories. On coding, the best open-weight model is about ten points behind the best proprietary one. On long-horizon agentic work, the kind that runs unattended for hours, the gap is more than forty points. The practical reading: open-weight models are ready for the bulk of coding work, including bug fixes, refactors, test writing, and supervised agent loops. For fully autonomous multi-hour tasks, a proprietary model still earns its price, and a common setup is to route between the two.

Are Open-Source Coding Models Really Free?

Free access to model weights does not mean zero cost. You still need GPUs, storage, networking, inference software, monitoring, security controls, upgrades, and engineering time. Large mixture-of-experts models may activate only a small share of their parameters for each token, but a serving system still needs the full set of weights in memory.

Open weights also come with license terms. MIT and Apache 2.0 grant broad rights to use, modify, and redistribute. Four of the nine models here use custom licenses with commercial conditions: Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and MiniMax M3.1 Flash.

Self-hosting is usually economical when you have steady, high usage, strict source-code privacy requirements, existing GPU capacity, or predictable workloads that keep the hardware busy. A hosted open-model API often makes more sense when usage remains uncertain, or you want to test several models before committing to infrastructure.

You can compare the two options with a simple calculation:

  • Hosted monthly cost = input-token cost + output-token cost, less any cached-input and Flex savings
  • Self-hosted monthly cost = GPU hours + storage + networking + monitoring + engineering operations

Where Do Open-Source Coding Models Deliver the Most Value?

Open-source coding models provide several operational advantages across different scenarios.

  • Private codebases: You can run the model inside controlled infrastructure when source code, credentials, customer data, or internal documentation cannot leave your environment.
  • High-volume agentic workflows: Self-hosting or low-cost open-model APIs give more predictable costs for repeated repository analysis, test execution, debugging, and tool calls.
  • Model customization: You can fine-tune the model, adjust its inference settings, add domain-specific tools, or train adapters for internal frameworks and programming languages.
  • Deployment control: Your team can pin a tested model version, choose the hardware, control latency, and decide when to apply upgrades. Hosted model IDs still get retired, so plan for deprecation either way.
  • Hardware-specific workloads: You can select a dense or MoE architecture based on available VRAM, throughput targets, quantization support, and expected context length.
  • Reduced provider dependence: Open weights make it easier to move between a hosted API, a private endpoint, and self-managed infrastructure without rebuilding the coding application.

Running Open-Source Coding Models Locally or Self-Hosted

Several serving frameworks support open coding models:

  • vLLM focuses on high-throughput GPU serving and production APIs.
  • SGLang provides efficient structured generation and agent-oriented serving. Our vLLM vs SGLang comparison covers how to choose between the two.
  • llama.cpp runs quantized models across CPUs, consumer GPUs, and Apple Silicon.
  • Ollama simplifies local model installation and API access.
  • LM Studio provides a desktop interface and a local OpenAI-compatible server.

When running a model locally, consider its size, precision, and context window. Two models in this guide are sized for it. Muse Glimmer 30B ships with quantized builds that Meta targets at 24GB and 32GB of VRAM. Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B dense model, so a four-bit build needs roughly 14GB for the weights alone, and a 24GB GPU is a practical starting point once you add runtime overhead and context.

Everything else here is a data-center model. The other seven (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3.1 Pro) run from 428 billion to 2.8 trillion parameters and need multi-GPU servers.

Local or hosted, these models connect to any coding tool that accepts an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including open agents such as OpenCode.

Running These Models on DeepInfra

If you want the model without building the serving layer yourself, the simplest approach is DeepInfra’s OpenAI-compatible API: the same request format and client as the OpenAI API, with the model chosen by name. Seven of the nine models above are available, and prices are per token with no minimum.

ModelInput ($/1M)Output ($/1M)Flex tier (0.8×)Est. monthly cost*
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017$0.098$0.294Yes$15.68
Qwen3.8-27B$0.15$1.875Yes$52.50
Muse Glimmer 30B$0.30$1.20No$54.00
MiMo-V2.6-Pro$0.387$0.783No$54.36
GLM-5.3$0.563$2.50Yes$106.30
DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813$1.30$2.60Yes$182.00
Kimi K3.1 Pro$1.90$9.50Yes$380.00

**Estimate for 100M input tokens and 20M output tokens a month at the standard tier, before cached-input savings. Prices are from DeepInfra’s model pages on November 17, 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, Qwen3.8-27B, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, GLM-5.3, and Kimi K3.1 Pro are at promotional rates; list prices are given in each model’s section above. MiniMax M3.1 Flash and Mistral Large 4 are not served; the earlier MiniMax-M3 is, at $0.28 and $1.10.*

The spread is the point. The same workload costs $15.68 on the model with the highest LiveBench coding score and $380 on the largest one, a 24-fold difference. Three settings bring the bill down further:

  • Flex tier. Models with the Flex tag run at 0.8× the standard price in exchange for slower responses and occasional unavailability. That fits batch refactors, test generation, and overnight agent runs. The DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 estimate above drops to about $12.54.
  • Cached input. Coding agents resend the same system prompt, tool definitions, and repository context on every step. Those repeated tokens bill at the cached-input rate: $0.10 instead of $1.30 per million on DeepSeek V4 Pro-0813, for example. Our guide to prompt hygiene covers how to structure prompts so the cache hits.
  • Reasoning effort. Several of these models accept a reasoning_effort setting. GLM-5.3 defaults to max; dropping to high or low for routine edits cuts output tokens.

For high-volume supporting work around a coding agent, such as reading build logs or triaging issues with screenshots, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a low-cost multimodal option at $0.15 input and $0.50 output per million tokens. It scores 54.1 in LiveBench 2.0 coding, so use it for the simple steps.

If response speed is the product, as in inline autocomplete, test providers built on speed-specialized hardware as well. For agents, batch work, and anything billed by volume, the per-token gap compounds.

Here is how to call one of these models with the Python client:

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPINFRA_API_KEY"],
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a coding assistant. Return only the refactored code."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Refactor this function for readability:\n\ndef f(a,b):\n    return [x for x in a if x not in b]"},
    ],
    temperature=0.2,
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)copy

To try a different model, change the model name.

The Bottom Line

The best open-source model for coding depends on the work.

For most teams, start with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017: it has the highest independent coding score among open-weight models, an MIT license, and the lowest price in this guide. If your agents run long, unattended tasks, test Kimi K3.1 Pro and MiMo-V2.6-Pro against it; they score close to it on long-horizon work, and MiMo does so on an MIT license at a low output price. For long-horizon coding with a security angle, GLM-5.3 is the one to evaluate, license permitting. If you need a small model you can run yourself, choose Qwen3.8-27B for scores or Muse Glimmer 30B for a ready-made local build. Mistral Large 4 nearly matches DeepSeek on coding and is the choice if a European-built model matters to you, as long as you can use Mistral’s API or host a trillion-parameter model yourself.

Whichever you shortlist, measure it on your own repositories before you commit. Vendor benchmarks use different harnesses, and the independent leaderboard does not yet cover every model here.

Visit the DeepInfra models page to compare open-source models across context window and pricing. For any questions or feedback, reach out to us at feedback@deepinfra.com. You can also join the community on Discord, or find us on X at @DeepInfra.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Prompt Hygiene: Cheaper, Faster LLM API Calls
item.content:encoded:
Prompt Hygiene: Cheaper, Faster LLM API Calls

Published on 2026.11.17 by DeepInfra

Prompt hygiene is the habit of writing prompts that are clean, minimal, and unambiguous. It sounds like a writing tip, but in production it behaves like an infrastructure optimization: it reduces token spend, improves latency, and lowers the retry rate by making model outputs more predictable.

When teams complain that LLM calls are “too expensive” or “too slow,” the root cause is often not the model. It’s the prompt. Bloated inputs, unclear instructions, and unbounded outputs quietly inflate cost and turn reliability into a gamble.

This article explains what prompt hygiene is, why it matters, and how to apply it in a way that makes your calls cheaper and faster without reducing quality.

Why prompt hygiene matters in production

In production, every LLM call has two things that show up on your bill: the tokens you send in and the tokens the model sends back. (If the arithmetic is new to you, Pricing 101 walks through it.) A long prompt costs more up front and usually takes longer to process. A vague prompt often costs even more on the way out, because the model fills the gaps by generating extra text you didn’t actually need, and output tokens are priced higher than input tokens on most models. Both add latency.

The real budget killer, though, isn’t a response that’s a bit wordy. It’s a response that comes back in the wrong shape—missing fields, wrong structure, impossible to parse—and forces you to run the call again. A retry doubles the cost of that call, and it also creates the kind of “random slow” tail latency that users notice right away. It is one of the quieter reasons an API bill can double without anyone changing the model.

Prompt hygiene is simply the easiest way to keep that variability under control.

What “dirty prompts” look like

Messy prompts tend to fail in the same few ways. First, they include too much context “just in case.” People paste whole documents, send full chat histories, or repeat the same instruction three different ways. That inflates token usage, but it rarely improves the answer.

Second, they contain unclear or conflicting constraints. Asking for something “detailed but concise” sounds reasonable to a human, but it forces the model to choose which instruction to prioritize. Sometimes it picks “detailed.” Sometimes it picks “concise.” That inconsistency is exactly what makes production behavior unpredictable.

And finally, dirty prompts often don’t define the output contract. If you want bullets but don’t say so, you’ll sometimes get paragraphs. If you want JSON but don’t specify the schema, you’ll get something that looks like JSON—until one day it doesn’t, and your parser breaks.

The goal: reduce ambiguity and bound the output

The core idea behind prompt hygiene is simple: reduce the number of decisions the model has to make.

When you specify a clear task, clear constraints, and a clear output format, you reduce “entropy” in the generation. Less entropy means the model is less likely to drift, ramble, or invent structure.

And when you bound the output length, you control cost directly. A good prompt could follow this outline:

  • Task: State the task in one sentence, early and explicitly.
  • Constraints: Add the rules that matter: length, tone if needed, allowed sources, and what to do when something is missing.
  • Output format: Describe the exact structure you want the model to return.
  • Input: Provide only the data necessary for this call.

This is not about being rigid for the sake of it. It is about giving the model a well-defined lane so you get consistent results cheaply.

The hygiene rules that save the most money

Rule 1: Put the task in the first two lines

Models respond best when the goal is front-loaded. If the task is buried after a long preamble, you increase the chance of misalignment.

A prompt that starts with “Summarize this…” gives the model less to misread than one that starts with “You are a helpful assistant…” followed by several paragraphs of scene-setting.

Rule 2: Remove anything that doesn’t change the answer

Every token has a cost. If a sentence does not improve correctness, formatting, or compliance, delete it. In practice, this means cutting motivational fluff, duplicate instructions, and “nice-to-have” background that does not affect output.

Rule 3: Cap output length with measurable limits

“Be concise” is subjective, and subjective constraints are ignored more often than teams expect. Hard limits work because they are measurable. You can constrain output with word count, bullet count, character count, or strict JSON keys. Even simple limits like “max 120 words” can cut spending dramatically, because output verbosity is where much of the bill hides.

Rule 4: Always specify an output format

If your downstream system parses the result, formatting is not a preference. It is a contract. Tell the model exactly what the output should look like. If you need JSON, provide the schema (our guide to JSON-only responses shows how to enforce it at the API level). If you need bullets, specify the number and style. If you need headings, specify the headings.

Add a line that prevents extra text, such as “Output only the result. Do not add explanations.”

Rule 5: Eliminate conflicting constraints

Prompts that contain contradictory instructions lead to inconsistent results. Instead of “be detailed but short,” define what “detailed” means. For example, require “exactly three risks” or “include two edge cases.” Then separately cap length. This turns a vague goal into a deterministic target.

Rule 6: Define what to do when information is missing

If you do not define missing-data behavior, the model will often guess. One sentence can prevent hallucinations and retries: “If the answer is not in the input, write ‘Not stated in source.’” Or: “If a field is missing, return null.” This improves reliability and reduces rework.

Production hygiene: what changes at scale

Once you’re calling a model repeatedly—especially behind an API—the biggest waste isn’t a single verbose prompt. It’s paying full price for the same tokens over and over again. Two habits make a huge difference here: separating stable instructions from per-request input, and being intentional about how you feed context.

  • Separate stable instructions from per-request input If you find yourself pasting the same policy, tone guide, or output format rules into every request, you’re paying a “tax” on every call. In production, it’s cleaner to split your prompt into two layers. The first layer is a stable, versioned wrapper that contains the rules that should always apply—things like output format, safety constraints, and how to handle missing data. The second layer is the per-request prompt, which stays short and contains only the actual user input and task-specific details. The API is stateless, so the wrapper still travels with every request, but a wrapper that is identical from call to call can be served from the prompt cache at a fraction of the input price (see the next section). It also makes behavior consistent across endpoints, because you’re not relying on copy-pasted instructions that slowly drift over time.
  • Prefer retrieval and trimming over dumping context Another common cost trap is sending an entire document because the answer is “somewhere in there.” You pay for that whole block of text every single time, even if the model only needs a small paragraph. A better pattern is to retrieve or pre-trim the relevant parts and pass only those into the prompt. Even without a full RAG pipeline, you can often cut token usage dramatically by selecting a specific section, pulling the few paragraphs around a keyword, or providing the top snippets that actually contain the answer. Smaller, more relevant context usually improves quality too, because it reduces noise and keeps the model focused.

Prompt caching: pay less for the part that never changes

A stable prefix is also a cacheable one. On DeepInfra, prompt caching is automatic on supported models: when the beginning of a prompt matches a prefix from a recent request on the same model, the cached state is reused, the model skips reprocessing that portion, and those tokens are billed at the model’s cached-input rate instead of the standard input rate.

Two hygiene rules follow directly from how the cache matches:

  • Put stable content first. The cache matches from the start of the prompt, so the system prompt, format rules, and few-shot examples go before the user’s input.
  • Keep the prefix byte-identical. A single changed character invalidates the match. Keep timestamps, user IDs, and anything else that varies out of the prefix.

Here is what that is worth. DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 lists standard input at $1.30 per 1M tokens and cached input at $0.10 per 1M. Take a 3,000-token stable wrapper sent on 200,000 requests a month, which is 600M prefix tokens:

Rate per 1M tokensMonthly cost of the prefix
Standard input$1.30$780
Cached input$0.10$60

That is an estimate with a generous assumption: every request hits the cache. Cache entries expire after a period of inactivity, so real hit rates depend on how steady your traffic is. You can measure yours from the prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens field in each response’s usage object. If you need a prefix to stay warm for a guaranteed window, prompt cache retention holds it for 5 minutes or an hour in exchange for a write premium on the first request.

A concrete before-and-after example

If you’re running prompts through DeepInfra, you feel the cost of messy prompts immediately: more input tokens, longer completions, and higher latency—especially when you’re calling models at scale or powering user-facing endpoints. The quickest win is to tighten the prompt so the model spends tokens only on the work that matters.

Before: a “messy” prompt that wastes tokens

This kind of prompt is common in prototypes:

“You are an expert assistant. Read the following carefully and provide a professional answer. Make sure it includes all relevant details and context. Be thorough but also concise.”

It sounds reasonable, but it’s expensive and unreliable in production:

  • It doesn’t state the task (what is the model actually supposed to do?)
  • It encourages verbosity (“relevant details and context,” “thorough”)
  • It contains conflicting instructions (“thorough but concise”)
  • It has no output contract, so formatting varies and parsers break

In practice, this typically means longer responses, more variance, and more retries—exactly the combination that increases spend and tail latency.

After: a “hygienic” prompt you can ship behind an API

Here’s a production-ready rewrite that is cheaper, faster, and easier to validate:

Task: Answer the question using only the provided text.
Constraints:
Use at most 6 bullet points
Each bullet must be ≤ 18 words
If the text does not contain the answer, write: Not stated in source.
Output format: Return only the bullet list (no intro, no closing line).
Text: …
Question: …

Why this works better:

  • Lower output tokens: the hard cap prevents runaway completions.
  • Lower latency: shorter generations generally complete faster and reduce tail latency.
  • Fewer retries: strict format + clear missing-info behavior makes responses easier to parse and validate.
  • Better caching opportunities: the instruction block is now a fixed prefix the prompt cache can reuse, and when outputs are consistent, you can also cache whole responses by (model, prompt version, input hash).

What the rewrite saves

Here is an estimate at DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813’s standard rates ($1.30 input, $2.60 output per 1M tokens). The assumptions: both prompts carry the same 1,500-token source text; the messy instructions are about 40 tokens and the rewritten ones about 75; the uncapped answer averages 400 tokens; and the capped answer tops out near 145 tokens (6 bullets × 18 words, at roughly 0.75 words per token).

Per 1M callsInput tokensOutput tokensInput costOutput costTotal
Before1,540M400M$2,002$1,040$3,042
After1,575M145M$2,048$377$2,425

The rewritten prompt is slightly longer on the way in and still comes out about 20% cheaper overall, because output cost falls by roughly 64%. Retries widen the gap: if one in ten of the “before” responses had to be re-run because it would not parse, that adds about $304 per million calls. And with the 75-token instruction block cached, the “after” row drops a little further.

Your numbers will differ with your model, your inputs, and how long your uncapped answers run. The method carries over: count tokens in and out, before and after, and price them at the rates on the model page.

A quick pre-launch checklist

Before you ship a prompt, run it through a small checklist:

  • Is the task stated clearly at the top?
  • Can you delete at least 20% of tokens without changing results?
  • Is the output length capped with a measurable rule?
  • Is the output format explicit and parseable?
  • Are there any conflicting instructions?
  • Is missing-data behavior defined?
  • Is only necessary context included?
  • Does the stable part of the prompt come first, unchanged from call to call, so it can be cached?

Prompts that pass this checklist tend to be cheaper, faster, and significantly easier to maintain.

Conclusion

Prompt hygiene is not about making prompts short. It is about making them disciplined.

When you remove unnecessary tokens, constrain output, define clear formats, and keep the stable part of the prompt cacheable, you reduce the model’s guesswork and stop paying full price for repeated text. That lowers cost, reduces latency, and—most importantly—cuts retries. In production, that reliability is often worth more than any single model upgrade.

Related articles

On June 15, 2026, claude-sonnet-4-20250514 and claude-opus-4-20250514 stopped answering requests. Anthropic had posted the notice 62 days earlier. Teams with either string in a call site learned about it from an error rate, not an email. […]</p>

That’s how most vLLM vs SGLang decisions start. A published test reports a 29 percent throughput gap, the number lands in Slack, and two weeks later you’re debugging kernel version conflicts at midnight while p99 latency sits […]</p>

Most million-token context claims come with practical asterisks — degraded retrieval, inconsistent behavior at range. Z-AI describes this as the first time that scale has been delivered with reliability for sustained, long-horizon work. The coding […]</p>
