item.title: [Anyscale] Ray Train: Diagnosing GPU Starvation in Model Training with…
item.description: Full title: Ray Train: Diagnosing GPU Starvation in Model Training with Data Ingest Observability
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Ray Train: Diagnosing GPU Starvation in Model Training with Data Ingest Observability

By Jason Li | November 17, 2026

Part 3 of our KubeRay series. This blog stands on its own, so you don't need the earlier posts to follow along. Part 2: KubeRay in production: best practices from the field covers how teams run KubeRay in production and how Anyscale KubeRay Connect fits on top of it.

The Anyscale platform has built-in observability for Ray workloads, and KubeRay Connect, introduced at the end of Part 2, brings it to the KubeRay clusters you already run. This post covers one of those features, built specifically for training workloads: Ray Train's data ingest observability.

LinkWhy GPU starvation is hard to catch

Model training is capital-intensive, so training teams need to pay close attention to GPU utilization. At the scale of hundreds or thousands of GPUs, even a small slowdown adds up to a lot of lost GPU-hours.

To keep GPUs busy, the next batch of data needs to be ready the moment the model finishes the current one. When it isn't, the GPUs sit and wait. That's GPU starvation, and it's one of the most common reasons utilization drops. It's also one of the quietest: nothing crashes, nothing alerts, and the job just keeps running a little slower than it should.

Teams usually notice one of two symptoms: GPU utilization that swings up and down instead of holding steady, or training runs that take longer than expected. In the run below, for example, SM activity on every GPU keeps rising and falling instead of reaching a plateau:

GPU SM Activity

That pattern is a typical sign of GPU starvation. Data loading and training run in parallel: while the GPU trains on one batch, the next batch is being prepared. When preparing a batch takes longer than training on it, the training step finishes first and the GPU sits idle until the next batch arrives:

Training steps

Each idle gap is one of the dips in the utilization graph above. The symptom is easy to spot. The cause is not. A batch can arrive late for a variety of reasons: a slow upstream data pipeline, data traveling over the network from another node, heavy preprocessing on the training worker such as an expensive collate_fn, or the host-to-device copy. Each cause has a different fix, so the first step is finding which stage is the bottleneck.

The rest of this post walks through the tools for doing that:

  • Data ingest metrics in open source Ray: how Ray Train and Ray Data time each stage of data loading, and how to read the Grafana graphs to see whether training is stalling on data, which stage is responsible, and what to change.
  • Data ingest observability on Anyscale: the same graphs with no setup, plus a live data ingest panel on the Ray Train dashboard that summarizes ingest health for every running dataset. KubeRay Connect brings both to KubeRay clusters you manage yourself.

LinkData ingest metrics in open source Ray

Starting in Ray 2.58, Ray Train and Ray Data record how long each batch spends in every stage of data loading, so you can see which stage is holding training back. If your Ray Train code already reads from Ray Data, no code changes are needed.

A typical setup looks like this. The driver defines a Ray Dataset, here Parquet files read from S3, and passes it to the trainer. Ray Train gives each of the eight training workers its own shard of the dataset. Each worker reads its shard with iter_torch_batches, which applies your collate_fn and returns batches of 64 rows as PyTorch tensors:

import ray
import ray.train
from ray.train import ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer

train_ds = ray.data.read_parquet("s3://my-bucket/train/")

def train_func():
    shard = ray.train.get_dataset_shard("train")
    for batch in shard.iter_torch_batches(batch_size=64, collate_fn=my_collate):
        ...  # your training step

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_func,
    datasets={"train": train_ds},
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=8, use_gpu=True),
)
trainer.fit()

That single iter_torch_batches call is where all of the data loading happens. Like every other Ray Data iterator, including iter_batches, iter_rows, and to_tf, it moves each batch through the same pipeline before handing it to your training loop.

Inside that call, each batch passes through six stages on its way from the Ray Data pipeline to your GPU. Any of them can be the bottleneck:

StageWhat it measures
Production waitWaiting for the upstream Ray Data pipeline to produce the next block
Data transferFetching blocks to the training worker, including from another node's object store
BatchingSlicing and combining blocks into batches, including any local shuffle buffer
FormatConverting each batch to the requested format, such as NumPy or pandas
CollateRunning your own per-batch preprocessing on the training worker, such as tokenizing text or padding sequences to a common length, passed in as collate_fn
FinalizeCopying the batch to the GPU (host-to-device transfer) in iter_torch_batches

These stages don't run one after another on your training thread. Instead, a pool of background threads runs them concurrently to prepare the next batch while your training step runs. As long as the next batch is ready before your training step finishes, all of this work is hidden and doesn’t cost you any wall-clock time. When the next batch isn't ready in time, the training loop waits and the GPU sits idle. That wait is the exposed data loading time. Ray records it on every training worker, along with the time spent in each stage.

In open source Ray, these metrics appear in the Data Ingestion section of the Train Dashboard in Grafana once you set up Prometheus and Grafana for your cluster. The graphs answer three questions in order, shown here for a run that's stalling on an expensive collate_fn:

  • Is training stalling on data? Max Exposed Data Loading Time shows how long the training loop waits for each batch on the slowest rank. If it's zero, data loading keeps up, and tuning the pipeline won't help. If it isn't, that time is GPU idle time on every step.

Max Exposed Data Loading Time

  • Which stage is responsible? Percentage Data Loading Breakdown by Stage shows each stage's share of data loading time, pooled across all ranks. A large production wait share means the upstream Ray Data pipeline can't produce data fast enough. A large share in any other stage points to work on the training worker itself.

Percentage Data Loading Breakdown by Stage

  • Is it every rank or just one? Each stage has its own graph broken down by rank. If one rank sits well above the rest, it's a straggler, and because ranks synchronize on every step, a single slow rank can hold back the entire run.

Production wait time by rank

Two throughput graphs round out the view. Data Ingest Throughput by Rank shows the rows per second each rank consumes, and Data Production Throughput shows the rows per second the Ray Data pipeline delivers to training. Together they show a healthy run's steady-state rate, so drops and imbalance across ranks stand out.

Data Ingest Throughput by Rank & Data Production Throughput

Knowing which stage is responsible is what makes the problem actionable, because each one points to specific things to check or change:

BottleneckWhat to try
Production waitCheck the Ray Data dashboard for the slowest operator in your upstream pipeline and tune its configuration. You can also add CPU-only nodes so Ray Data can scale out preprocessing, or cache the preprocessed dataset in memory with materialize() if it fits.
Data transferIncrease prefetch_batches so blocks start transferring ahead of the training step. Higher values hold more batches in memory, so watch memory usage on the training nodes.
BatchingIf you use local_shuffle_buffer_size, reduce it or shuffle upstream instead, such as with a map_batches shuffle or by shuffling file order at read time.
FormatIncrease prefetch_batches so more batches are converted ahead of the training step.
CollateMove heavy preprocessing out of collate_fn and into the Ray Data pipeline with map_batches, where it scales out across the cluster instead of running on the training worker. For lighter collate work, increasing prefetch_batches can also help by preparing more batches ahead of the training step.
One straggling rankCheck what's different about that rank's node. Common causes are Ray Data tasks competing with the training worker for CPU or memory, and blocks that are repeatedly fetched from remote nodes. If Ray Data tasks are competing for resources, keep them off the training nodes by pinning the dataset to CPU-only nodes with a label_selector.

LinkData ingest observability on Anyscale

On Anyscale, you get all of these Grafana graphs with no setup. Anyscale collects the metrics for every training run and shows the graphs on the Ray Train dashboard, so there's no Prometheus or Grafana to host.

On top of the Grafana graphs, the Ray Train dashboard on Anyscale includes a live data ingest panel. Instead of reading through a dozen graphs, you get one live view of data ingest health across your whole cluster. The sped-up recording below shows it on a run that's stalling on collate:

Live data ingestion health

For each Ray Data dataset that's currently executing, the panel shows the following. Per-batch metrics are for the rank you select; the recording shows the slowest rank.

  • Ingestion progress: how far training has gotten through the dataset, as rows ingested out of the total.
  • Throughput: rows per second produced by the upstream data pipeline and ingested by training in total.
  • Exposed data loading stall: how long the training loop waits on data for each batch.
  • Training compute time: how long the training step takes for each batch.
  • Batch cycle: each batch's total time, split between training compute and the exposed stall.
  • Stage breakdown: time per batch in each of the six data loading stages, so the bottleneck stands out. In the recording, collate takes almost all of it, which points straight at the collate_fn.
  • Link to Grafana: one click to the full Data Ingestion graphs, for historical metrics and more detail.

Everything in this section is part of the observability built into the Anyscale platform. If you run your own KubeRay clusters, KubeRay Connect brings it to them without migrating workloads.

With these metrics, unstable GPU utilization becomes something you can trace to a single bottleneck, instead of something you guess at. Fix that stage and your GPUs stay fed: utilization rises and holds steady, and the same run finishes sooner on the same hardware.

To go deeper, see these guides in the Ray docs:

  • Debug data loading bottlenecks covers the full drill-down and the fix for each result.
  • How does Ray Data iterate over data? covers the threading model behind the six stages.

LinkSummary

Unstable GPU utilization tells you that something is wrong without telling you what. Starting in Ray 2.58, per-stage data loading metrics in Ray Train and Ray Data close that gap. They tell you whether data loading is what's holding training back and, if it is, where the bottleneck is, so you know where to look next. In open source Ray, the metrics show up in the Train Dashboard in Grafana. On Anyscale, you get the same graphs with no setup, plus a live data ingest panel that summarizes every running dataset.

LinkNext steps

GPU starvation is one of several issues that make production training hard to debug, and the Ray team is continuing to build observability into Ray Train for the most common ones. Here's what we're working on next:

  • Automatic hang detection and stack trace capture. Ray Train will detect when training stops making progress and automatically capture stack traces from every worker, so you can see where each one is stuck without reproducing the hang.
  • Health monitoring. More extensive monitoring of training health, including hardware health checks, to surface the problems that slow down or stop production training runs.

If you run into a data ingest issue these tools don't cover, or have ideas for what we should build next, file an issue on GitHub.

Table of contents

  • Why GPU starvation is hard to catch
  • Data ingest metrics in open source Ray
  • Data ingest observability on Anyscale
  • Summary
  • Next steps

Sharing

item.title: [xAI Grok] Building an accounting team with Grok Bot
item.content:encoded:
Back to newsNov 16, 2026

Building an accounting team with Grok Bot

By Annay (Paul) Bains, Will Smerdon, and Erin Jenks

Five Grok Bots at SpaceXSI each own an accounting job end to end, from provisioning a customer account to collecting payment. They only involve a person when the work needs judgment.

Download for macOSContact sales

Most accounting teams organize their work around a set of well-defined jobs, from managing customer accounts to billing and collecting payments.

At SpaceXSI, we're starting to assign those jobs to Grok Bots. Each Bot takes responsibility for an entire process, working independently and involving us when it encounters something that requires human judgment or approval. They're allowing us to handle more work without increasing headcount at the same rate.

We've built five Team Bots, each with a carefully scoped responsibility:

  • Provisioning Bot checks contracts and sets up or closes customer accounts.
  • Billing Bot verifies contract details and generates invoices.
  • Billing Support Bot answers billing questions and takes action on requests from our go-to-market team, such as updating customer records or retrieving invoices.
  • Cash Applications Bot applies incoming payments, investigates discrepancies, writes off bank fees, and flags short payments for collections.
  • Collections Bot handles customer billing inquiries and coordinates requests such as refunds.

Setting them up has taught us a lot about what it takes to make Bots reliable enough to own important business processes. Here's how we've approached building our team and what each Bot does.

How we build and manage our accounting Bots

Our initial experiments with Grok Bot involved some trial and error as we figured out how best to organize the work. We eventually settled on assigning each Bot an existing well defined and scoped accounting process to own from beginning to end. Rather than asking a Bot to help with various tasks, we give it a specific job that a person on our team would otherwise perform.

One common misconception about AI agents is that they should be able to do a job as soon as you give them access to the right systems. In practice, we've found that Bots need the same investment in documentation, onboarding, and ongoing coaching as new employees.

That takes time upfront, but once trained, they can work around the clock and handle far more volume with greater accuracy than a person doing the same job. When we teach a Bot a new skill, it's like uploading a new capability that it can immediately put to work.

Build reliable processes before assigning them to Bots

A Bot will struggle to run a process that people haven't already figured out how to perform reliably. If the workflow is poorly defined or depends on undocumented knowledge, giving it to a Bot won't solve those problems.

For that reason, we've invested in building applications that make our accounting processes more structured. We use Grok Build to create applications with interfaces that define how a process works and what actions are permitted. This gives the Bot a controlled environment to work in, rather than leaving it to figure out how to perform each task from scratch.

For example, we built an internal provisioning application that provides a defined way to enable customer accounts, with controls on what actions can be taken. Our Provisioning Bot now operates that application. This gives us a reliable process with a logged audit trail of actions taken that both people and Bots can use.

Document each job as if you're onboarding an employee

We maintain a Notion document that serves as each Bot's operating manual. It contains the knowledge and instructions the Bot needs to do its job, from how to verify contract details before issuing an invoice to which billing adjustments require human approval.

Each night, the Bots consult these documents to refresh their knowledge and flag any discrepancies with their existing instructions. They cannot edit the documents themselves. Only the people responsible for each process have that permission.

When we change a policy or discover a better way to handle a transaction, we update the documentation and teach the Bot the new procedure. The people who know the job best remain responsible for defining how it gets done.

Give Bots clear permissions and approval requirements

Accounting processes require careful controls because they affect financial reporting and may be subject to audit requirements or control frameworks. Our Bots can read the information they need, but their ability to change records is more restricted.

Grok Bot can also connect securely to internal systems through integrations such as Tailscale. This allows Bots to access private tools and data without exposing those systems to the public internet. Companies can control which resources a Bot can access, with access policies tied to the identity of the person who authorized the connection.

We allow them to execute lower-risk tasks independently and require approval for sensitive actions such as issuing credits or refunds. We also control who can authorize those actions. For example, anyone with appropriate access can ask Billing Support Bot to explain an invoice, but only designated people can authorize changes to billing records.

Train Bots before letting them work independently

We train new Bots the same way we train new employees. We start by teaching them how the job works, then have them observe us performing the work before gradually giving them responsibility for completing tasks on their own. This gives us time to identify gaps in their knowledge and correct mistakes before they start working independently. Our typical onboarding process now takes about three weeks:

  • Week one: Build the Bot's knowledge base and have it observe how we perform the job.
  • Week two: Let the Bot propose actions and explain what it intends to do, with a person approving its work.
  • Week three: Allow the Bot to execute routine work independently and escalate exceptions.

Our first Bots took longer to develop. Billing Support Bot, for example, took four to five weeks to roll out. As we've learned how to structure the work, we've been able to build subsequent Bots much faster. We continue to coach them after launch, correcting mistakes and updating their instructions, while they handle work that would otherwise require several full-time employees.

Provisioning Bot sets up and closes customer accounts

Provisioning Bot makes sure customers receive the correct access to our products when they sign a contract, and that access is removed when their contract ends. It uses an internal application we built with Cursor to manage this process, which previously required someone on our team to handle manually.

When a deal closes, Provisioning Bot compares the executed contract against the corresponding CRM records. It checks that the order details match, then uses our provisioning application to enable the customer's account. Afterward, it verifies the entitlements against the contract and notifies the sales rep in Slack that provisioning is complete.

When a customer churns or a contract ends, the Bot also removes the corresponding entitlements. This helps us avoid provisioning errors that could leave customers without the access they've purchased or allow access to continue after a contract ends.

Billing Bot generates invoices and checks for errors

Billing Bot takes over once a customer account has been provisioned. It checks that the information in our billing system matches the terms of the executed contract before generating, and sending an invoice.

To do this, the Bot compares the contract against the customer records that flow from the CRM into our Billing System. If it finds a discrepancy, it corrects the information in the Billing System so invoicing can proceed and alerts the appropriate team to fix the underlying CRM record(s). It then sends the invoice and notifies the sales rep.

This has reduced the time required to issue an invoice from roughly 24 hours to minutes.

Billing Bot also checks for missing tax information. For example, if a customer hasn't provided a VAT or GST identification number, the Bot notifies the sales rep of the tax that will be assessed and gives them 24 hours to provide the missing information. Previously, we might have sent the invoice and resolved the issue only after the customer raised a question. Now we can address it before the invoice goes out.

The Bot can also handle credits and rebilling, subject to additional permissions and approvals.

Billing Support Bot answers questions from our go-to-market team

Billing Support Bot handles requests from our go-to-market team about customer billing. It connects to our core accounting systems, allowing sales reps to get answers and make routine updates without involving someone on our accounting team.

For example, a customer might notice that the usage shown on an invoice doesn't match their dashboard. Billing Support Bot can investigate the underlying records to explain why the two amounts differ.

The Bot can also take action directly. If a rep needs to update a customer's billing email or add additional recipients, they can ask the Bot in Slack. It verifies that the new addresses match the customer's domain, then updates the billing records automatically.

Previously, our team handled these requests one at a time, even when the underlying work was straightforward. Now the Bot can resolve many of them from start to finish. We estimate that Billing Support Bot has freed up approximately eight hours a day across our accounting team's work.

Cash Applications Bot reconciles customer payments

Cash Applications Bot reconciles incoming customer payments against outstanding invoices. Beyond matching payments automatically, it investigates discrepancies and handles routine adjustments that would otherwise require an accountant to intervene.

The Bot checks our payment feed twice daily and automatically applies payments that match outstanding invoices exactly. When a payment doesn't match, it searches our customer support system for remittance advice that can help identify which invoices the payment covers.

The Bot also automatically writes off bank fees that cause discrepancies between payment and invoice amounts. If a customer has paid less than they owe, it flags the short payment to our collections team for follow-up.

This process ordinarily takes an accountant three to four hours. The Bot completes it in roughly 30 minutes.

Collections Bot handles customer-facing billing inquiries

Collections Bot is our first accounting Bot to communicate directly with customers. It monitors our accounts receivable inbox, answers billing questions, and coordinates requests that require action from other Bots.

For example, if a customer requests a refund, Collections Bot works with Billing Bot and Cash Applications Bot to investigate the request and prepare the necessary actions. The Bots must obtain approval from an authorized person before processing the refund.

We spent approximately three months training Collections Bot because customer-facing communication introduces additional security requirements. In particular, the Bot must verify that someone requesting account information is authorized to receive it.

It does this by checking the sender's email address against approved contact information in the CRM and our billing system. A similar-looking email domain isn't sufficient. If the information doesn't match, the Bot escalates the inquiry to a person rather than release sensitive information.

Building toward an SI accounting team

Without Grok Bot, we estimate that the work we're assigning to these five Bots would require more than doubling the headcount on our team. Instead, we're building a team in which Bots handle routine processes and our accountants focus on managing the work, improving the systems, and resolving exceptions.

The biggest lesson from our experience is that building an effective AI team requires the same attention we'd give to building a human one. We need to define jobs clearly, document how they're performed, and invest in training. Once we've done that, we can give Bots responsibility for work that previously depended on people being available to do it.

Try Grok Bot today

Download for macOSContact sales

item.title: [Cohere] Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library…
item.description: Full title: Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library searchableIntroducing precise, timestamped video retrieval for enterprise search and AI agents.
item.content:encoded:
Nov 16, 2026

4 minute read

Video intelligence: Make every moment in your video library searchable

Introducing precise, timestamped video retrieval for enterprise search and AI agents.

Enterprises have vast amounts of valuable information locked inside recorded meetings, training videos and media archives. But unlike documents, video remains difficult for AI applications to search and use.

Today, we're introducing Video Intelligence in Compass, enabling AI applications and agents to search across video collections, find relevant moments and retrieve timestamped evidence alongside documents.

Compass understands both what's said and what's shown on screen. Instead of returning an hour-long recording, it retrieves the exact moment that answers a question, with a timestamped clip, transcript and visual description.

We're now recruiting design partners. Register your interest.

Search for moments, not just files

Consider the questions people actually ask of video:

  • When did the team agree to move the launch to Q3?
  • Where does the presenter explain revenue trends on the whiteboard?
  • When did a particular player get sent off during the game?

Answering them takes more than matching keywords in a transcript or scanning individual frames. It takes an understanding of what's said, what's shown and how events unfold over time. A single frame can show a player leaving the pitch, but only the sequence shows they were sent off. A presenter can describe improving KPIs while the chart on screen tells a different story.

Timing matters too. A clip that begins two minutes early, or cuts off before the answer, still leaves someone scrubbing through the footage.

Compass makes video searchable by meaning, context and precise moments in time.

From raw footage to discoverable intelligence

A single search returns the exact moment in a recording alongside the matching page, slide and sheet from related documents, all drawn from one index that respects what each user is allowed to see.

Finding the right moment in a video is only part of the challenge. AI applications also need to retrieve that information, verify its source and use it alongside other enterprise knowledge.

Compass brings video into the same retrieval system as documents, with the precision and controls needed for enterprise AI applications.

  • Precise moments, not predefined clips: Rather than relying on fixed video segments, Compass determines the relevant start and end times at search time, returning the moment that answers the question.
  • Video and documents in one search: Applications and AI agents can retrieve relevant footage alongside documents, bringing video into enterprise search, RAG and agentic workflows.
  • Evidence you can verify: Every result links back to the original footage, with timestamps, transcripts and visual descriptions so users can check the source.
  • Built for enterprise requirements: Permission-aware retrieval ensures users only access authorized content, while configurable fields, model choices and deployment options let organizations adapt the solution to their needs.

Connect your agent to the Compass MCP server so it can reason over what's shown on screen, such as slides, charts and demonstrations, not just what's said.

Unlock new applications for your video data

Compass makes video accessible to AI applications, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agentic search. By making spoken and visual content searchable alongside documents, Compass gives your applications and AI agents eyes and ears to reason over new modalities and use information that was previously difficult to access.

Meetings and enterprise knowledge: Build AI assistants that surface decisions, forecasts and commitments from recorded meetings, research presentations, earnings calls and analyst briefings. Find exactly when something was discussed and retrieve the relevant clip, rather than searching through hours of recordings.

Education and training: Help employees and learners find answers across recorded lectures, onboarding sessions and training libraries. Retrieve the precise explanation relevant to a question, making educational content easier to discover, reference and reuse.

Sports and media archives: Search large video libraries for specific plays, players, events, camera angles or visible brands. Accelerate highlight creation, footage discovery, content licensing and sponsor reporting without manually reviewing recordings.

Legal and compliance: Find statements, disclosures and other relevant moments across recorded footage. Retrieve timestamped clips with supporting transcripts and visual context, enabling reviewers to locate and verify information against the original source.

Video Intelligence turns recorded meetings into a searchable record of decisions, returning just the minute where something was agreed so anyone can check it against the source.

Strong retrieval performance across enterprise video

Good moment retrieval means finding the most relevant moments and identifying precisely where they start and end. We evaluated Compass against seven video embedding models across 11 datasets, including six public benchmarks and five internal enterprise video datasets.

Compass ranks first on average, with an nDCG@10 (how accurately the top ten search results are ranked) 4.4 points ahead of the strongest alternative. The lead holds up across all three domains, even as the strongest competitor rotates from one domain to the next:

  • Public benchmarks: 2.4 points ahead of Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, averaged across six widely used open-source moment and video retrieval benchmarks.
  • Sports: 5.1 points ahead of Gemini Embedding 2 on soccer broadcast footage, where queries look for specific players, teams, and plays.
  • Enterprise knowledge: 2.0 points ahead of Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B on business meetings, lectures, and workplace-safety training.

Cohere Video Intelligence ranks first across our evaluation suite. Scores are nDCG@10 over 11,133 queries across 11 datasets, including open-source public benchmarks (six datasets), enterprise knowledge (meetings, lectures and safety training; three datasets) and sports (two soccer broadcast datasets).

Build with Video Intelligence

We're inviting design partners to test and shape Video Intelligence using real-world workloads.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight…
item.description: Full title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Published November 16, 2026

Update on GitHub

42

Célina Hanouti

celinah

Victor Mustar

victor

Bertrand Chevrier

kramp

Lucain Pouget

Wauplin

Pierric Cistac

pierric

Eliott Coyac

coyotte508

Julien Chaumond

julien-c

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

Run them with the tools you already use

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

How open-weight models are used

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

Routing powered by OpenRouter

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

zai-org/GLM-5.3            # default: best mix of price, speed and reliability
zai-org/GLM-5.3:fastest    # highest throughput
zai-org/GLM-5.3:cheapest   # lowest price
zai-org/GLM-5.3:novita     # only Novita

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video and audio generation

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

See where your requests go

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Breaking change: custom provider keys

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

What's next

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

  • Connect your OpenRouter account to Hugging Face.
  • More tasks routed through OpenRouter.

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

item.title: [OpenRouter] OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face
item.content:encoded:
OpenRouter Now Powers Inference on Hugging Face

Sasha Blumenfeld ·11/16/2026

We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond. Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face. Chat models on Hugging Face Inference Providers now run through OpenRouter, with the same routing across providers that OpenRouter customers already rely on.

The integration also runs the other way. OpenRouter can now send a trace of each request to a Hugging Face Storage Bucket you own, so the prompts and responses from your real traffic sit next to the models and datasets you would use to evaluate or fine-tune on them. The setup guide has the steps.

What you get on Hugging Face

Many chat models on Hugging Face are served by more than one provider. OpenRouter’s provider routing now powers routing on Hugging Face Inference Providers, and it picks the provider for each request based on live price, speed, and reliability. You don’t have to set anything up, and your existing Hugging Face token and code keep working.

You also get automatic failover. If a provider slows down or starts failing, requests go to other providers until it recovers. If a provider returns an error, the request is retried on the next one inside the same call.

When we rebuilt this routing in October, a live experiment measured 46% fewer requests hitting a capacity error, 16.9% faster time to first token, and 16.3% higher throughput, for 6.0% higher cost per request. Everyone building on Hugging Face now gets the same routing.

You stay in control of the trade-off. Adding a suffix to the model ID, such as :fastest, :cheapest, or a provider name, tells OpenRouter what to prioritize, and requests work through OpenAI’s Chat Completions and Responses APIs or Anthropic’s Messages API. A conversation also stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache.

Each model page has a new Providers tab with live price, speed, and uptime for every provider. You can see your spend by provider and turn off any provider you don’t want to use.

160 models from 38 labs are available this way today, which is every model OpenRouter serves that has a page on the Hub. They include the open-weight models developers use most on OpenRouter, where open-weight models carried about 70% of paid tokens in October:

  • DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
  • MoonshotAI Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3
  • Z.ai GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash
  • Qwen3.8 27B
  • MiniMax M3.1 Flash
  • Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6-Flash
  • NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra
  • OpenAI gpt-oss-120b

Your traces can live on the Hub

Add Hugging Face Storage Buckets as a Broadcast destination (it’s in beta) and OpenRouter sends each request as a JSON file to a bucket you own. Each file holds the input messages, the model’s output, token counts, and cost. Images and other media are left out.

That’s the raw material for an evaluation set or a fine-tuning run on an open-weight model. You can organize the files by date or by API key.

Get started

On Hugging Face:

  • Create a token at hf.co/settings/tokens with the “Make calls to Inference Providers” permission.
  • Open any supported model’s page on the Hub. Chat with it there, or click View code for setup steps for your code or your coding agent, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Hermes Agent.
  • To choose which providers can serve your requests, go to Inference Providers in your Hugging Face settings.

To send traces to a Storage Bucket:

  • Create a Storage Bucket on Hugging Face.
  • Create an access token with Write permission and generate S3 credentials from it.
  • In OpenRouter, go to Settings > Observability, turn on Broadcast, and open Hugging Face Storage Buckets.
  • Enter your namespace, bucket name, access key ID, and secret access key. A path template such as {apiKeyName}/{date} is optional.
  • Click Test Connection, then save.

The full setup guide covers path templates and the trace file format.

Try a model in the Hugging Face Playground, or send your traces to a Storage Bucket.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Tighter Access Controls for Management Keys
item.content:encoded:
Tighter Access Controls for Management Keys

Sasha Blumenfeld ·11/16/2026

Management keys no longer have to come with full admin access to your whole organization. Now you can make a key read-only, limit it to one workspace, or both, so each key can only do the job it was created for. Read-only keys can view API keys, activity, and usage, and read/write keys can also create, update, and delete API keys. If a key leaks or gets misused, the damage stays contained.

Available today to every organization, on every plan. Create a key from your workspace’s Keys page or from Management API Keys, and see the management API keys guide for the routes each kind of key can call.

Teams run their own workspace, and now their automation can too

As organizations grow on OpenRouter, they split their work into workspaces, often one per team. Each team runs its own workspace, and Organization Admins look after what everyone shares: credits, budgets, and organization settings.

Until now, a management key always had full read and write access to the whole organization. A team that wanted to automate its own workspace had to use a key that could reach every other workspace too.

Now each key has two settings. Scope sets where a key works: one workspace, or the whole organization. Access level sets what it can do there: read only, or read and write. Workspace Admins can create keys for their own workspace, so a deploy pipeline can rotate a team’s API keys, an agent can set up guardrails, or a script can add teammates to the workspace, without any of them reaching another team’s workspace.

Scope keeps a key inside one workspace

A workspace-scoped key only works on its own workspace. If a request names another workspace, or a resource that belongs to one, OpenRouter refuses access. A buggy agent or a leaked key can’t reach the rest of your organization.

Inside its workspace, the key can manage API keys, members, guardrails and guardrail policies, your own provider keys, observability destinations, and presets. It can read the workspace’s budgets, activity, and analytics.

Budget limits, credits, and organization settings stay with your Organization Admins. A team can automate everything inside its workspace and still can’t raise its own workspace budget. Setting a workspace budget, creating or deleting workspaces, managing organization members, and private endpoints still need an organization key, which works the way it always has.

Read-only access lets tools look without changing anything

Access level is the second setting, and it applies to workspace keys and organization keys alike. A read-only key can call the read routes its scope allows, including analytics queries. Any request that would create, change, or delete something returns an error.

That fits the tools that only need to look. A cost dashboard can pull usage, a monitoring agent can watch activity, and an audit script can list keys, guardrails, and provider keys. You can connect a new reporting or audit tool without giving it write access to your account.

Give each job a key with only the access it needs

Scope and access level combine into four kinds of key:

  • An agent that creates and rotates API keys for one team gets a read/write key for that team’s workspace.
  • A usage dashboard for one team gets a read-only key for that team’s workspace.
  • An organization-wide audit or cost tool gets a read-only organization key.
  • Anything that creates workspaces or sets budget limits keeps a read/write organization key.

Both settings are fixed when you create a key, so a key can’t gain access later. To change either, create a new key and delete the old one.

Create a key in the dashboard

  • Open the workspace, go to Keys, and select the Management keys tab. Workspace Admins can create keys for their own workspace, and Organization Admins can create them for any workspace.
  • Click New management key. The dialog shows which workspace the key is scoped to.
  • Enter a name, choose an expiration, and pick Read only or Read and write under Access level.
  • Copy the key when it’s shown. You won’t see it again.

For a key that covers the whole organization, Organization Admins use the Management API Keys page.

Your agents and tools use the key the way they use a management key today, as a Bearer token on the management API:

curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MANAGEMENT_KEY"

To review the management keys you already have, open Security settings, go to Key safety, open Filter keys, and select Show management keys. Each active key is listed with its owner, last use, and expiration. The management API keys guide lists every route each kind of key can call.
