These are list prices; enterprise contracts are negotiated, and every row above machine translation includes human review or project management that our figure leaves out. The closest like-for-like option is Smartling’s machine translation, and our pipeline costs about 6% as much.

What you can reuse

If you are localizing your own product, four parts of this design carry over directly.

  • Fingerprint every translation against its English source, so stale entries requeue themselves.
  • Let code reject broken placeholders, plural branches, tags, and forbidden terms before any model reviews the meaning.
  • Use a verifier that names each error and its severity, and send those objections back to the translator.
  • Turn every mistake a person catches into a glossary rule, a style note, an override, or an eval case.

Send us your feedback

Some wording will be off while we’re in beta, and the quickest way to fix it is to report it with select-to-report in the Language dialog. We review every report and turn it into a glossary rule, a style note, or an override.

Frequently asked questions

Which languages does OpenRouter support?

OpenRouter is available in English, Simplified Chinese, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, German, French, Japanese, and Korean. Localization is in beta.

How do I change the language on OpenRouter?

Pick a language from the account menu, or open a localized address such as openrouter.ai/ja.

Which models translate OpenRouter?

GPT-6.1 Sol (openai/gpt-6.1-sol) translates each string, and a second call to the same model verifies it against the English. Both run through the OpenRouter API.

How much does it cost to translate the whole site?

A full retranslation of today's 16,918 strings into 7 languages costs about $460, translation and verification included, which is under half a cent per string per language. The same job costs about $7,200 at Smartling's published machine translation rate and about $57,300 to $191,000 at published AI and human translation rates.

How do I report a bad translation?

Turn on select-to-report in the Language dialog, highlight the text that reads wrong, add a note, and submit it.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Self-Hosted LLM vs API: When Does Self-Hosting Pay Off
item.content:encoded:
Self-Hosted LLM vs API: When Does Self-Hosting Pay Off

OpenRouter ·11/12/2026

If you pay an API bill for an open-weight model, you may wonder whether your own GPU would cost less. GPU rent is charged every hour, busy or idle, while an API charges only for the tokens you use.

A self-hosted LLM costs less only when your traffic keeps the GPU busy enough of the time. At October 8, 2026 prices, a 27B model on one rented RTX 3090 breaks even at about 12% load, while a large mixture-of-experts model on rented H200s never beats the cheapest zero-data-retention (ZDR) API endpoint.

This post works out the break-even with live per-provider prices from our API, then shows how our data controls cover privacy.

TL;DR

  • Break-even load is the GPU’s hourly rent divided by what the same hour of tokens would cost through the API. Below that load, the API is cheaper.
  • DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on four rented H200s never breaks even against the cheapest ZDR endpoint. On two B200s, it needs 76% load at the lowest rent we found.
  • At October 8 prices, Qwen3.8 27B on one RTX 3090 at $0.50 an hour breaks even at 6 to 12% load, but each user gets only about 15 tokens per second.
  • Published self-hosting costs of around a cent per million tokens mostly count cached input tokens, which are nearly free through the API too.
  • Most privacy requirements don’t need self-hosting. provider.zdr limits a request to zero-data-retention endpoints, and our EU and US domains keep requests in-region.

How do you work out whether self-hosting pays off?

Take one hour of a GPU’s time and price it two ways. On one side is the rent. On the other is what the API would charge for the tokens that GPU can serve in an hour, at a speed your users accept.

break-even load = GPU rent per hour / API cost of one fully loaded GPU-hour of tokens

A break-even of 30% means the GPU has to be busy for 30% of the hours you rent it before it costs less than the API. Anything above 100% means the API wins even if the GPU never rests.

Both sides have to be priced on the same token mix, because input, cached input and output tokens have very different API prices. We also left out engineering time and the spare capacity you’d keep for traffic peaks, so every break-even in this post is a lower bound.

What does the API cost for the same open-weight model?

Most open-weight models are served by many providers. Each one runs its own copy of the weights on its own hardware and sets its own price. Our endpoints API (GET /api/v1/models/{author}/{slug}/endpoints) returns every provider’s price and precision for a model, and GET /api/v1/endpoints/zdr lists the endpoints with a ZDR policy. As of October 8, 2026, they returned:

ModelEndpoints (ZDR)Input $/MCached input $/MOutput $/M
qwen/qwen3.8-27b18 (14)0.024 to 0.990.02 to 0.991.49 to 5.25
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash31 (24)0.016 to 0.450.0007 to 0.200.14 to 1.80

For the same weights, the most expensive provider charges 3.5 times the cheapest for Qwen3.8 27B output, and nearly 13 times for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. A break-even worked out against a single list price can be far off. Providers also serve different precisions, from fp4 to bf16, and our LLM quantization post measures how much that changes the answers.

What we paid for real workloads

Reasoning models spend output tokens thinking before they answer, and agents resend their whole context every turn. So we ran two workloads per model with ZDR enforced and priced each request with GET /api/v1/generation, which reports the tokens and cost the provider actually billed:

WorkloadModelRequestsInput tokens (% cached)Output tokens (% reasoning)CostPer 1M output tokens
Chat over a 5k-token documentDeepSeek V4.1 Flash1053,330 (68%)12,476 (97%)$0.0110$0.88
8-turn agent, 60k-token contextDeepSeek V4.1 Flash8504,747 (75%)28,509 (83%)$0.0243$0.85
Chat over a 5k-token documentQwen3.8 27B1072,329 (56%)25,084 (97%)$0.0694$2.77
7-turn agent, 85k-token contextQwen3.8 27B7595,223 (100%)81,870 (99%)$0.1900$2.32

The last column divides the full cost, input included, by the output tokens. Almost every output token was reasoning, and a self-hosted copy of the model would spend the same GPU time producing them. Qwen3.8 27B also hit our 16,000-token cap while still thinking on 3 of its 7 agent turns. Every API run for this post cost $0.49 in total.

What does a self-hosted LLM cost to run?

We didn’t rent these GPUs ourselves. The self-hosted side uses published benchmarks and rental prices, so treat each row as an assumption:

SetupThroughput per GPUSourceRent per GPU-hour
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 4x H200, vLLM fp4, 32 concurrent sessions35,084 input + 231 output tok/s, 95% of input cached, 71 tok/s per userInferenceX agentic traces, 2026-09-21$2.90 (InferenceX retail tier), $4.59 (RunPod)
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 2x B200, vLLM fp4, 32 concurrent sessions117,225 input + 683 output tok/s, 96% cached, 232 tok/s per userInferenceX, 2026-10-03$3.70 (InferenceX retail), $6.79 (RunPod), $6.89 (Lambda)
Qwen3.8 27B, 1x RTX 3090, vLLM W4A16, 64 concurrent942 output tok/s at 128 tokens in / 512 out, about 15 tok/s per userHyperQwen benchmarks$0.50 (RunPod), or about $0.05 in power for a card you own (250 W at the EIA July 2026 US residential rate)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has 552B backbone parameters, so it needs a multi-GPU node. Qwen3.8 27B is a dense model that fits on one 24 GB card at 4 bits.

Throughput is per GPU, the way InferenceX reports it, so every cost in this post is per GPU-hour. Per-user speed counts only the time a response is being generated, and these agentic sessions spend much of their time on prefill, so it doesn’t multiply out to the total. The 3090 figure comes from HyperQwen’s heavily patched vLLM build, so treat it as a best case.

We used its end-to-end figure, which includes prefill, rather than its 1,035 tok/s decode-only headline. HyperQwen benchmarked 128-token prompts, and our chat prompts are much longer, so for our chat mix we estimated 565 output tokens per second from its measured prefill and decode rates.

When does self-hosting pay off?

For each setup, we took the hour of tokens the benchmark measured, split it into uncached input, cached input and output, and priced that mix at every ZDR endpoint for the model, then divided the rent by the result. API prices are from October 8, 2026:

SetupRent per GPU-hourAPI cost of the same hour, cheapest ZDR / median ZDRBreak-even load vs cheapest ZDRBreak-even load vs median ZDR
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 4x H200$2.90$1.70 / $3.54never82%
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 4x H200$4.59$1.70 / $3.54nevernever
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 2x B200$3.70$4.87 / $9.9576%37%
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 2x B200$6.79$4.87 / $9.95never68%
Qwen3.8 27B, 1x RTX 3090, short prompts$0.50$5.89 / $8.358%6%
Qwen3.8 27B, 1x RTX 3090, our chat mix (estimated)$0.50$4.33 / $6.1412%8%
Qwen3.8 27B, own RTX 3090, power only$0.05$5.89 / $8.351%1%

“Never” means the rent is higher than the API cost even at 100% load. Prices move quickly. On October 19, a new ZDR endpoint for Qwen3.8 27B charged $0.50 per million output tokens, which moves the short-prompt break-even to about 29%.

Start from the load you actually have. Traffic that only arrives during working hours, 40 of the week’s 168 hours, keeps a GPU busy at most 24% of the time. At October 8 prices, that rules out every DeepSeek row and leaves the 3090. Against the October 19 endpoint, the 3090 would need about 29%, so check current prices before you buy. A batch pipeline running around the clock can reach 70%, which brings both B200 rows into range against the median ZDR price, but neither against the cheapest.

In monthly terms, the rented 3090 costs $365 and pays for itself after about 170 million output tokens of our chat mix. The two-B200 node costs $5,402 a month at retail rent and has to serve 2.7 billion output tokens before it beats the cheapest ZDR endpoint.

The small model comes out ahead because its API prices are high compared with the hardware it needs. Providers charge $1.49 to $5.25 per million output tokens for Qwen3.8 27B, and a $0.50-an-hour card produces about 3.4 million of them an hour. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is the opposite case. Twenty-four ZDR endpoints compete for its traffic, and the cheapest charges $0.18 per million output tokens.

The 3090’s low cost comes with a speed trade-off. It reaches that throughput by serving 64 requests at once, at about 15 tokens per second each. That’s slow for a chat interface, and slower still for a reasoning model that writes thousands of hidden tokens before its answer. Across the 18 API endpoints for Qwen3.8 27B, the median ran at 45 tokens per second in the 30 minutes before our pull, and the fastest at 474.

Why do published self-hosting costs look so low?

If you’ve seen self-hosting quoted at around a cent per million tokens, the token mix is usually the reason. InferenceX puts DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on H200 at $0.012 per million tokens at hyperscaler pricing. That figure is per million total tokens, and in its agentic workload, 99% of tokens are input, 95% of them served from the prefix cache. Through the API, cached input for that model costs $0.0007 to $0.20 per million, so those tokens are cheap either way.

Priced per output token, the same H200 at the $2.90 retail rent costs $3.49 per million before any input is counted. The cheapest ZDR endpoint charges $0.18.

Do you need to self-host for privacy?

Privacy is the other common reason to self-host, and you can get most of it through the API. Setting provider.zdr on a request limits it to endpoints whose providers don’t store your prompts or completions. If your ZDR setting also allows Safety Retention endpoints, those may keep prompts and responses to detect abuse, so choose ZDR only when you need no retention at all. Providers with implicit caching may also hold derived KV-cache data for a short time, as our implicit caching explainer describes. You can also enforce ZDR account-wide, per model group, or in a guardrail that covers specific API keys. On the Business and Enterprise plans, requests sent to eu.openrouter.ai or us.openrouter.ai run only on endpoints in that region, and they fail rather than leave it.

This script tries both, including two requests we expected to fail:

"""The privacy paths: ZDR per request, a ZDR conflict, and EU in-region routing."""
import os

import requests

KEY = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['OPENROUTER_API_KEY']}"}
MSG = [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the word ok."}]

def ask(base, model, provider=None):
    body = {"model": model, "messages": MSG, "max_tokens": 400, "provider": provider or {}}
    r = requests.post(f"{base}/api/v1/chat/completions", json=body, headers=KEY, timeout=120)
    data = r.json()
    if r.status_code == 200:
        return f"{r.status_code} served by {data['provider']}"
    return f"{r.status_code} {data['error']['message']}"

GLOBAL, EU = "https://openrouter.ai", "https://eu.openrouter.ai"

print("1. ZDR on, any provider:     ", ask(GLOBAL, "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash", {"zdr": True}))
print("2. ZDR on, only DeepSeek API:", ask(GLOBAL, "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash", {"zdr": True, "only": ["deepseek"]}))
print("3. EU domain, DeepSeek:      ", ask(EU, "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash"))
print("4. EU domain, GLM 5.3 + ZDR: ", ask(EU, "z-ai/glm-5.3", {"zdr": True}))

eu_models = requests.get(f"{GLOBAL}/api/v1/models", params={"region": "eu"}, timeout=60).json()["data"]
print(f"5. models eligible for EU in-region routing: {len(eu_models)}")

Output recorded October 8, 2026:

1. ZDR on, any provider:      200 served by Decart
2. ZDR on, only DeepSeek API: 404 No endpoints found matching your data policy (Zero data retention). Configure: https://openrouter.ai/settings/privacy
3. EU domain, DeepSeek:       404 No endpoints found supporting your data region.
4. EU domain, GLM 5.3 + ZDR:  200 served by Inceptron
5. models eligible for EU in-region routing: 72

Both filters run before we pick a provider, so they shrink the list of candidate endpoints instead of rerouting after the fact. With zdr on, DeepSeek’s own API drops out because it retains data. Pinning the request to that provider with only leaves no endpoint at all, which returns the first 404. The EU domain keeps only endpoints we’ve onboarded in Europe. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash had none, so the third request failed instead of quietly going to the US. To use EU routing, pick a model with EU endpoints from GET /api/v1/models?region=eu, which listed 72 models, including GLM 5.3.

ZDR has one limit. Your prompts are still processed on a provider’s GPU, so it doesn’t give you control of the hardware. If your policy requires the model to run on a deployment you control, Private Endpoints (Enterprise plan) add your own dedicated or fine-tuned deployment to a catalog model’s provider list. It must be hosted with a provider we support for BYOK, your team calls it with the same slug, and public endpoints stay available as fallbacks if you list them. If data must never leave hardware you operate, self-host and size the hardware from the break-even table above. Our ZDR explainer and data residency guide compare the options in more detail.

Can you self-host and use the API together?

Yes, and for most teams the break-even table points to this setup. A GPU only pays off at high load, so size your own for the steady base of your traffic, where it stays busy, and send the peaks to the API, where you pay only for what you use.

This works because vLLM and SGLang expose the same OpenAI-compatible chat API we do. A client moves between them by changing the base URL, key and model name. Fall back to the API on a connection error, or on the 429 or 503 your server returns when its queue is full. Set provider.zdr on the API side so overflow traffic keeps zero data retention. If your policy requires prompts to stay on hardware you control, don’t overflow to the API.

Two things can go wrong with this setup. If your local copy runs at a different precision from the API endpoint, the same prompt can get different answers, so pin the API side to a matching quantization with provider routing. And a conversation that switches backends partway through loses its prompt cache, so keep each conversation on one side once it starts.

Frequently asked questions

Is self-hosting an LLM worth it?

For cost alone, only if you can keep the GPU busy. In our numbers, Qwen3.8 27B on a rented RTX 3090 breaks even at 6 to 12% load. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on rented data-center GPUs needs 37% load or more, and against the cheapest zero data retention endpoint it often never breaks even. Privacy and control can justify self-hosting at any load.

Which LLM is best for self-hosting?

Models that fit on one GPU are the best fit, because they avoid multi-GPU servers and their API prices leave the most room to save. Qwen3.8 27B, for example, runs on one 24 GB card at 4 bits. Our rankings and the open-weight vs closed-weight comparison show which models developers use most.

What is the cheapest self-hosted LLM option?

A GPU you already own. An RTX 3090 limited to 250 W costs about $0.05 an hour in electricity at the July 2026 US residential average, so it beats the cheapest zero data retention endpoint for Qwen3.8 27B once it’s busy about 1% of the time. The trade-offs are slower responses for each user and your own time spent on maintenance.

Can I host my own model and still use it through OpenRouter?

Yes, on the Enterprise plan. Private Endpoints route a catalog model’s slug to your own dedicated or fine-tuned deployment, hosted with a provider we support for BYOK. Only the users and organizations you approve can see or call it.

Next steps

  • Zero Data Retention: enforce ZDR per request, per model group, in a guardrail or account-wide.
  • In-Region Routing: send requests through the EU and US domains, and enforce a region with a guardrail.
  • The model pages for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8 27B list current per-provider prices and throughput.

item.title: [Anyscale] Real-time inference for JEPA world model architectures with…
item.description: Full title: Real-time inference for JEPA world model architectures with Ray
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Real-time inference for JEPA world model architectures with Ray

By Omar Shorbaji and Ian Jordan, PhD | November 12, 2026

With V-JEPA2-AC the system decides what a robot arm should do next by assessing hundreds of possible futures and picking the one closest to the goal. It takes a significant amount of time between moves. This document presents a design and tested implementation for getting that under a second by moving the search into a Ray cluster.

Link01 · A Primer on Robotics

A robot perceives a partial observation of the environment, selects an action via some policy, executes it through a controller, and repeats this at control-loop frequency. Classically, each of those three functions is solved in closed form, and a CPU on the robot is enough to run all of them.

Classical robotics built each of those three boxes from first principles: hand-derived kinematics for perception, trajectory optimization for planning, PID or model-predictive controllers for control. This approach, depicted in Figure 1, underlies decades of industrial automation, but every new task, object, or environment typically requires new engineering.

Classical robotics — ~1 ms / action

Figure 1. The loop every robot runs. Perception turns sensor readings into state, planning produces a path, control executes it, and the arm closes the loop through the physical world. All three are solved in closed form on one on-board CPU. What it costs is engineering: the policy only covers the task it was derived for.

Figure 1. The loop every robot runs

Physical AI aims to replace some or all of those boxes with networks trained on data, trading hand-derived precision for generality: a model trained on sufficient data transfers to situations not explicitly programmed for.

LinkHow the JEPA architecture fills the "plan" box

V-JEPA2-AC is one such model. It is built on the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA). In this architecture, the system decides what a robot arm should do next by assessing hundreds of possible futures using the model and picking the one closest to the goal. Figure 2 shows the whole loop in place on the hardware that runs it.

Deployed zero-shot on Franka arms in two labs, with no fine-tuning for the specific environment, V-JEPA2-AC reports 65–80% success on pick-and-place with novel objects. This ran on a single RTX 4090. However, that configuration takes 16 seconds to plan every single action. It is not fast enough to run continuously.

LinkWhere the sixteen seconds actually goes

It is worth walking one planning step end to end, because the arithmetic explains the rest of this document. The arm holds still. The camera frame and the goal image are encoded once. The search algorithm, CEM, then draws 800 candidate action sequences from a Gaussian centered on its current best guess, pushes every one through the predictor, scores the results against the goal embedding, keeps the best 80, and re-centers the Gaussian on them. That is one round, and it happens ten times: roughly 8,000 predictor evaluations for one small movement of one arm. The system then executes only the first action of the winning sequence, throws the rest away, and starts over from a fresh frame. The cost is structural, and it recurs at every step.

V-JEPA2-AC on one on-board GPU — 16 s / action

Figure 2. Only the plan box changes. The robot still captures a camera frame and its joint state, and control is untouched, but the closed-form planner is replaced by the model and a search around it. The encoder is part of the model, so encoding happens here, once per step; the ten-round loop that follows is the expensive part.

Figure 2. Only the plan box changes

The controller is also blocking: it waits for the previous action to complete before sending the next, so planning never overlaps with motion. The robot pauses, plans for sixteen seconds, moves, and pauses again. That stutter, not the model's accuracy, is the problem this document sets out to fix.

Link02 · The Approach

We take the approach of, first, moving world model inference off the robot and into a cloud server. While this introduces the new cost of a network round trip on every control step, that is offset by other improvements. First, it opens the opportunity of serving the model on a more powerful GPU. In this implementation we use NVIDIA A100-40GB GPUs, which have more memory than the 24 GB RTX 4090 used in the paper and substantially more bf16 throughput.

The same search on one cloud GPU — 21.4 s / action (measured, A100, optimized model)

Figure 3. The plan block lifts the inference off the robot. What stays local is sensing and actuation, so what crosses the network is one camera frame plus its joint state, and one action vector back.

Figure 3. The plan block lifts the inference off the robot

On its own, a bigger GPU is not enough. Meta's reference planner, run unmodified on one A100 with these settings, takes 81.8 s per action; with the model-level optimizations in Section 05 it takes 21.4 s. Our 81.8 s is slower than the paper's 16 s on a 4090 because we ran Meta's released planning code as-is (fp32, 800 candidates × 10 rounds, a two-step horizon); the paper's timing likely reflects different settings or precision. Every speedup in this post is measured against our own 81.8 s baseline on the same hardware. Faster, but the arm still stops between moves.

The second step is to distribute the load across multiple GPUs. The opportunity comes from noting that within a single CEM refinement round rollouts can be computed independently and gathered before the round moves on. The paper runs them as one large batch on one GPU; nothing requires them to stay on one GPU. In our implementation we use one eight-GPU node (8× A100-40GB) on Anyscale.

The search distributed across a Ray cluster — 2.86 s / action (measured, 8× A100); 0.86 s with 3 rounds per step

Figure 4. One step inside the plan block changes. The 800 candidates in a round are independent, so the predict step fans out across warm replicas that already hold the model and gathers before scoring. The ten rounds are still sequential, which is what sets the floor.

Figure 4. One step inside the plan block changes

We implement this using Ray.

Link03 · A Primer on Ray

LinkA general framework for turning Python into a cluster program

Ray is an open-source framework, originally built at UC Berkeley's RISELab and now maintained by Anyscale, for scaling ordinary Python from a laptop to a cluster without rewriting it as a distributed system. It exposes a small set of primitives and preserves mostly-sequential code structure.

LinkRay Core

Ray Core has two building blocks that matter here. A @ray.remote function becomes a task, scheduled somewhere in the cluster and returning a future. A @ray.remote class becomes an actor: a stateful worker pinned to a machine, and optionally a GPU, that keeps loaded model weights resident between calls. Tasks suit one-off parallel work; actors suit a process that pays to load a 1.2-billion-parameter checkpoint once and then answers many cheap requests.

LinkRay Serve

Ray Serve sits on top of Ray Core: a @serve.deployment declaration is enough for Ray to manage a pool of replicas, route requests, and scale under load. Ray Core answers how to run a function on many workers; Ray Serve answers how to expose it as a service other systems call, which is the shape a robot's control loop needs, a low-latency endpoint hit once per step.

Link04 · Implementation

LinkTwo Ray Serve deployments, composed

The design is two Ray Serve deployments and a handle between them. WorldModel is the GPU tier: one replica per GPU, each holding the encoder and predictor (we ran 8 replicas on 8 A100s). Planner is the driver: it runs the ten-round CEM loop, fans each round out across those replicas, and serves the endpoint the robot calls once per control step. Composing them this way, rather than as loose Ray Core actors, puts them under Serve's control: placement, health checks, restarts, and a declarative config a KubeRay RayService can roll out without downtime. The shape below elides the internals; what matters is where the fan-out sits. See figure 5 for a diagram of the deployment layout.

serve_app.py — Ray Serve · the shape, details elided

from ray import serve
Import ray
from ray.serve.handle import DeploymentHandle

# The GPU tier. One replica per GPU, pinned, weights resident between calls.
@serve.deployment(
    num_replicas=8,  # one per GPU
    ray_actor_options={"num_gpus": 1},
    max_ongoing_requests=1,          # one shard at a time, so fan-out maps 1:1
)
class WorldModel:
    def __init__(self, checkpoint): ...        # paid once, when Serve starts it
    def encode(self, frame, proprio): ...      # the encoder is part of the model
    def score(self, ctx, actions): ...   # one shard, one GPU batch

# The driver. Holds a handle to the GPU tier and runs the search.
@serve.deployment(num_replicas=2)
@serve.ingress(app)
class Planner:
    def __init__(self, model: DeploymentHandle):
        self.model = model

    @app.post("/plan")
    async def plan(self, frame, proprio, goal_image):
        obs, goal = await asyncio.gather(      # encode once per control step
            self.model.encode.remote(frame, proprio),
            self.model.encode.remote(goal_image),
        )
  ctx = ray.put((obs, goal))  # once per plan, read from shared memory
        mean, std = init_distribution(horizon, action_dim)

        for _ in range(10):                    # CEM rounds: sequential, the floor
            cands = sample(mean, std, n=800)
            scores = await asyncio.gather(*[   # fan out one shard per replica
                self.model.score.remote(ctx, shard)
                for shard in np.array_split(cands, 8)
            ])                                 # gather before the round refits
            mean, std = refit(cands, scores, elite_frac=0.1)

        return {"action": mean[0].tolist()}    # first action only, then re-plan

app_builder = Planner.bind(WorldModel.bind(CHECKPOINT))

Two choices carry the design. The GPU tier is pinned at num_replicas=8 rather than autoscaled, because a search whose replica count changes mid-round has unpredictable latency, and the point is a stable per-step budget. max_ongoing_requests=1 makes each replica take one shard at a time, so an 8-way fan-out lands one shard per GPU instead of queueing several on a subset. Underneath, each replica is still a Ray Core actor, which is why the weights stay resident; the difference is that Serve owns the lifecycle.

Figure 5: Ray Serve on Anyscale connects the robot-facing Planner deployment to warm WorldModel replicas through a DeploymentHandle, with one model

Figure 5 Ray Serve on Anyscale connects the robot-facing Planner deployment to warm WorldModel replicas through a DeploymentHandle, with one model

What we learned building it. Three details decided the latency. First, the observation and goal latents (2.8 MB) go into Ray's object store once per plan with ray.put; every replica reads them from shared memory and caches them on its GPU, so each round moves only about 5 KB of candidate actions out and the energies back, and Ray's whole share of a round (fan-out, gather, refit) is under 10 ms. Second, with max_ongoing_requests=1 Serve's default power-of-two-choices router occasionally placed two shards on one replica while another sat idle, doubling that round; Serve's round-robin request router lands the shards of a round on consecutive replicas, one per GPU (zero collisions in 50 rounds). Third, our Serve replica processes started with TORCHDYNAMO_DISABLE=1 in their environment, which silently turned torch.compile into a no-op; clearing it in the replica's constructor recovered a 1.35× speedup.

Source. The full implementation, including model loading, the fast scoring path, the complete CEM refinement step, the two Serve deployments, every benchmark script and a runnable notebook, lives in the companion repository: https://github.com/anyscale/robotics_world_model_inference/tree/main/v3_realtime_inference_for_jepa

Link05 · Results

LinkMeasured on 8× A100

We built the design above and measured it on one Anyscale node with eight A100-40GB GPUs, using the search settings from Section 01 (800 candidates × 10 rounds, keep 80, horizon 2). The anchor is Meta's reference planner, run unmodified in fp32 on one A100: 81.8 s per action. Before adding GPUs we made the model itself faster on one GPU: a KV cache across rollout steps (the predictor is frame-causal, so earlier frames never need recomputing), bf16 with FlashAttention, and torch.compile. The result matches the reference energies (Pearson r = 0.9999) and brings one GPU to 21.4 s per action, 4× faster.

Figure 6. Measured planning time per action. Ray Serve fans each round out over 8 A100s (2.86 s, 29× the reference). Running 3 search rounds per step instead of 10 reached the same accuracy in closed-loop tests (Section 06), giving 0.86 s per action, 96× the reference.

Figure 6. Measured planning time per action

Then the fan-out. Each round's 800 candidates are split across W WorldModel replicas, one GPU each. Going from 1 to 8 GPUs cuts a plan from 21.4 s to 2.86 s, a 7.5× speedup. Same seeds give identical plans at every GPU count, so sharding changes the speed of the search but not its answer. The latency model proposed in the first draft of this post holds up: calibrated on our measured single-GPU round (2.14 s), it predicts 2.94 s at 8 GPUs against 2.86 s measured.

LinkPlanning latency vs. cluster size

A100-40GB replicas on one 8-GPU node. Points are measured; the line is the latency model.

2.86 s / action at 8 A100 workers. This is 7.5× faster than one A100 and 29× faster than Meta's reference planner.

Figure 7. Plan latency vs. number of GPU replicas, measured on 8× A100 (points) against the latency model calibrated on the measured single-GPU round (line; dashed beyond 8 GPUs = projection).

Figure 7. Plan latency vs. number of GPU replicas

Model: time(W) = 10 × ( r / effective(W) + 0.001s × (W − 1) ), where effective(W) = W / (1 + 0.008×(W−1)) and r is the measured single-GPU round, 2.14 s on an A100. Beyond 8 GPUs the curve flattens, because each GPU's share of the 800 candidates gets small. Larger clusters pay off mainly by serving more robots, or larger searches, from the same tier.

Two things remain unmeasured: network latency between an on-premises robot and a cloud region, and performance on a physical arm (our closed-loop tests use the world model as the simulator). Cold start stays off the request path: replicas load and compile in about 50 s at deploy time, before they take traffic. Batching candidates differently does not change accuracy: the plans are identical at 1, 2, 4 and 8 GPUs.

Link06 · Further Optimization

LinkWhat to try once the search itself is no longer the bottleneck

Once each round is as fast as the GPUs allow, what remains is the chain of ten sequential rounds, and the next gains come from restructuring the loop rather than adding GPUs.

LinkA. Non-blocking control

Start planning step t+1 while the robot is still executing step t. That hides planning latency behind execution time instead of adding to it, and it is a controller change, not a model change.

Measured. We simulated an arm that takes 1 s per action and lands with 4 mm of execution error. A blocking controller spent 1.86 s per step (plan, then move). Non-blocking control, planning step t+1 from the world model's prediction of where step t will land, spent 1.04 s per step, i.e. the motion itself plus 40 ms. It reached the same final accuracy, and a 12-step episode took 15.3 s instead of 25.3 s.

Figure 8. Closed-loop episodes toward a goal 21.6 cm away, with the world model standing in for the robot. Left: 3 search rounds per step reach the same accuracy as 10 in a third of the planning time. Right: non-blocking control removes the planner from the robot's critical path.

Figure 8. Closed-loop episodes toward a goal 21.6 cm away

LinkB. Warm-started CEM

Receding-horizon control throws away everything but the first action. Re-using the rest to seed the next step's distribution, instead of a fresh Gaussian, lets each replan converge in fewer than ten rounds, shrinking the sequential chain parallelism cannot touch.

Measured. In closed-loop tests, 3 rounds per step (0.86 s on 8 A100s) reached the same accuracy as the full 10 (2.83 s): both settle about 4 cm from a goal that starts 21.6 cm away. Warm-starting from the previous plan worked, but on this task a fresh 3-round search did equally well, so the gain came from running fewer rounds. How many rounds a task needs is worth tuning per task.

LinkC. Fleet-level batching

A GPU tier sized for one robot is idle between its requests. Behind a Serve endpoint the same tier serves a fleet, and request batching can pack shards from different robots into one GPU batch, amortizing the same warm GPUs across many arms.

LinkD. Model compression

Distilling or quantizing the predictor shrinks the compute term itself, independent of how many workers it is split across. It stacks with distribution rather than competing with it.

LinkE. Serving-level optimization

The predictor rolls forward step by step over the horizon, so what LLM serving already relies on carries over: KV caching across rollout steps, prefill and decode disaggregation, continuous batching. These shrink the same compute term from a different direction, inside the same Serve deployment.

Implemented. KV caching across rollout steps, together with bf16, FlashAttention and torch.compile, is part of the measured system. It gives 4× on a single GPU and matches the reference energies to r = 0.9999.

Link07 · Takeaways

The sixteen seconds is not an implementation defect. It follows from a deliberate architectural choice: a JEPA model predicts state rather than actions, so an action has to be searched for at inference time instead of read off a policy head. That is the same trade agentic systems make when they sample many candidates and score them, and it comes with the same benefit, a system that can be pointed at a new goal without retraining.

The four setups make the trade concrete. A hand-written policy buys millisecond actions and pays for them in task-specific engineering. V-JEPA2-AC trades that speed for a system that accepts any goal you can photograph. Moving the search to a cluster buys the speed back without giving up the generality, and does it in infrastructure rather than in the model. Measured on one node of eight A100s, Ray Serve takes the full search from 82 s to 2.9 s per action, with distribution doing most of the work and Ray adding under 10 ms per round. The ten sequential rounds set the floor that more hardware cannot move. Attacking that floor with fewer rounds per step brings it to 0.86 s, and non-blocking control hides what remains behind the arm's own motion.

LinkReferences

  • Assran, M. et al. V-JEPA 2: Self-Supervised Video Models Enable Understanding, Prediction and Planning. arXiv:2506.09985, 2025. arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985
  • Meta AI. Introducing the V-JEPA 2 world model and new benchmarks for physical reasoning. ai.meta.com/blog/v-jepa-2-world-model-benchmarks
  • Ray Project. Ray Core: Key Concepts, Tasks and Actors. docs.ray.io/en/latest/ray-core
  • Ray Project. Ray Serve documentation. docs.ray.io/en/latest/serve
  • Ray Project. KubeRay: RayService. docs.ray.io/en/latest/cluster/kubernetes

Planning-time and success-rate figures are as reported in the V-JEPA2-AC paper (arXiv:2506.09985). Cluster sizing, the CEM parallelization design, the latency model, and all code shown are an independent engineering implementation built on top of that published work, not affiliated with or endorsed by Meta AI or the Ray project. Latency measurements in Sections 05 and 06 were taken on one 8× A100-40GB node on Anyscale (November 2026); the extension of Figure 6 beyond 8 GPUs is a projection.

Table of contents

  • 01 · A Primer on Robotics
  • How the JEPA architecture fills the "plan" box
  • Where the sixteen seconds actually goes
  • 02 · The Approach
  • 03 · A Primer on Ray
  • A general framework for turning Python into a cluster program
  • Ray Core
  • Ray Serve
  • 04 · Implementation
  • Two Ray Serve deployments, composed
  • 05 · Results
  • Measured on 8× A100
  • Planning latency vs. cluster size
  • 06 · Further Optimization
  • What to try once the search itself is no longer the bottleneck
  • 07 · Takeaways
  • References

item.title: [xAI Grok] Introducing Grok Bot 1.0
item.content:encoded:
Back to newsNov 2, 2026

Introducing Grok Bot 1.0

Bots now work with your whole team, take on work without being asked, and get more done, faster.

Download for macOSContact sales

0:00 / 0:00

Today we’re launching Grok Bot 1.0, a major update to our AI teammates. Since introducing Grok Bot in beta, we’ve made three major improvements:

  • Multiplayer teammates. You can share Bots and bring them into Slack, Microsoft Teams, and video calls. Bots learn from everyone they work with and keep improving their understanding of the team’s knowledge and preferences.
  • Proactive teammates. Bots can recognize work that needs to be done and offer to take it on. They can follow up on unfinished tasks, anticipate what a team needs next, and bring people in when a decision requires their judgment.
  • More capable teammates. Bots are faster and more reliable at using the browser and completing complex work, including writing documents and building presentations. We’ve also made them more efficient, reducing the resources required to complete tasks.

Grok Bot began as a way to hand off work to an AI teammate. With 1.0, those teammates understand the work your team is doing and the people doing it, so they can contribute like any other colleague.

Bots work together alongside your team

With Team Bots, everyone on a team can work with the same AI teammate. Since we launched Team Bots, we’ve made a number of improvements to make them easier to share and manage. As a Bot works with different people, it learns more about the team’s work and how each person contributes, becoming more useful to everyone over time. Sharing is more flexible too. Share a Team Bot with specific people or groups, and work with it in Slack or Microsoft Teams.

In conversations, Bots can follow discussions involving multiple people, understand who’s involved, and contribute relevant information or offer to pick up work. During a product launch, for example, a Bot might notice that new customer research points to a different message than the team is considering. It can bring that into the discussion, then coordinate with another Bot to update campaign materials once the team agrees on a direction.

Bots can also join video calls and participate through the chat, bringing information from earlier conversations into the discussion. They keep track of decisions and learn more about the team’s work, allowing them to become more useful over time.

Bots take initiative

Grok Bot can spot work before anyone asks. It can monitor ongoing projects, recognize when something needs attention, and suggest next steps based on what it knows about the team’s goals, processes, and priorities.

For example, a Bot helping with a product launch might notice an upcoming deadline and prepare the materials the team needs. It can also follow up on unfinished work, coordinate with other Bots, and bring people in when a decision requires their judgment.

Bots learn and improve as they work

As people work with a Team Bot, it builds an understanding of how the team operates. It learns individual preferences, remembers decisions, and draws on the expertise of different team members. When someone teaches a Bot a better way to complete a task, that improvement can benefit everyone who uses it. Bots can also suggest changes to how they work based on what they learn from the team.

We’ve also added safeguards for working in shared spaces. Bots respect each person’s permissions, ask before taking sensitive actions, and check whether information is appropriate to share in a public channel. This allows teams to give Bots more responsibility while maintaining control over what they can access and do.

Bots are smarter, faster, and more capable

Beyond the changes to how Bots work with teams, we’ve continued improving the overall Bot experience. Some of the biggest changes since beta include:

  • Better browser use. Bots navigate websites more reliably, handle sign-ins more smoothly, and complete tasks with fewer interruptions.
  • Stronger writing and presentations. Bots produce better documents and slide decks, and can now create interactive Pages that you can edit together or ask them to keep updated.
  • More ways to work across apps. Bots have improved connections to tools like Gmail, Google Calendar, and GitHub, allowing them to complete more work directly.
  • Smarter approvals. Bots better understand when you’ve already authorized an action and when they need to ask, reducing unnecessary interruptions while protecting sensitive information.
  • New Bot settings and analytics. Manage what a Team Bot knows and see how your team uses it.

Get started with Grok Bot 1.0

Grok Bot 1.0 is available starting today. You can create a Bot for yourself, share it with your team, or bring it into Slack, Microsoft Teams, and your video calls.

Team Bots are available on Team and Enterprise plans. Meetings are available on Team, Enterprise, and Ultra plans. Enterprise admins can turn on Meetings in settings.

We’re excited to see what you build with your new teammates.

Try Grok Bot today

Download for macOSContact sales

item.title: [Hugging Face] BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Para…
item.description: Full title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

Team Article

Published November 11, 2026

2

Milan Gritta

milangritta

qvac

Jihye Back

happy-jihye

qvac

JinUk, Cho

jucho2725

qvac

ohjoon kwon

joooon

qvac

Patrik Lambert

patrik-lambert

qvac

Mathias Buus

mafintosh

qvac

Amril Nurman

Nurman

qvac

Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)

Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead.

Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages.

Copyright Complaints

We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement.

Key Highlights

Benchmark results

  • Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets).
  • Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus.
  • Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5).

Model capabilities

  • More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9).
  • Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model.
  • Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested.

Safety, efficiency and deployment

  • Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%.
  • More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device.
  • Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp.

Broader Vision

Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives.

Methodology

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: BotPsy training recipe. The student goes through four stages. Three specialist Qwen3.5-4B teachers, each RL-trained for one skill, guide it during the distillation stage.

Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT)

We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Learning from teachers (MOPD)

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Figure 4: Mean score of each capability group after each training stage. SFT boosts tool use but pushes knowledge and instruction following below the base model; distillation brings both back above base, and the RL stages add further gains on all three.

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Data composition

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

Figure 5: Approximate training-data composition per stage, grouped by capability.

Results

Tool use & agents

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

BenchmarkBotPsy-0.8B oursQwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1×Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5×LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5×MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25×
BFCL v4¹44.023.437.728.122.8
ACEBench²58.730.155.439.424.5
τ-bench³51.523.246.56.528.8
Claw-Eval⁴46.539.348.931.631.0
BrowseComp-Plus⁵4.51.92.80.20.8
ToolSandbox⁶64.630.541.245.728.1
Average45.024.738.825.322.7

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Knowledge

Tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

BenchmarkBotPsy-0.8B oursQwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1×Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5×LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5×MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25×
GPQA Diamond⁷38.133.259.935.015.8
MMLU-Pro⁸48.941.665.539.440.0

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Instruction following

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

BenchmarkBotPsy-0.8B oursQwen3.5-0.8B-Think base · 1×Qwen3.5-2B-Think 2.5×LFM2.5-1.2B-Think 1.5×MiniCPM5-1B-Think 1.25×
IFEval⁹90.859.780.085.678.4
IFBench⁹55.922.040.933.940.6
Multi-IF¹⁰67.243.266.968.253.4

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Multi-turn conversations

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

Figure 6: Multi-turn agentic tasks: BFCL v4 multi-turn, ACEBench Agent, τ²-bench (retail, telecom) and τ³-bench (banking). BotPsy leads four of the five benchmarks; on τ³-banking, every model stays below 5.

Weak spots

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

Where it works: app-level performance breakdown

BotPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Single tool calls work well everywhere

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

Figure 7: Mean per-scenario score (0–100, higher is better) by app group, for simple (left) and complex (right) scenarios. n gives the number of simple / complex scenarios in each group; the bottom row is the unweighted mean of the seven groups.

The largest gains are in multi-step tasks

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Multi-step information retrieval is the weak spot

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

Inference efficiency

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Figure 8: Accuracy against reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench. Tokens are measured on questions all five models answer correctly; accuracy is over all questions. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Figure 9: Pass rate against assistant turns per solved task on τ²-bench retail and telecom. Turns are measured on tasks all five models solve; pass rate is over all tasks. Top-left is better; the dashed line is the Pareto frontier.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):

  • τ²-retail: 10.7 turns, against 11.7 for the base (9% fewer) and 10.6 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think.
  • τ²-telecom: 13.1 turns, against 17.6 for the base (26% fewer) and 13.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think (5% fewer).

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

Intended Use and Limitations

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

Citation

@misc{botpsy2026,
  title  = {BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model},
  author = {{Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. d.b.a. Tether AI Research}},

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

Evaluation Footnotes

  • All scores are percentages (higher is better).
  • All models were evaluated in thinking (reasoning) mode.
  • All benchmarks that use an external API were run on November 3, 2026.
  • ¹ BFCL v4: overall score calculated using the official weighted formula (40% Agentic, 30% Multi-Turn, 10% Live, 10% Non-Live, and 10% Hallucination), averaged over 3 runs.
  • ² ACEBench: overall accuracy. All models were evaluated in function-calling (FC) mode; mean of 2 runs.
