item.description: Full title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

Enterprise Article

Published November 6, 2026

5

Kyle Wiggers

Ai2Comms

allenai

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

How ToyBlocks works

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

Research building on ToyBlocks

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models: VLA spatial generalization

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

High-level reasoning: vision-language models

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

High-level reasoning: agentic systems

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models as simulators

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Real-world experiments with high- and low-level models

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

Opening the tools for further research

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Introducing the New Auto and Auto Code Routers
item.content:encoded:
Introducing the New Auto and Auto Code Routers

Brian Thomas ·11/6/2026

Today we’re launching the next generation of Auto Router. Taking all we’ve learned from running Auto Router for the past 3 years, we rebuilt it from the ground up on an entirely new technical foundation that outperforms the old router by up to 4× depending on the benchmark, with a routing step that is 3× faster at the p90 in our live test (0.65s against 1.96s).

It’s easier for a router to score well on benchmarks than to perform well in practice. Auto Router sees over 2.5T tokens from over 100k people every month, so it has to hold up in the real world.

This launch includes a brand new router specialized for coding work, Auto Code (openrouter/auto-code), alongside our flagship general purpose Auto Router (openrouter/auto).

Try it now by setting model to openrouter/auto or openrouter/auto-code in any request, or open Auto Router in the chatroom. Check out the Auto Router docs for all the details.

What’s new in this generation

The previous Auto Router relied on a couple of imprecise signals, such as task type, to drive model selection, a limit required to keep latency low and judgments consistent. The new Auto Router and Auto Code choose models by weighing eleven factors about each request and combining them with live pricing, provider health, and cache status.

This new process lets Auto Router work with any set of models. You can apply any governance policies, including guardrails, zero data retention requirements, provider restrictions, allowed model lists, and BYOK keys. Auto Router makes efficient choices from the models available to you.

We introduced the new Auto Code router based on feedback about what it was like to use a general purpose router in a coding harness. This router is tuned from the ground up for coding performance by including a higher tier of coding models and optimizing for latency. Across the five benchmarks below, Auto Code scores in line with Claude Opus 5.5 while costing 74% less per task.

In the previous generation, we also observed that the remarkable efficiency of the lowest cost models had caused Auto router to drift lower on cost per task, leaving out many exceptional models. We made a decision with this release to return to pricing closer to where Auto was a few months ago in order to introduce a greater variety of models. If you preferred the previous behavior, you can set the cost_tier to low to get similar cost performance.

See the reasoning behind routing decisions in the chatroom

The easiest way to start learning how these new routers work is to pick Auto Router or Auto Code in the chatroom. A routing insights panel appears beside each reply showing why the router picked that model. The same analysis is available via the API when you enable router metadata.

Watch the live routing mix on each model page

The Auto Router and Auto Code model pages now show which models each router picks most often, split by session type, and how the mix shifts as difficulty rises.

Compare performance against other routers and single models

Auto Router and Auto Code benchmark results are published on the model routing benchmarks page alongside the other routers on OpenRouter and single-model baselines. We rerun them periodically, so you can track how each router keeps up as new models are released.

Built upon years of lessons from running Auto Router

Auto Router is coming up on its third birthday. If you set openrouter/auto in an agent years ago, you’re still getting the latest cost-optimal choice today. We’ve learned a lot about where automatic model selection goes wrong, and built the new generation to avoid those problems. Some examples:

We separated out Auto Code to optimize for harnesses. The most common complaint about previous versions of Auto Router was how it performed in coding harnesses. Auto Code favors a slightly more expensive tier of models whose strengths match coding work. It weighs speed more heavily because responsiveness matters while you build. It also penalizes failures more harshly, so it course corrects faster on work where success and failure are clear cut.

It’s restrained about switching to protect caching benefits. Switching models costs extra while the new model rebuilds the input token cache. Auto Router favors a change in reasoning effort when that’s enough, and switches only when the gain is worth the cache it gives up. In our beta period it stayed on the same model for nearly nine of every ten agent turns.

It adapts to failures. When a session is going wrong in ways that point at the model, such as the same error coming back or tests failing after an edit, those signals raise the odds of a switch. That makes it much less likely a session stays stuck with a model that was the wrong pick early on.

It’s tuned based on both real usage as well as benchmarks. Auto Router gets better with every benchmark run and every real routing decision it sees. Through typesafe/jev-router and openrouter/auto-beta we have already verified it on production workloads, while respecting zero data retention throughout. In our beta, against the previous router, invalid tool calls were 4× lower and agentic responses were cut off half as often.

Model Routing built upon the leading Provider Routing foundation

Model routers like Auto Router and Auto Code pick which model will process the request. Provider routing picks who will serve that model. OpenRouter has done this for every request since the beginning: once the model is picked, the provider router chooses among the providers hosting it using your provider preferences, live uptime and latency, price, and whether a provider already holds your prompt cache.

A model router can only be as good as the underlying provider router. We built Auto Router to be aware of our entire catalog, so it adapts to governance restrictions, benchmark results, and market signal from new model releases as they happen. Every one of the 600+ models on OpenRouter enters the consideration set the day it’s added, and benchmarks and popularity signals decide whether it earns a place in the cost-optimal set.

How a request moves through Auto Router

  • Auto Router narrows the model pool. Guardrails, zero data retention, model capabilities, provider restrictions, BYOK keys, and any allowed or excluded model lists decide which models are considered.
  • A fast decision model processes the request. In one call it rates eleven things, such as what kind of task this is, whether the task just changed, how hard it is, whether speed matters, whether it needs vision or knowledge of a codebase, and whether a bigger model, more thinking, or a cheaper model would serve it better.
  • The routing policy chooses the model. It weighs live prices, cache status, and benchmark performance to pick both the model and the reasoning effort.
  • The request goes through the same provider routing a direct request to that model would, so it lands on the best provider for that model.
  • The results of each turn inform the next turn’s model selection. The router carries signals like whether the model is struggling and what’s already cached into the next decision.

Routers versus single models

Benchmarks consistently show that no router on the market beats the single best frontier model at every point on the cost and quality curve. The new Auto Router is no exception, and we publish its benchmarks to show its strengths and weaknesses plainly.

Routers earn their place when the work is varied, when an organization needs to hold costs steady, and for people who don’t have the time or interest to keep up with the constant stream of model releases. Choosing Auto Router or Auto Code over a single model trades a little peak performance for consistent, cost efficient performance over time.

If you know the model that works best for your specific work, keep using it. If you’d rather choose once and stay focused on the work itself, a router is the way to do that.

Get started

Auto Router and Auto Code work wherever you’d put a model string:

curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "openrouter/auto-code",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Add a retry with backoff to fetchUser in api/users.ts"}]
  }'

Read the Auto Router docs for the full settings, or open Auto Router in the chatroom and send it the prompt you’d normally hand-pick a model for. Tell us what it gets right and wrong in #feedback on Discord.

Frequently asked questions

What do I need to change to switch from the old Auto Router?

Nothing at all. The slug is still openrouter/auto and the auto-router plugin settings cost_tier, allowed_models, and excluded_models still work.

What is the difference between Auto Router and Auto Code?

Both run on the same routing engine. Auto Router is the general purpose router for mixed traffic and general agents, and favors a cost-efficient tier of models. Auto Code is specialized for coding agents and harnesses, starts in a higher cost tier, and weighs measured pass rate, speed, and cost per solved task across models and reasoning efforts.

Is model routing the same as provider routing?

No. Model routing picks which model handles a request; provider routing picks which provider serves that model. Auto Router and Auto Code do the first, then OpenRouter’s provider routing does the second with your provider preferences, uptime data, and prompt cache state.

Do the routers respect my guardrails and data policies?

Yes. Guardrail policies, zero data retention requirements, provider restrictions, allowed and excluded model lists, and BYOK keys define the model pool, and the router picks the cost optimal model inside it.

Does a router cost extra?

No. You pay the standard price of whichever model serves the request, and the response’s model field tells you which one it was.

What is openrouter/auto-beta?

Auto Router Beta is the release channel for the next version of Auto Router. New routing changes ship to openrouter/auto-beta first and graduate to openrouter/auto once they prove out, so use it to see what is coming in advance. If you try it, tell us what it gets right and wrong in #feedback on Discord.

item.title: [Mistral AI] Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.
item.content:encoded:
Studio

Le Chonk brings the brains. Studio puts it to work.

7 min read

Copy url to clipboardCopied

Thinking

Summary

Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) enhances enterprise AI with advanced coding, cybersecurity, and document reasoning, while Mistral Studio provides a flexible platform for deploying agents, workflows, and apps across cloud, VPC, or on-premises environments. New features like managed agents, workflows, and enterprise context streamline business processes, enabling faster development and deployment of AI solutions. Customers like ABANCA and BNP Paribas already use Studio to automate tasks, improve efficiency, and maintain full control over their AI systems.

Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) pushes the frontier of what enterprises can build with open models. It does great for coding, delivers advanced defensive cybersecurity capabilities, and brings powerful reasoning to complex documents and business tasks.

Mistral Studio is our enterprise AI platform for putting that intelligence to work in your business. It lets your teams activate models quickly through agents, workflows and apps connected to your enterprise data and systems. Deploy them wherever you choose: in the cloud, in your own VPC, on-premises or across a combination of environments. And retain full control and understanding of the intelligence you create, from how your systems work to the knowledge they build.

Today, we’re expanding Studio with managed agents and apps, alongside new capabilities for workflows, enterprise context, agent observability and evaluations.

Customers and partners including ABANCA, Accenture, Alten, BNP Paribas, Capgemini, CMA CGM and Tata Consultancy Services already use Studio in production. With this release, your developers can build and deploy new use cases faster, then reuse that work across more of the business.

Mistral Studio is our platform for building enterprise AI applications. Running it in our own cloud environment, with inference provided by Mistral, allows us to bring AI into the business while retaining control over our infrastructure and how sensitive customer data is accessed and used.

Jose Jorge Garcia Romaris, Head of Data Engineering & AI

Our clients are looking beyond isolated AI use cases to reinvent how work gets done across the enterprise. Mistral Studio gives us the foundation to build, orchestrate and scale AI solutions tailored to their business needs, while securing control over their data and deployment. Combined with our industry expertise and delivery capabilities, it allows us to turn technology into real business impact at scale.

Gregory Christophe, Accenture x Mistral Business Group

Most industrial AI projects still stall at the pilot stage. We'll build agents and workflows for our clients' engineering and R&D teams on Mistral Studio to take their pilots into production. We're training our developers on the platform.

Gualtiero Bazzana, ExCom Member and CAIO

The AI systems we build run some of our most sensitive processes, so we run Mistral Studio on our own infrastructure and keep those systems under our control.

Su YANG - Head of Artificial Intelligence & IT Innovation, BNP Paribas

AI creates lasting value only when enterprises can trust it within their operations. Mistral Studio aims to let us decide exactly which systems the agents can access, and brings the observability and evaluation needed to turn a promising PoC into a system they can operate, measure, and rely on. That’s one of the gaps our clients are looking to close leveraging Mistral.

Fernando Alvarez, Capgemini Group Chief Strategy & Development Officer, Group Executive Board Member

We've built AI systems with Mistral's engineers for some of our most critical processes, from cargo release and customer assistance in shipping to transport orders in logistics. They run on Mistral Studio, where each new process we automate is production-ready in weeks rather than months. With the new version of Studio, our own teams and partners will do more of the building themselves, so we can take more of our processes to production and keep the know-how in-house.

Julien Smadja, VP AI

The future of enterprise AI will be defined by an ecosystem that balances innovation with trust, giving organizations the flexibility to adopt the right AI technologies while maintaining control. Through our partnership with Mistral, TCS is helping enterprises harness advanced AI capabilities while maintaining sovereignty, governance, security, and deployment flexibility. As one of the first global systems integrators investing in the Mistral ecosystem, we are enabling clients to build, deploy, govern, and scale AI with confidence. Together, we are accelerating the adoption of trusted AI and helping enterprises convert AI ambition into business outcomes.

Amit Kapur, Chief AI & Services Transformation Officer

Agents, workflows and apps for your business processes

Agents, workflows and apps serve different parts of a business process. An agent investigates and acts, a workflow coordinates execution and approvals, and an app gives employees a way to use these systems.

Studio brings all three together on shared infrastructure. You start with a model like Le Chonk and connect it to your enterprise data and systems through connectors and MCP servers. That foundation lets you easily build agents, workflows and apps with access to the context they need. Studio manages how they run and lets teams inspect what happened.

Through the new Mistral MCP server, developers can build with Mistral Vibe or the coding agent they already use, test locally and deploy to their Studio environment with one command. Studio handles hosting and execution, so teams can build on that foundation to get each new use case into production faster.

Build managed agents that investigate and act

In Studio, developers can now build agents that carry out complex, multi-step tasks. Developers can equip them with skills that capture the team’s procedures, sandboxes where they can run code, and subagents to delegate parts of a task. Hooks let developers add custom logic at key points in execution, shaping how the agent works and integrates with existing systems.

Studio manages the runtime behind all that work, using the proven infrastructure that supports millions of Mistral Vibe sessions each week. Developers can focus on the agent’s capabilities and behaviour, while setting boundaries on the tools, data and actions it can access. That means getting capable agents into production faster, with less infrastructure to build and more control over how your agents operate.

Our engineering team built an agent in Studio to investigate production incidents. When an alert fires, engineers need to work out what happened, often under pressure to resolve the issue. The agent starts the investigation: it follows the team’s runbook, asks for approval before taking sensitive actions and posts its findings in Slack. Engineers pick up the investigation with useful context already gathered, saving the team hundreds of hours each month.

Automate processes with workflows

Workflows define how a process runs: which steps follow fixed rules, where an agent reasons and when a person decides. Interrupted runs can resume where they left off. Teams can describe a process in Mistral Vibe and use it to generate, test and deploy a workflow, with code they can inspect and edit. Today’s release also adds event triggers from enterprise systems and a visual graph that makes each workflow’s logic easier to inspect.

Our product operations team built a workflow in Studio to sort ideas from internal teams and feedback from customers. Routing each submission to the right people is one of the team’s routine tasks, but one that takes time. A model identifies bugs and feature requests, then routing rules send them to the appropriate team. This saves the product operations team about 35 hours a week.

Build apps ready for enterprise use

Coding agents make it easy to build an application, but putting it to work across an enterprise means meeting requirements for security, access and reliability. Studio provides hosting, authentication and access controls, helping developers get applications ready for enterprise use faster. Teams can build with pre-approved, reusable components, reducing the amount of new code that needs security review.

These applications can use agents and workflows, retrieve enterprise documents through search indexes and access shared context in Studio. Developers can test locally, then deploy with one command to make the application available at its own link or inside Mistral Vibe.

Our Applied AI team, which helps customers build AI solutions, built a staffing app in Studio. Previously, staffing a project meant manually matching team profiles and past experience against requirements spread across documents and tools.

The app uses an agent to recommend people and explain how their experience fits the project. Staffing leads get a shortlist with supporting evidence ready to review, helping Mistral assemble teams faster and uncover expertise that might otherwise be overlooked when staffing complex customer AI projects.

Each use case leaves the enterprise better equipped to build the next. More engineering effort goes into improving operations, with less time spent rebuilding the infrastructure around them.

Keep your AI sovereign

Studio gives you control over where your AI runs, how it operates and the intelligence you build. Deploy both the models and the platform in your own cloud, VPC or on-premises environment. You can also use Mistral-hosted deployments or combine environments to meet your requirements. Sensitive data and the processes built around it can stay within your perimeter.

You choose the models, govern access to data and tools, and decide which actions require human approval. OpenTelemetry traces show each step of a run, including model calls, tool use and approvals, so your teams can see where a process slows down or fails. Evaluations let them test changes to prompts, models or tools against your own datasets before release. Those traces and evaluations remain theirs, preserving the operational knowledge they build through use.

Customers are already putting this into practice with systems built alongside our Solutions team. From penetration testing to KYC onboarding, they’re bringing AI into critical operations while keeping sensitive data and specialist knowledge under their control.

Get started

Choose a process your team wants to improve and put Le Chonk to work in Studio.

  • Build an agent: Managed Agents documentation· Incident investigation cookbook
  • Automate a process: Workflows documentation · Workflow cookbooks
  • Create an app: Apps documentation · Document review cookbook

Explore interactive demos and enterprise use cases, or read the release notes for the full list of updates.

For an enterprise rollout or a business-critical implementation, talk to our team about what you want to automate and where it needs to run.

item.title: [Hugging Face] A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Devic…
item.description: Full title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Published November 5, 2026

Update on GitHub

20

Olesia Krizhevich

olesiagradium

gradium

Laurent Mazare

lmz

gradium

Eric Bezzam

bezzam

Eustache Le Bihan

eustlb

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Why a voice should live on your device

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

What we released

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

Demos and first projects

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

Inference

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration

model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")

print(f"{model.num_parameters():,}")  # 30,788,354
print(f"{processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,}")  # 10,305,313

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file

path = hf_hub_download("gradium/phonon-voices", "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors")
voice = load_file(path)["speaker_wavs"][0].T  # (num_frames, 512)

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

conversation = [
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "Hello from Phonon."}]}
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    processor_kwargs={"audio_prompt_latents": [voice]},
).to(model.device)
# prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|>

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

outputs = model.generate(**inputs)  # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32)
audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask)
processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav")

See the docs 🤗 for more!

What's next

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

item.title: [Hugging Face] New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simula…
item.description: Full title: New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

Enterprise + Article

Published November 5, 2026

10

Pranjali Joshi

PranjaliJoshi

nvidia

Rick Z

rickznv

nvidia

Yao Xu

yaoxuhf

nvidia

Qianli Ma

qianlim

nvidia

Chen-Hsuan Lin

chenhsuanlin

nvidia

Ming-Yu Liu

mingyuliutw

nvidia

Xiang Li

ryanxli

nvidia

Zhengfei Kuang

zhengfei-nvidia

nvidia

Zhonghao Wang

zhonghaow

nvidia

Jiaxiang Tang

ashawkey

nvidia

TL;DR

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

  • 🌦️ Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto : Generate multi-view driving data with varied weather, lighting, and time of day.
  • 🚗 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto : Stream synchronized camera and LiDAR observations for driving simulation.
  • 🎨 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer : Turn simulator controls and a text prompt into photorealistic video.
  • 🤖 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual : Predict video from robot or camera actions.

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

Why do you need these checkpoints?

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Build Autonomous Vehicle Worlds with Cosmos3-Nano

🌦️Transfer-Auto: driving scenarios → multi-sensor data

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Prefer a notebook? Open Transfer-Auto.

🚗Sim-Auto: driving controls → streaming observations

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Prefer a notebook? Open Sim-Auto.

🎨 Sim-Transfer: simulator controls → RGB

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

  • Depth: relative distance from the camera.
  • Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.
  • Edges: scene contours.
  • Blur: coarse appearance and layout.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Depth control to video

Segmentation control to video

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Prefer a notebook? Use Transfer.

🤖 Sim-Bimanual: actions → video

Input Frames

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

See the data contract and action schema.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Prefer a notebook? Open Bimanual

How streaming generation works

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

The four-stage training recipe

  • Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.
  • Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.
  • Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.
  • Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

🛠️ Adapt with your data

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

  • Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.
  • Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.
  • Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.
  • Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Best MiMo-V2.6-Pro API Providers in 2026
item.content:encoded:
Best MiMo-V2.6-Pro API Providers in 2026

Published on 2026.11.05 by DeepInfra

As large language models continue to push the boundaries of context length and multimodal capabilities, Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro has emerged as a strong entrant among open-weight models. With its native omnimodal architecture — supporting text, image, video, and audio — and a 1,048,576-token context window, it opens up new paradigms for agentic workflows, long-document analysis, and complex reasoning tasks. Deploying and scaling a model of this magnitude, however, introduces real infrastructure challenges. Managing GPU memory requirements, optimizing inference latency, and controlling API costs are critical pain points for developers and enterprise architects alike.

This article surveys the SaaS tools, API providers, and infrastructure platforms available for MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Whether you need dedicated autoscaling endpoints, privacy-first routing, or cost-effective API access, this guide is meant to help identify the right environment for production workloads.

Summary of the Best MiMo-V2.6-Pro Providers

For a quick recommendation based on specific architectural needs, the table below summarizes the options covered in this guide:

ProviderBest For
DeepInfraDevelopers and enterprises seeking reliable, optimized, well-rounded API access.
XiaomiOrganizations wanting to self-host the open weights or use the official direct API.
BazaarLinkTaiwan-based enterprises needing localized billing and OpenAI-compatible API access.
EmpirioLabs AIDevelopers building agentic workflows that require live web search and structured JSON outputs.
LLM APIDevelopers building autonomous AI agents that need to manage their own API credits — see note below.
FlexAIEnterprise teams requiring dedicated, high-throughput compute and autoscaling infrastructure.
CometAPIBusinesses wanting a single API key for failover routing across hundreds of models.
MofCloudGlobal cloud teams needing regional token plans and FinOps tools — see note below.
TrustedRouterPrivacy-conscious users needing verifiable zero-logging policies and performance-based routing.

Two entries in this list — MofCloud and LLM API — could not be independently confirmed when this guide was fact-checked, and are flagged with notes in their own sections below. The other seven providers were individually verified.

DeepInfra

DeepInfra is a strong overall option for accessing and deploying MiMo-V2.6-Pro alongside other top-tier AI models. For developers and enterprises seeking a balance of performance and cost-effectiveness, DeepInfra provides an optimized inference engine that abstracts away the complexity of managing underlying GPU hardware.

Key Features

  • Strong overall solution for MiMo-V2.6-Pro
  • High-performance infrastructure
  • Cost-effective API access

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

When dealing with a model capable of processing over a million tokens, inference speed and cost predictability are paramount. DeepInfra differentiates itself with a reliable API that handles large context loads without compromising on latency, which makes it a solid choice for teams that want production-ready access to MiMo-V2.6-Pro without the overhead of managing their own clusters. Current rates are on the DeepInfra pricing page, and the quickstart guide has you making calls in minutes.

Explore MiMo-V2.6-Pro on DeepInfra.

Xiaomi

As the creator and official publisher of the MiMo-V2.6-Pro model, Xiaomi provides the foundational architecture that powers this ecosystem. By releasing the model weights under an open MIT license, Xiaomi has enabled the broader developer community to build on it freely.

Key Features

  • Official publisher of the MiMo-V2.6-Pro model
  • Provides open weights under an MIT license
  • Native omnimodal capabilities (text, image, video, audio)
  • 1,048,576-token context window

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

Xiaomi’s primary differentiator is its position as the source. For organizations with strict data governance requirements, or those with the internal MLOps expertise to manage large-scale GPU clusters, downloading the MIT-licensed weights directly from Xiaomi allows for complete control. Xiaomi also offers an official MiMo Open Platform API for direct access.

BazaarLink

BazaarLink is an OpenAI-compatible API provider that brings specialized billing and localized features to the Asian market, specifically tailored for Taiwan. It supports MiMo-V2.6-Pro’s full 1M-token context window and omnimodal inputs.

Key Features

  • $0.435 input and $0.87 output per 1M tokens
  • Cache read pricing at $0.0036 per 1M tokens
  • Supports text, image, video, and audio inputs
  • TWD billing and Taiwan uniform invoices available

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

BazaarLink is positioned for cost-efficiency in repetitive tasks through its cache read pricing, which is attractive for MiMo-V2.6-Pro users who frequently query the same large documents or system prompts. Its localized TWD billing and uniform invoices also make it a low-friction choice for Taiwan-based enterprises.

EmpirioLabs AI

EmpirioLabs AI focuses on supporting the MiMo V2.6 series for complex, long-horizon tasks. It provides an API platform that natively integrates external tooling, which suits developers building more sophisticated AI agents.

Key Features

  • Native web search integration included
  • Reasoning enabled by default
  • Function calling and structured JSON output up to 131,072 tokens
  • OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

While MiMo-V2.6-Pro has a 1M-token context window, extracting structured data reliably from massive contexts can be challenging. EmpirioLabs AI differentiates itself by guaranteeing function calling and structured JSON outputs for contexts up to 131,072 tokens. Combined with built-in web search and default reasoning, it is a solid fit for agentic workflows that need live data retrieval and strict output formatting.

LLM API

Verification note: a provider named “LLM Gateway” was independently confirmed to serve this model. A distinctly named “LLM API” with the specific “agent storefront for autonomous purchasing” feature described below could not be independently confirmed, and may be a conflation of the two. Confirm this listing directly before publishing.

LLM API is described as an infrastructure provider tailored for the machine-to-machine economy, offering MiMo-V2.6-Pro access designed for autonomous AI agents that manage their own resources.

Key Features

  • $0.435 input and $0.87 output per 1M tokens
  • Described as including a dedicated agent storefront for autonomous purchasing (unverified)
  • OpenAI-compatible client integration
  • Live prices and self-serve payment options

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

For teams building autonomous agents, the described appeal is a dedicated agent storefront that would let agents autonomously purchase API credits and manage their own usage via self-serve payment methods. At a competitive per-token rate, it could be worth evaluating — but confirm the storefront capability directly, since it wasn’t independently verifiable for this guide.

FlexAI

FlexAI targets the enterprise sector by offering MiMo V2.6 Pro RL as a dedicated, autoscaling endpoint. Instead of shared, rate-limited API access, FlexAI provisions dedicated hardware for specific workloads.

Key Features

  • Dedicated endpoint provisioned per customer
  • Runs on 16x H100 GPUs
  • Billed per minute at $33.60 per hour
  • Autoscales with traffic volume

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

Running a 1M-context omnimodal model requires serious compute. FlexAI provisions 16x H100 GPUs per customer, providing the dedicated VRAM and throughput needed for high-volume, low-latency production environments. The per-minute billing ($33.60/hour) and autoscaling make it well suited to enterprise teams with variable, high-throughput traffic spikes.

CometAPI

CometAPI is a unified API aggregator that simplifies model routing and failover. It provides access to MiMo V2.6 Pro alongside a large catalog of other AI models through a single integration point.

Key Features

  • Unified API for 500+ models
  • Discounts available below list price
  • Unified billing and failover routing
  • Supports the full 1M-token context window

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

For production systems where uptime is critical, CometAPI’s built-in failover routing is designed to redirect MiMo-V2.6-Pro requests automatically if one upstream provider experiences downtime. Access to the full 1M-token context window alongside unified billing across hundreds of models — compare the full DeepInfra model catalog for a sense of scale — makes it a useful option for complex AI stacks.

MofCloud

Verification note: this provider could not be independently confirmed when this guide was fact-checked — no independent sources turned up for MofCloud. Confirm it exists and that the figures below are current before publishing this section.

MofCloud is described as a global cloud infrastructure provider that pairs MiMo-V2.6-Pro access with enterprise-grade FinOps and cloud cost management tooling.

Key Features (as described)

  • $0.45 input and $0.89 output per 1M tokens
  • Zero cost for cache tokens
  • Regional token plans for China, Europe, and Singapore
  • FinOps and AI cost management tools

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

MofCloud’s stated differentiator is a zero-cost cache token policy, which would reduce the cost of large-context, repetitive queries, along with regional token plans and integrated FinOps tooling aimed at global teams. None of this was independently verifiable for this guide, so treat it as unconfirmed until checked directly.

TrustedRouter

TrustedRouter is an attested API gateway designed for organizations with strict data privacy and security requirements. It acts as a secure intermediary, routing requests to upstream MiMo-V2.6-Pro providers such as Lightning AI.

Key Features

  • Zero prompt or output logs policy
  • Routes to upstream providers like Lightning AI
  • Measures uptime and speed via routed probes
  • Verifies gateway attestation for security

Differentiators for MiMo-V2.6-Pro

When sending highly sensitive, million-token documents to an LLM, data leakage is a real concern. TrustedRouter’s zero prompt/output logs policy, backed by gateway attestation, combined with ongoing uptime and speed measurement via routed probes, is built to let privacy-conscious users avoid trading performance for security.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Deploying Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro requires weighing an application’s specific needs — whether that means managing massive context windows, handling omnimodal inputs, or controlling inference costs.

  • For enterprise and high-throughput needs: teams needing guaranteed compute and autoscaling should look to FlexAI for dedicated 16x H100 deployments.
  • For agentic workflows: developers building autonomous systems should consider EmpirioLabs AI for structured JSON and web search capabilities, or LLM API if agents require autonomous purchasing power (pending confirmation of that capability — see note above).
  • For privacy and security: TrustedRouter is a strong choice for organizations requiring verifiable zero-logging and attested routing.
  • For global and regional operations: MofCloud is described as offering FinOps tools for global teams (unconfirmed — see note above), while BazaarLink is a solid option for Taiwan-based localized billing.

The Best Overall Solution

The right fit depends on specific architectural needs, but for the majority of developers and enterprises, DeepInfra remains a strong overall solution. It offers reliable, high-performance, cost-effective API access for MiMo-V2.6-Pro, letting teams focus on building applications rather than managing complex infrastructure. For a closer look at pricing across recent releases, see our Kimi K3 vs. Claude Opus 4.8 vs. GPT-5.6 Sol comparison.
